stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with GuardDuty managed by a delegated administrator in its security-tooling account, and every existing account is already a member with the detector enabled. During a coverage review, the delegated administrator notices that S3 Protection is disabled in several member accounts because account teams changed the setting, and that accounts recently created through Account Factory join the organization without S3 Protection turned on. The security team requires S3 Protection to be enabled uniformly across all current and future member accounts, and the team wants the solution that requires the LEAST recurring operational effort. What should the security engineer do?

options.text: Deploy a scheduled AWS Lambda function in the delegated administrator account that calls the UpdateMemberDetectors API every week to detect drift and re-enable S3 Protection in any member account where an account team has turned it off.

In the delegated administrator account, set the S3 Protection auto-enable configuration to ALL so that the protection plan is enabled for every existing member account and is applied automatically to accounts that join later.

Attach a service control policy to the organization root that denies the guardduty:UpdateDetector and guardduty:UpdateMemberDetectors actions so that member account teams can no longer change any GuardDuty protection plan settings in their accounts.

Publish a runbook that instructs each account team to enable S3 Protection in its own account, and add a verification step to the Account Factory provisioning checklist so newly created accounts enable the feature.

explanation: B is correct. The auto-enable setting for a GuardDuty protection plan supports an ALL mode that turns the plan on for all existing member accounts and applies it automatically to every account that later joins the organization, which fixes the current drift and covers future accounts with no recurring work. A is wrong because a scheduled remediation function is custom code that must be maintained and leaves windows of up to a week during which drifted accounts are unprotected. C is wrong because a service control policy only prevents future changes; it does not re-enable S3 Protection where it is already disabled and does not enable it for new accounts. D is wrong because manual runbooks and provisioning checklists are exactly the recurring operational effort the team wants to avoid and depend on account teams complying.

stem: A security engineer in a company's security operations center is triaging a GuardDuty finding of type UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS that references the IAM role attached to a production Amazon EC2 instance. The instance runs a public-facing web application behind an Application Load Balancer, and the application recently added a feature that fetches user-supplied URLs on the server side. The finding's severity is High, and it names the role session that belongs to the instance's profile. Before escalating the finding to the incident response team, the engineer must state precisely what condition GuardDuty has observed so that responders scope the investigation correctly. What does this finding indicate?

options.text: The instance has fallen back from IMDSv2 to IMDSv1, which exposes the role's credentials to server-side request forgery attacks against the instance metadata service on the affected instance.
The temporary credentials that were issued to the instance's role were used to call AWS APIs by an Amazon EC2 instance that belongs to a different AWS account but remained inside the AWS network.
The role attached to the instance repeatedly attempted API actions that were blocked by a service control policy, which suggests that an automated process is probing the permissions of the role.

The temporary credentials issued through the instance's instance profile were used to call AWS APIs from an IP address outside AWS, which indicates the credentials were likely stolen from the instance.

explanation: D is correct. The InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS variant fires when credentials created exclusively for an EC2 instance through its instance profile are used from an IP address outside AWS, a strong indicator that the credentials were exfiltrated, for example through the server-side request forgery exposure that the new URL-fetching feature creates. A is wrong because GuardDuty does not generate this finding for metadata service version changes; IMDS configuration is a preventive posture concern, not what this finding reports. B is wrong because use of the credentials from an EC2 instance in another AWS account produces the InsideAWS variant of the finding, not the OutsideAWS variant. C is wrong because API attempts denied by a service control policy appear in CloudTrail as access-denied errors and do not produce this finding type, which is about where the credentials were used from.

stem: A company runs containerized microservices on an Amazon EKS cluster that uses managed node groups. GuardDuty foundational threat detection is enabled across the organization and already analyzes VPC flow logs, DNS query logs, and CloudTrail events. After a red-team exercise, the security team learns that a simulated attacker started a reverse shell inside a running container and executed a cryptocurrency-mining binary, and that no finding was generated for either action. The team must detect this kind of operating-system-level activity inside the containers, and it wants the option that requires the LEAST deployment and maintenance effort from the platform team. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring for EKS and use the GuardDuty-managed security agent so that the agent is deployed and kept up to date automatically on the cluster's nodes.
Enable GuardDuty EKS Audit Log Monitoring so that GuardDuty analyzes the Kubernetes control-plane audit logs from the cluster and raises findings for suspicious cluster activity.
Enable Amazon Inspector container image scanning for the Amazon ECR repositories that hold the cluster's images so that vulnerable packages in the images are reported continuously.

Send the EKS control-plane audit logs to CloudWatch Logs and create metric filters and alarms that match any interactive exec commands that users or automation issue against the running pods in the cluster.

explanation: A is correct. Runtime Monitoring instruments the operating system of the cluster's nodes with an eBPF-based security agent, detecting process-level events such as reverse shells and known cryptocurrency-mining binaries, and the GuardDuty-managed agent option handles deployment and updates without platform-team effort. B is wrong because EKS Audit Log Monitoring analyzes only Kubernetes API-server audit events, so activity that happens entirely inside a container's operating system never appears in that log source. C is wrong because Inspector reports vulnerable software in stored images; it does not observe running workloads and cannot detect an active reverse shell or miner. D is wrong because metric filters on audit logs see only Kubernetes API operations such as exec requests, they miss shells spawned by exploited application processes, and the filter patterns require ongoing maintenance.

stem: A media company operates a portal where external partners upload documents to an Amazon S3 ingest bucket. An AWS Lambda function processes each uploaded object and copies results into an internal bucket that many downstream teams read. The security team must ensure that every newly uploaded object is examined for malware before the Lambda function processes it, and that objects in which malware is found are never processed. The company requires a fully managed capability and will not operate or patch its own scanning software or signature databases. The pipeline must continue to run automatically without a person approving each object. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable GuardDuty S3 Protection for the account so that GuardDuty monitors data-plane activity on the ingest bucket and raises findings about suspicious object uploads before processing begins.
Run a scheduled Amazon Macie discovery job against the ingest bucket every hour and configure the Lambda function to skip any object that appears in the job's findings.

Enable GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 on the ingest bucket with object tagging enabled, and change the pipeline so that the Malware Protection scan-result event invokes the Lambda function, which processes only objects whose scan-status tag shows that no threats were found.

Deploy an open-source antivirus engine in a container fleet behind an Amazon SQS queue, scan each object as it is uploaded, and refresh the engine's signature database through a nightly maintenance job that the operations team owns.

explanation: C is correct. Malware Protection for S3 scans each newly uploaded object in a protected bucket, and with tagging enabled it applies a GuardDutyMalwareScanStatus tag that the pipeline can require to equal NO_THREATS_FOUND before the Lambda function processes the object, keeping infected files out of the workflow with no scanning infrastructure to run. A is wrong because S3 Protection detects anomalous access patterns from S3 data-plane events; it does not inspect object content for malware. B is wrong because Macie identifies sensitive data such as personal information, it is not a malware scanner, and an hourly job cannot gate each upload. D is wrong because a self-hosted antivirus fleet with nightly signature maintenance is exactly the self-operated scanning software that the company has ruled out.

stem: A company stores regulated documents in several hundred Amazon S3 buckets. The security team wants to detect anomalous data-plane activity, such as an unusually high volume of GetObject calls from an unfamiliar network, or API patterns that resemble data exfiltration from the buckets. The company's CloudTrail configuration records management events only; a proposal to enable data events for every bucket was rejected last quarter because of the projected logging cost. GuardDuty foundational threat detection is already enabled in every account. The team wants the detection capability that adds the LEAST additional cost and ongoing configuration effort. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable CloudTrail data events for all of the buckets, deliver them to CloudWatch Logs, and create metric filters and alarms that fire on high GetObject volumes from any single source.
Enable S3 server access logging on each bucket, deliver the access logs to a central bucket, and schedule Athena queries that look for unusual request volumes against the documents.
Enable GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 on the buckets so that GuardDuty examines activity on the objects and raises findings when access patterns become anomalous.
Enable S3 Protection in GuardDuty, which analyzes S3 data-plane events through an independent stream without requiring the company to enable or pay for CloudTrail data events.

explanation: D is correct. S3 Protection extends GuardDuty to monitor S3 data-plane operations, producing anomaly findings such as unusual GetObject volume and exfiltration-style access, and GuardDuty consumes this telemetry through an independent event stream, so the company does not have to enable data events on its trails or pay CloudTrail delivery costs. A is wrong because it requires exactly the bucket-wide data-event logging that was rejected for cost, plus hand-built thresholds that miss novel anomalies. B is wrong because server access logs are delivered on a best-effort basis with delay, and scheduled queries with static thresholds provide slow, coarse detection with real operational effort. C is wrong because Malware Protection for S3 scans newly uploaded objects for malicious content; it does not analyze access patterns for anomalies.

stem: A security team runs an authorized vulnerability-scanning appliance from a shared-services VPC. Every night the scanner probes EC2 instances across the company's accounts, and GuardDuty generates dozens of Recon:EC2/PortProbeUnprotectedPort findings that reference the scanner as the remote source. An EventBridge rule forwards all new GuardDuty findings to an alerting service, so the nightly scans repeatedly page the on-call engineer during every scanning window. Company audit policy requires that GuardDuty continue to generate and retain these findings so that reviewers can confirm the scanner's activity later. The team must stop the nightly pages with the LEAST operational overhead. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a GuardDuty suppression rule in the administrator account that matches the finding type and the scanner's source so matching findings are archived automatically on arrival and no longer flow to EventBridge.

Add the scanner appliance's IP address to a GuardDuty trusted IP list in the administrator account so that GuardDuty stops treating network traffic from the scanner as suspicious activity in any of the member accounts.
Insert an AWS Lambda function between the EventBridge rule and the alerting service that inspects each finding and drops the findings whose recorded source matches the scanner appliance.
Disable the Recon:EC2/PortProbeUnprotectedPort finding type on the GuardDuty detector in each affected account so that the nightly probes from the scanner stop producing findings.

explanation: A is correct. A suppression rule automatically archives new findings that match its filter criteria, so the findings are still generated and remain reviewable in GuardDuty for auditors, but archived findings are not delivered to EventBridge and therefore stop paging the on-call engineer. B is wrong because trusted IP lists stop GuardDuty from generating findings for traffic involving those addresses at all, which violates the requirement to keep generating and retaining the findings. C is wrong because a filtering function is custom code that must be deployed and maintained when a native rule meets the requirement. D is wrong because GuardDuty does not support disabling individual finding types on a detector, and stopping generation would violate the audit requirement anyway.

stem: A company uses AWS Organizations and has designated a delegated administrator account for AWS Security Hub CSPM (formerly Security Hub). An internal audit finds that several member accounts have disabled the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark standard, that other accounts never enabled Security Hub CSPM in two Regions the company recently expanded into, and that control parameters differ between accounts. The security team must enforce one consistent configuration, with Security Hub CSPM enabled and a defined set of standards and controls, across every account and every company Region. Member account teams must not be able to change the configuration, and the team must manage everything from one place. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy an AWS Config organization conformance pack that evaluates whether Security Hub CSPM and the required standards are enabled in each member account and reports any account that is noncompliant.

Use CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions to enable Security Hub CSPM and the required standards in every account and Region, and redeploy the stack set whenever configuration drift is detected in any member account.

Enable central configuration from the delegated administrator's home Region, create a configuration policy that enables Security Hub CSPM with the required standards and controls, and associate the policy with the organization root.

Attach a service control policy to the organization root that denies the securityhub:BatchDisableStandards and securityhub:DisableSecurityHub actions so that member account teams cannot turn the required configuration off.

explanation: C is correct. Security Hub CSPM central configuration lets the delegated administrator define configuration policies that specify whether Security Hub CSPM is enabled and which standards and controls apply, and associating a policy with the organization root enforces it across all member accounts and all linked Regions; centrally managed accounts cannot override the policy locally. A is wrong because a conformance pack only detects that accounts are noncompliant; it neither enables Security Hub CSPM nor prevents members from disabling standards. B is wrong because stack sets can enable the service, but member administrators can still change standards afterward, leaving drift to be discovered and redeployed repeatedly. D is wrong because a service control policy can block disable actions but cannot enable Security Hub CSPM in the unconfigured Regions or align the control parameters that already differ.

stem: A company's security operations center monitors workloads that run in six AWS Regions. AWS Security Hub CSPM (formerly Security Hub) is enabled in every account and Region through the organization's delegated administrator. Analysts complain that investigating an issue requires switching the console between Regions, and the team's ticketing integration must call the Security Hub CSPM API separately in each Region to collect findings. The team wants analysts and the integration to be able to see and search all findings and insights from every Region at a single endpoint, and it wants Regions the company adopts in the future to be included without additional work. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure Security Hub CSPM in each Region to export findings to a central Amazon S3 bucket and build Athena queries and QuickSight dashboards over the exported findings data.
Designate one Region as the Security Hub CSPM aggregation Region, link the other five Regions to it, and enable automatic linking so that future Regions are included when they are enabled.
Create EventBridge rules in each Region that forward Security Hub CSPM findings to a custom event bus in one Region and store the findings in DynamoDB for the integration to query.

Rely on the delegated administrator account, because designating a delegated administrator automatically consolidates the findings of every member account and every Region into that account's home Region.

explanation: B is correct. Cross-Region aggregation continuously replicates findings, insights, and their updates from linked Regions into the designated aggregation Region, so analysts and API integrations work against one Region, and the automatic-linking option includes newly enabled Regions with no further configuration. A is wrong because an export-and-query pipeline must be built and maintained, adds delay, and does not give analysts a live console view or a single Security Hub CSPM API endpoint. C is wrong because per-Region forwarding rules and a custom DynamoDB store duplicate what aggregation provides natively and add undifferentiated maintenance. D is wrong because a delegated administrator consolidates findings across accounts, not Regions; without aggregation, each Region still holds only its own findings.

stem: A company aggregates AWS Security Hub CSPM (formerly Security Hub) findings from every organization account into a delegated administrator account. Accounts in a sandbox organizational unit run short-lived experiments, and their resources are tagged Environment=sandbox. These resources generate a stream of findings for a control that the security team has decided is acceptable in sandboxes, and the noise pushes production findings down the analysts' queue. The team wants findings whose resources carry the sandbox tag to be set automatically to severity INFORMATIONAL with workflow status SUPPRESSED as they arrive, while the findings remain recorded for later reference. Production findings must be untouched, and the team will not write or operate custom code. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an EventBridge rule that matches Security Hub CSPM findings with the sandbox resource tag and invokes an AWS Lambda function that calls BatchUpdateFindings to lower the severity and suppress each matching finding.

Use Security Hub CSPM central configuration to disable the control in every account that belongs to the sandbox organizational unit so that the noisy findings are no longer generated in those accounts.

Create a GuardDuty suppression rule in the delegated administrator account that matches the Environment=sandbox resource tag so that the matching findings are archived automatically at the moment they are generated.

Create a Security Hub CSPM automation rule in the delegated administrator account whose criteria match the Environment=sandbox resource tag and whose actions set the severity to INFORMATIONAL and the workflow status to SUPPRESSED.

explanation: D is correct. Automation rules run in the delegated administrator account and act on findings as they are ingested, and a rule whose criteria match the resource tag can natively apply actions that update the finding's severity and workflow status, so sandbox findings are recorded but demoted with no code to operate. A is wrong because an EventBridge-and-Lambda pipeline achieves the outcome only by introducing exactly the custom code the team refuses to operate. B is wrong because disabling the control stops the findings from being generated at all, which loses the record the team wants and affects every resource in those accounts, not only tagged ones. C is wrong because GuardDuty suppression rules apply to GuardDuty findings inside GuardDuty; they cannot act on Security Hub CSPM control findings or change severity and workflow status.

stem: A company runs a commercial vulnerability scanner in its on-premises data center to assess workloads that have not yet migrated to AWS. The scanner is not available as an AWS Security Hub CSPM (formerly Security Hub) integration in the partner catalog. The security team wants the scanner's results to appear in Security Hub CSPM alongside findings from GuardDuty and Amazon Inspector so that analysts can search them with the same filters, track them with workflow statuses, and let automation rules act on them. New scanner results must appear in Security Hub CSPM within minutes of each scan completing. The team already operates a small integration service that can call AWS APIs with appropriate credentials. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Map each scanner result to the AWS Security Finding Format and have the integration service call the BatchImportFindings API to send the results into Security Hub CSPM as findings from a custom product.
Publish each scanner result as a custom event to the default EventBridge event bus with a Security Hub CSPM detail type so that Security Hub CSPM ingests the events and records them as findings.
Write the scanner results to a CloudWatch Logs log group and create a subscription filter that streams the log events into Security Hub CSPM so that they are indexed as findings.
Convert the scanner results to the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework and write them to the company's Amazon Security Lake so that the results become available to analysts inside Security Hub CSPM.

explanation: A is correct. Security Hub CSPM ingests third-party and in-house findings through the BatchImportFindings API when they are formatted as ASFF, and findings imported this way are first-class: analysts filter them, set workflow statuses, and automation rules act on them, with ingestion happening at call time so results appear within minutes. B is wrong because Security Hub CSPM does not consume findings from EventBridge; the integration flows the other way, with Security Hub CSPM emitting its findings to EventBridge. C is wrong because CloudWatch Logs subscription filters deliver to destinations such as Kinesis and Lambda; there is no subscription destination that feeds Security Hub CSPM. D is wrong because Security Lake is a data lake that normalizes and stores OCSF security logs for analytics tools; writing to it does not create Security Hub CSPM findings with workflow tracking.

stem: A company builds container images in a CI/CD pipeline and pushes them to Amazon ECR repositories, where basic scanning with scan-on-push is enabled. Last month a critical CVE was published that affected a library present in dozens of images that had been stored for months; because the affected images were never pushed again, no scan ran, and the vulnerability went unnoticed until a routine review. The security team requires stored images to be re-evaluated automatically whenever new vulnerability intelligence is published, and it wants the resulting findings delivered into AWS Security Hub CSPM together with the company's findings from other services. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Keep basic scanning enabled and schedule an AWS Lambda function that calls the StartImageScan API for every image in every repository once each week so that stored images are re-checked.
Activate Amazon Inspector ECR enhanced scanning with continuous scanning for the repositories so that stored images are automatically re-scanned as Inspector's vulnerability intelligence is updated.
Enable GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring for the workloads that run the images so that GuardDuty detects whenever a vulnerable library is loaded into memory by one of the running containers.
Add a nightly stage to the CI/CD pipeline that rebuilds and re-pushes every image in the registry so that scan-on-push evaluates each image against the latest vulnerability data.

explanation: B is correct. Enhanced scanning is provided by Amazon Inspector, and its continuous scanning option re-scans images already stored in ECR whenever Inspector's vulnerability database changes, so a newly published CVE surfaces on existing images without any push or manual action, and Inspector findings flow into Security Hub CSPM through the native integration. A is wrong because basic scanning limits how often each image can be scanned in a day, the weekly schedule leaves a multi-day detection gap, and the function is custom code to maintain. C is wrong because Runtime Monitoring detects active threats such as malicious processes; it does not report CVEs present in stored images. D is wrong because rebuilding every image nightly consumes pipeline capacity, can introduce unintended image changes, and is a wasteful workaround for a native capability.

stem: A company must produce vulnerability findings for its entire Amazon EC2 fleet as part of a compliance program. Most instances are managed by AWS Systems Manager, but an inventory review shows that several hundred older instances run a hardened build on which the operations team is prohibited from installing any additional agents, including the SSM Agent. The security team wants a managed service that identifies operating system and software package vulnerabilities on every instance, including the agent-prohibited ones, with all findings available in one place. New instances launch weekly, so coverage must extend to them automatically, and the team will not build scanning infrastructure. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Install the CloudWatch agent on the older instances, stream each instance's installed-package inventory to CloudWatch Logs, and build queries that compare the package versions against public vulnerability feeds.
Use AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to scan the entire fleet for missing patches on a recurring schedule and treat the resulting patch-compliance report as the vulnerability findings.

Enable Amazon Inspector EC2 scanning with the hybrid scan mode so that SSM-managed instances are scanned through the agent and the remaining instances are assessed through agentless snapshot-based scanning.
Enable GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring across the fleet so that the GuardDuty security agent inspects the packages on each instance and reports the vulnerable software that it discovers.

explanation: C is correct. Inspector's EC2 hybrid scan mode combines agent-based scanning for instances managed by Systems Manager with agentless scanning, which assesses software inventory from EBS snapshots, so the agent-prohibited instances are still evaluated, coverage extends automatically to new instances, and findings are consolidated in Inspector and Security Hub CSPM. A is wrong because the CloudWatch agent is still an additional agent on instances where agents are prohibited, and hand-built feed comparison is scanning infrastructure by another name. B is wrong because Patch Manager requires a working SSM Agent and reports missing patches rather than CVE findings, so the agent-prohibited instances are not covered. D is wrong because Runtime Monitoring requires deploying a security agent and detects active threats at runtime rather than cataloging vulnerable packages.

stem: A financial services company stores loan documents in three Amazon S3 data-lake buckets that together hold roughly 40 TB of objects. Compliance requires the company to locate every object that contains the company's proprietary customer account number, a format of two letters followed by ten digits that no AWS managed data identifier matches. The review must examine every object in the three buckets rather than a sample, must repeat every week, and repeated runs must not re-analyze objects that were already examined and are unchanged, so that cost stays proportional to new data. Findings must be available for the compliance team's review. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable Amazon Macie automated sensitive data discovery for the account and rely on its continual evaluation of the account's buckets to surface the customer account numbers stored in the three buckets.

Create a weekly scheduled Amazon Macie discovery job that is scoped to the three buckets and configure the job to use all of the managed data identifiers that are available in the financial information detection categories.
Create an AWS Glue crawler over the three buckets and schedule Athena queries that apply a regular expression for the account number format to the crawled tables every week.

Create a custom data identifier with a regular expression for the account number format, and run a weekly scheduled Macie discovery job scoped to the three buckets that includes all objects and uses the custom identifier.

explanation: D is correct. A custom data identifier lets Macie match the proprietary two-letter, ten-digit format, a scoped discovery job can be configured without sampling so that every object is analyzed, and a scheduled job automatically analyzes only objects that were added or changed after previous runs, which keeps weekly cost proportional to new data. A is wrong because automated sensitive data discovery analyzes a representative sample of objects to build sensitivity profiles, so it cannot guarantee that every object was examined. B is wrong because managed data identifiers detect known data types such as payment card and bank account numbers; none of them matches the proprietary format, so the job would miss the target data. C is wrong because Glue and Athena work on structured, queryable data, would re-read unchanged data every week, and cannot parse the range of document formats that Macie inspects natively.

stem: A company's organization contains more than three thousand Amazon S3 buckets across 45 accounts, and Amazon Macie is already enabled with a delegated administrator account. The security team has no current picture of where sensitive data lives and wants continuous, organization-wide visibility: an interactive assessment that ranks each bucket by how likely it is to contain sensitive data, updates as bucket contents change, and stays within a predictable monthly budget. The team will use the ranking to choose a small number of buckets for exhaustive review later. Running full discovery jobs across every bucket was rejected because the estimated cost scaled with total storage. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable Amazon Macie automated sensitive data discovery across the organization so that Macie continually samples objects from all buckets and maintains a sensitivity score for each bucket.
Create one scheduled Amazon Macie discovery job per account that analyzes every object in every bucket each day and aggregates all of the findings in the delegated administrator account.
Enable GuardDuty S3 Protection for all of the accounts so that GuardDuty evaluates each bucket's contents and reports which of the buckets hold sensitive information.
Enable Amazon S3 Storage Lens advanced metrics for the organization and use its dashboard to identify the buckets that are most likely to contain sensitive customer data.

explanation: A is correct. Automated sensitive data discovery continually selects and analyzes representative samples of objects across the organization's buckets, maintains per-bucket sensitivity scores on an interactive summary, updates as bucket contents change, and its sampling model keeps cost predictable rather than proportional to total storage, which is exactly the triage input for choosing targeted follow-up jobs. B is wrong because daily full jobs across three thousand buckets have the storage-proportional cost profile that was explicitly rejected. C is wrong because S3 Protection detects threats in access patterns; it never inspects object contents and produces no sensitivity assessment. D is wrong because Storage Lens reports usage and activity metrics such as object counts and request rates and has no awareness of data sensitivity.

stem: When GuardDuty raises a finding about anomalous behavior by an IAM principal, a company's analysts reconstruct the activity by exporting CloudTrail logs and writing ad hoc Athena queries to answer questions such as which API calls the principal made over the preceding weeks, which IP addresses and geolocations it used, and which EC2 instances and roles it interacted with. Each investigation takes hours of query writing before conclusions can be drawn. The security team wants analysts to pivot directly from a GuardDuty finding into an interactive view that already contains this historical context, with the LEAST analyst effort per investigation. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a CloudTrail Lake event data store for the organization and build a library of saved SQL queries and dashboards that analysts run for each principal that comes under investigation.

Enable Amazon Detective for the organization and have analysts open findings in Detective, which maintains a behavior graph of each principal's historical API activity, IP usage, and related entities.
Enable Security Hub CSPM cross-Region aggregation and create Security Hub CSPM insights that group each principal's findings so that analysts can review the grouped results during an investigation.

Stream the organization's CloudTrail logs into an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain and build dashboards that visualize each principal's API activity, source addresses, and resource interactions over time.

explanation: B is correct. Detective continuously ingests CloudTrail events, VPC flow logs, and GuardDuty findings into a behavior graph that retains up to a year of activity, so an analyst can pivot from a GuardDuty finding straight into entity profiles that already show the principal's API call history, source IP addresses and geolocations, and related resources, without writing queries. A is wrong because CloudTrail Lake still requires analysts to author and run SQL for each investigation, which is the per-investigation effort the team is eliminating. C is wrong because Security Hub CSPM insights group findings; they do not reconstruct a principal's underlying API activity, network usage, or resource relationships. D is wrong because an OpenSearch pipeline must be built, secured, and maintained, and its dashboards still leave the correlation work to the analyst.

stem: A company's compliance framework requires the security team to be notified within a few minutes whenever the root user of any account in the organization is used, whether for an AWS Management Console sign-in or for API activity, in any Region. The company already operates an organization CloudTrail that records management events from every account and delivers them both to a central Amazon S3 bucket and to a CloudWatch Logs log group in the security account. The team wants to meet the requirement by building on this existing pipeline rather than deploying new per-account monitoring components. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable the AWS Config managed rule that checks whether the root user of each account has MFA enabled, and configure the rule to notify the security team whenever any account in the organization becomes noncompliant with the rule.
Create an EventBridge rule in every member account and Region that matches console sign-in events for the root user and forwards each matching event to a central SNS topic.

Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter on the organization trail's log group that matches events where the user identity type is Root, and create an alarm on the metric that notifies the security team through SNS.
Enable CloudTrail Insights on the organization trail so that unusual patterns of activity by the root user raise Insights events that are delivered to the security team for review.

explanation: C is correct. The organization trail already streams every account's management events into the central log group, so a metric filter matching a Root user identity type captures both console sign-ins and API calls from any account and Region, and a CloudWatch alarm on the filter's metric notifies within minutes using only the existing pipeline. A is wrong because the MFA configuration rule evaluates account posture; it says nothing about whether the root credentials were actually used. B is wrong because per-account, per-Region EventBridge rules are exactly the distributed components the team wants to avoid, and console sign-in events alone miss root API activity. D is wrong because CloudTrail Insights flags unusual volumes of API calls and would not alert on a single root action, which is precisely what must be caught.

stem: A company manages GuardDuty for its 80-account organization from a delegated administrator account, where findings from every member account are visible. The on-call security engineer must be paged in near real time whenever a finding with a severity of 7.0 or higher is generated for any member account, and lower-severity findings must not page anyone. The paging service is already subscribed to an SNS topic in the delegated administrator account. The team will not write or operate custom code, refuses to add configuration to individual member accounts because account baselines are frozen during an audit, and the solution must keep working automatically as new accounts join the organization. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: In the delegated administrator account, create an EventBridge rule that matches GuardDuty finding events with a numeric severity of 7.0 or greater and targets the existing SNS topic.
In each member account, create an EventBridge rule that matches high-severity GuardDuty findings and forwards the matching events to a central event bus in the delegated administrator account.
Configure GuardDuty findings export to publish all findings to an S3 bucket, and trigger an AWS Lambda function on object creation that filters for high severity and publishes to the SNS topic.
Create a Security Hub CSPM insight that groups findings with a severity of 7.0 or higher and configure the insight to publish its results to the SNS topic each time the grouped results change.

explanation: A is correct. In a GuardDuty organization, the delegated administrator account receives EventBridge events for findings from every member account, EventBridge supports numeric matching on the severity field in the finding detail, and a single rule targeting the existing SNS topic delivers pages in near real time, involves no custom code, and covers new members automatically with no member-account changes. B is wrong because it adds a rule to every member account, which the frozen baselines forbid, and it duplicates events the administrator account already receives. C is wrong because new findings reach the S3 export only after a delay of several minutes, and the filtering function is exactly the custom Lambda code that the team will not operate. D is wrong because Security Hub CSPM insights are saved queries for the console and API; an insight does not publish notifications to SNS when its results change.

stem: A company must detect, across all accounts in its organization, any security group that allows inbound access from 0.0.0.0/0 to TCP port 22 or port 3389. The detection must evaluate a security group as soon as it is created or its rules are modified, must include security groups that are not attached to any network interface, and the compliance state of every account must be visible from a central security account. Findings should also appear in AWS Security Hub CSPM, where the security team already triages issues from other services, and the company prefers AWS managed detection logic over custom code. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable Amazon Inspector network reachability findings for the organization so that Inspector reports the EC2 instances that are reachable from the internet on port 22 or port 3389.
Enable GuardDuty in all of the organization's accounts so that GuardDuty raises findings whenever a security group is configured to allow unrestricted inbound access to management ports.
Enable VPC flow logs in every account and schedule Athena queries that search for accepted inbound connections to ports 22 and 3389 that originate from public source addresses.

Deploy the restricted-ssh and restricted-common-ports AWS Config managed rules as organization Config rules with change-triggered evaluation, and review compliance through an aggregator in the security account.

explanation: D is correct. The managed Config rules evaluate the security group resources themselves, change-triggered evaluation runs the moment a security group is created or modified, unattached security groups are still recorded resources and are therefore evaluated, organization rules deploy the logic to every account, and an aggregator centralizes compliance state while Config findings also flow into Security Hub CSPM. A is wrong because network reachability analysis evaluates network paths to running instances, so an over-permissive security group that is not attached to anything produces no finding. B is wrong because GuardDuty analyzes threat telemetry such as flow logs and CloudTrail; it does not evaluate resource configurations against compliance rules. C is wrong because flow logs reveal only traffic that actually occurred, so a dangerous rule that has not yet been exploited stays invisible, and the scheduled queries are custom code run in every account.

stem: GuardDuty generated a Recon:EC2/Portscan finding for an application server in a production VPC; the finding names the instance but does not enumerate every target it probed. Before approving containment, the incident commander asks the detection team to establish the blast radius: exactly which internal subnets the instance probed, which destination ports it targeted, how many connection attempts were rejected, and when the scanning began. VPC flow logs for the affected VPC have been delivered to a CloudWatch Logs log group for the past year. The team must produce these details from data that already exists, without deploying anything new. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Search CloudTrail management events for API calls made with the instance's role credentials during the scanning window and reconstruct the probed targets from the recorded request parameters.

Query the Route 53 Resolver query logs for the VPC to list the internal hostnames that the instance resolved and infer the probed subnets and services from those recorded DNS lookups during the scanning window.

Run CloudWatch Logs Insights queries over the VPC flow logs that filter records where the instance's private address is the source, aggregating by destination address, destination port, action, and start time.
Enable VPC Traffic Mirroring on the instance's elastic network interface and analyze the mirrored packets to enumerate the subnets, destination ports, and rejected connection attempts involved.

explanation: C is correct. Flow log records carry source and destination addresses, destination ports, the ACCEPT or REJECT action, and timestamps, so Logs Insights aggregations over the existing year of data can enumerate every probed subnet and port, count rejected attempts, and establish when the scanning began, all from data already collected. A is wrong because CloudTrail records control-plane API calls; network connections between instances never appear in it. B is wrong because Resolver query logs show only DNS lookups, and port scans typically target IP address ranges directly without resolving names, so the logs cannot enumerate ports or attempts. D is wrong because Traffic Mirroring captures packets only from the moment it is enabled, so it cannot answer historical questions about scanning that has already happened.

stem: A company's threat intelligence team maintains a proprietary list of malicious domains that is updated hourly. The team must be able to hunt retroactively: whenever domains are added to the list, the team needs to search at least 30 days of DNS activity from workloads in all of the company's VPCs to find any instance that resolved those domains. The workloads use the default Route 53 Resolver at each VPC's .2 address, and GuardDuty is enabled in all accounts. VPC flow logs are already enabled, but the team found that they do not contain the query names needed for this analysis. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Upload the proprietary domain list to GuardDuty as a threat list so that GuardDuty's DNS monitoring produces findings whenever a workload in any VPC resolves one of the listed domains.
Enable Route 53 Resolver query logging for every VPC with delivery to Amazon S3, and have the team run Athena queries that join the stored query names against the current domain list.
Deploy Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall with a custom domain list that is built from the proprietary feed and set the rule action to ALERT so that matching queries generate findings for the team.
Add a custom field configuration to the VPC flow logs so that each flow record includes the DNS query name for the traffic that the workloads send to the Resolver's address.

explanation: B is correct. Resolver query logging records every DNS query that VPC resources make through the Route 53 Resolver, including the full query name, and delivering the logs to S3 builds the durable history that Athena can search whenever the intelligence list changes, which satisfies the 30-day retroactive hunting requirement. A is wrong because GuardDuty threat lists contain IP addresses rather than domain names, and GuardDuty does not expose its internal DNS log stream for customer queries against past activity. C is wrong because DNS Firewall evaluates queries only from the moment a rule exists, so a domain added today produces no signal about lookups that happened during the previous 30 days. D is wrong because flow logs describe IP-level flows and have no field, custom or otherwise, that records DNS query names.

stem: A developer accidentally committed an IAM user's access key to a public repository, and the key has been deactivated. The security team must now determine every API action the key performed: the investigation spans the organization's 40 accounts and all Regions and must cover the past 90 days. The organization trail delivers all management events to a central S3 bucket in the log-archive account; the trail is not configured to send events to CloudWatch Logs. The team has query access to the log-archive account and wants the approach that answers the question fastest with the LEAST new setup. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Open the CloudTrail console's Event history in each of the 40 accounts and filter the last 90 days of events by the exposed access key ID in each Region that the company uses.
Create a CloudTrail Lake event data store in the log-archive account and run a SQL query against the data store that filters the organization's events by the exposed access key ID.
Create a CloudWatch Logs Insights query that scans the organization trail's log group in the log-archive account for all events whose access key ID matches the exposed key.
Create an Athena table over the organization trail's S3 location in the log-archive account and run a query that selects all events whose access key ID matches the exposed key.

explanation: D is correct. The 90 days of organization-wide activity already sit in the central S3 bucket, and an Athena table defined over the trail's prefix can be created in minutes and queried by access key ID across every account and Region in one pass, with no new data collection or ingestion. A is wrong because Event history is viewed per account and per Region, so the team would repeat the search hundreds of times and still lack a consolidated result. B is wrong because a new event data store collects events from its creation onward; answering questions about the past 90 days would first require a separate import of the existing trail logs, which is additional setup and time. C is wrong because the trail does not deliver to CloudWatch Logs, so no log group containing the historical events exists to query.

stem: A company has finished consolidating 60 AWS accounts into a single organization and is standing up threat detection. The security-tooling account must manage GuardDuty for the whole organization: findings from every existing account must be visible to it, accounts created in the future must be covered without manual work, and monitoring must operate in each Region the company uses. GuardDuty is not yet enabled anywhere. The platform team that manages account baselines wants to avoid per-account console work, and the security team has administrative access to both the management account and the security-tooling account. Which combination of steps establishes this configuration? (Choose two.)

options.text: From the organization's management account, designate the security-tooling account as the GuardDuty delegated administrator in each Region where monitoring is required.
From the security-tooling account, send a GuardDuty membership invitation to each of the 60 accounts and ask each account's owner to accept the invitation.
Attach a service control policy to the organization root that denies the guardduty:DeleteDetector action so that member accounts cannot remove their detectors.
Enable GuardDuty in the management account only, because a detector in the management account automatically monitors the activity of every account in the organization.
In the security-tooling account, add all existing organization accounts as GuardDuty members and turn on the auto-enable setting so GuardDuty is enabled for accounts that join later.

explanation: A and E are correct. GuardDuty administration is Regional, so the management account must delegate the security-tooling account as administrator in every Region to be monitored, and the delegated administrator must then enroll the existing accounts as members and turn on auto-enable so that future accounts are covered the moment they join. B is wrong because organization integration makes invitations unnecessary; the delegated administrator adds organization accounts directly without owner acceptance. C is wrong because a service control policy is a preventive guardrail that hardens the deployment but neither enables GuardDuty nor enrolls any account. D is wrong because a GuardDuty detector monitors only the account it belongs to; there is no automatic organization-wide monitoring without designating an administrator and enrolling members.

stem: A company's finance team escalates a sudden, unexplained increase in EC2 compute spending. The security team suspects that attackers have compromised instances in several accounts and are running cryptocurrency miners, a pattern the company has seen before in its industry. The affected accounts run both standalone applications on EC2 instances and containerized workloads on Amazon ECS. The team must put detection in place that identifies cryptocurrency mining on the fleet, both by recognizing the network and DNS behavior of miners communicating with mining pools and by observing the mining processes themselves as they execute on the hosts. Which combination of capabilities meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable Amazon Inspector EC2 scanning across the accounts so that instances running vulnerable packages that mining malware commonly exploits are reported to the security team.

Enable GuardDuty foundational threat detection in all accounts so that CryptoCurrency finding types fire when instances query mining-pool domains or connect to addresses associated with mining activity.
Deploy AWS Config custom rules across the accounts that evaluate each EC2 instance's recorded configuration to detect the presence of unauthorized cryptocurrency-mining software.
Create CloudWatch alarms on the CPUUtilization metric for every instance in the fleet and page the security team whenever sustained utilization exceeds a defined threshold.
Enable GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring for the EC2 instances and the ECS workloads so that the security agent detects mining processes and related runtime behavior on the hosts.

explanation: B and E are correct. Foundational GuardDuty analyzes DNS query logs and VPC flow logs and raises CryptoCurrency findings when an instance resolves mining-pool domains or communicates with mining-related addresses, and Runtime Monitoring adds an on-host security agent that observes execution, detecting miner processes on both the standalone instances and the ECS workloads. A is wrong because Inspector inventories vulnerable software; it cannot determine whether mining is actually occurring on a host. C is wrong because AWS Config evaluates resource configuration recorded by the service, not the processes or software running inside an instance's operating system. D is wrong because a CPU alarm flags any sustained load, including legitimate batch work, and identifies nothing specific about mining, so it produces pages without providing detection.

stem: During an audit-readiness review, a company's security team receives two requirements for its organization CloudTrail, which delivers logs to a dedicated S3 bucket in the log-archive account where access is already restricted to the audit team. First, the team must be able to demonstrate cryptographically that log files delivered by CloudTrail have not been modified, deleted, or forged since delivery. Second, the team must be alerted promptly if anyone stops logging, deletes the trail, or changes what the trail records. The team will implement both requirements with native AWS capabilities rather than custom tooling. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Encrypt the trail's log files with an AWS KMS customer managed key and restrict the kms:Decrypt permission so that only members of the audit team can read the delivered files.
Enable S3 Versioning on the logging bucket so that earlier versions of any log file that is modified or deleted can be recovered and compared during an investigation.
Enable CloudTrail log file validation on the trail and use the CLI validation command against the delivered digest files to prove the integrity of the log files.
Enable CloudTrail Insights on the trail so that unusual changes in the volume of logged management activity raise Insights events for the security team to review.

Create an EventBridge rule in the organization's management account that matches the StopLogging, DeleteTrail, and UpdateTrail API calls for the organization trail and sends a notification to the security team's SNS topic.

explanation: C and E are correct. Log file validation makes CloudTrail deliver digitally signed digest files that chain hashes of each delivered log file, and the CLI validation command uses that chain to prove whether any file was modified, deleted, or forged after delivery, which is the cryptographic demonstration auditors require; an EventBridge rule in the management account, where the organization trail's configuration calls are made and logged, notifies the team promptly when anyone tampers with the logging configuration. A is wrong because KMS encryption controls who can read the logs; it provides no verifiable statement about whether files changed after delivery. B is wrong because versioning aids recovery but cannot prove integrity and raises no alert when tampering happens. D is wrong because Insights detects unusual API call volumes; it does not watch for specific trail-configuration actions and provides no integrity evidence.

stem: A healthcare analytics company ingests customer datasets into a set of Amazon S3 buckets in its data account, where Amazon Macie has not yet been enabled. A new privacy control states that the data-governance team must identify objects in these buckets that contain personal health information and other personally identifiable information, and must receive a notification within minutes whenever such an object is found so that the team can quarantine it before analysts use the dataset. Findings must also remain available for later compliance review. The company wants managed AWS services rather than custom classification code. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable GuardDuty S3 Protection for the data account so that GuardDuty inspects newly written objects and reports the ones that contain personal or health-related information.
Enable Amazon Macie in the data account and configure sensitive data discovery over the buckets using the managed data identifiers for health information and personally identifiable information.
Enable Amazon Inspector in the data account and add the buckets to its scanning scope so that newly uploaded objects are assessed for sensitive content as they arrive.
Create an EventBridge rule that matches Macie sensitive-data findings and targets an SNS topic that the data-governance team subscribes to for quarantine notifications.
Configure S3 Event Notifications for object-created events on the buckets and send the notifications to the data-governance team's SNS topic as each new object arrives.

explanation: B and D are correct. Macie is the managed classification service: its managed data identifiers recognize health-related and personally identifiable information, discovery over the buckets produces a sensitive-data finding for each affected object that remains available for compliance review, and Macie publishes findings to EventBridge as they are created, so a rule targeting the governance team's SNS topic delivers notification within minutes. A is wrong because S3 Protection analyzes access patterns for threats and never classifies object contents. C is wrong because Inspector assesses EC2 instances, container images, and Lambda functions for vulnerabilities; it has no capability to scan S3 objects. E is wrong because object-created notifications announce every upload regardless of content, telling the team nothing about which objects contain sensitive data.

stem: A company's security team must improve detection of compromised long-term IAM access keys across its organization, where an organization trail already records management events in every account. Two behaviors must be covered: first, use of an access key from infrastructure that is associated with anonymizing proxies or known-malicious hosts; second, a key suddenly issuing an abnormal burst of write management API calls that departs from its established baseline. The team wants managed anomaly detection rather than hand-tuned thresholds, and alerts for both behaviors must flow promptly into the team's existing EventBridge-based alerting pipeline. Which combination of capabilities meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable GuardDuty for the organization through a delegated administrator so that findings are generated when credentials are used from Tor exit nodes or known-malicious addresses in any account.
Schedule a daily job that downloads each account's IAM credential report and flags access keys whose last-used data shows services or Regions that the key has not used before.
Enable CloudTrail Insights for write management events on the organization trail so that unusual bursts of API call volume raise Insights events that the pipeline can consume.
Enable IAM Access Analyzer with the organization as the zone of trust so that its findings identify the credentials that are being used from outside the organization's boundary.
Enable Amazon Security Lake for the organization so that CloudTrail activity is normalized into the OCSF format and stored durably for the alerting pipeline to consume.

explanation: A and C are correct. GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail activity with threat intelligence and machine learning, generating findings when credentials are used from anonymizing proxies or known-malicious infrastructure, and it delivers findings to EventBridge in near real time; CloudTrail Insights baselines normal management-event volume and raises Insights events when write API call rates deviate abnormally, which the EventBridge pipeline can also consume. B is wrong because credential reports show metadata such as key age and last-used service; a daily download detects nothing in near real time and observes no per-call behavior. D is wrong because Access Analyzer findings describe resource policies that grant external access; they say nothing about how or where an access key is being used. E is wrong because Security Lake normalizes and stores logs for analytics; it performs no detection and raises no alerts by itself.

stem: A security engineer receives an automated alert that a developer committed an IAM user's long-term access key pair to a public GitHub repository approximately three hours ago. GuardDuty has not yet produced findings for the key, and the full exposure window is unknown. The IAM user is used by a scheduled reporting job that runs once each night, and no other credentials exist for the user. The company's incident response playbook requires the engineer to contain the exposure before performing eradication or recovery, and investigators must be able to attribute every API call that occurred during the exposure window. Which action should the engineer take FIRST?

options.text: Delete the IAM user and its access keys immediately, and create a replacement user with new credentials for the reporting job before the next nightly run.
Deactivate the exposed access key so that it can no longer authenticate, and preserve the key ID to search CloudTrail for all activity during the exposure window.
Enable GuardDuty in the account and wait for it to raise findings that identify any unauthorized use of the exposed access key before changing the key's status.
Create a second access key for the IAM user, update the reporting job to use it, and schedule the exposed key for deletion after the next nightly run.

explanation: B is correct. Deactivating the exposed key immediately stops it from authenticating, which contains the incident, while keeping the key and its key ID intact supports the required CloudTrail attribution of every call made during the exposure window. A is wrong because deleting the user and keys is an eradication step taken before containment is verified, and it removes context, such as the user's attached policies and key metadata, that investigators need. C is wrong because GuardDuty is a detection capability; enabling it neither prevents the attacker from continuing to use the key nor retroactively analyzes the exposure window. D is wrong because rotating in a new key while leaving the exposed key active until after the next run leaves the attacker with working credentials for many more hours.

stem: An application in a production account assumes an IAM role that grants write access to several DynamoDB tables. A security engineer confirms that temporary security credentials for the role were exposed through a misconfigured log aggregation pipeline and might be held by an external party. The role's maximum session duration is 12 hours, so exposed sessions could remain valid for the rest of the day. The application assumes the role continuously to obtain fresh credentials, and the business requires that the application keep running throughout the response without any configuration or deployment changes. Which action invalidates the exposed temporary credentials while meeting these requirements?

options.text: Update the role's trust policy to deny all new sts:AssumeRole requests until the investigation is complete, which forces every outstanding session for the role to expire immediately.
Delete the role and recreate it with the same name and permissions so that sessions issued by the original role stop being honored when the role's unique identifier changes.

Attach an inline policy to the role that denies all actions for sessions whose aws:TokenIssueTime is earlier than the current time, so existing sessions lose access while newly issued sessions work normally.
Detach all of the role's permissions policies, wait for the 12-hour maximum session duration to elapse so the exposed sessions expire, and then reattach the permissions policies.

explanation: C is correct. The revoke-sessions pattern denies every action to sessions issued before the policy's timestamp, which immediately neutralizes the exposed credentials, while the application's next automatic AssumeRole call yields a session with a later token issue time that is unaffected, so the application keeps running with no configuration change. A is wrong because changing the trust policy only prevents new role sessions, which breaks the application, and has no effect on temporary credentials that were already issued. B is wrong because deleting and recreating the role interrupts the application while the role is absent, and it invalidates the exposed credentials only as a side effect of an outage-causing action. D is wrong because removing the permissions policies revokes access for the application's legitimate sessions as well, causing up to 12 hours of downtime.

stem: During an active incident, a security engineer must isolate a compromised Amazon EC2 instance that has a single elastic network interface in a VPC subnet whose network ACL allows all inbound and outbound traffic. The engineer creates a security group with no inbound rules and no outbound rules and replaces all of the instance's security groups with it. Several minutes later, network monitoring shows that an established outbound session from the instance to an external command-and-control address is still transferring data. The instance is not part of an Auto Scaling group. Why is the session still active, and what should the engineer do to interrupt it immediately?

options.text: Established connections are tracked, and removing security group rules does not interrupt existing tracked flows; add deny rules for the destination to the subnet's network ACL to break the session.
Security group changes on a running instance take effect only after the instance is stopped and started; stop the instance and start it again so the isolation security group is enforced.
Traffic that has already been routed is governed by the route table rather than by security groups; remove the internet gateway route from the subnet's route table to stop the outbound flow.

The network interface retains its previous security group associations until it is detached from the instance; detach the elastic network interface and attach it to a quarantine instance in a forensic subnet.

explanation: A is correct. Security groups use connection tracking, and an existing tracked connection is not interrupted when the rules that allowed it are removed, so the established command-and-control session survives the isolation security group; network ACLs are evaluated per packet, so adding deny entries for the destination interrupts the flow immediately. B is wrong because security group changes take effect on running instances right away for new flows; no stop and start is required, and stopping the instance would also destroy volatile memory evidence. C is wrong because security groups do govern this traffic, and deleting the internet gateway route would cut connectivity for every workload in the subnet rather than the single malicious session. D is wrong because security group changes apply to the network interface immediately; there is no association that persists until detachment, and moving the interface would change the evidence environment.

stem: A GuardDuty finding indicates that an Amazon EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group is communicating with a known malware domain. The security team must preserve both the instance's volatile memory and its disk state for forensic analysis, must prevent accidental destruction of the instance during the response, and must then take the instance out of service for offline analysis. The instance is managed by AWS Systems Manager; the VPC has no Systems Manager VPC endpoints, and the instance reaches Systems Manager through a NAT gateway. Which sequence of steps meets these requirements?

options.text: Move the instance to standby in the Auto Scaling group. Stop the instance. Capture a memory image by using a Systems Manager Run Command forensic tool. Create EBS snapshots of all attached volumes. Enable termination protection on the instance.

Create EBS snapshots of all attached volumes. Terminate the instance so that the Auto Scaling group replaces it. Enable termination protection on the replacement instance. Capture a memory image from the replacement instance by using Systems Manager.

Enable termination protection on the instance. Replace the instance's security groups with a no-rule isolation security group. Move the instance to standby in the Auto Scaling group. Capture a memory image by using a Systems Manager Run Command forensic tool. Create EBS snapshots of all attached volumes. Stop the instance.

Enable termination protection on the instance and move it to standby in the Auto Scaling group. Capture a memory image by using a Systems Manager Run Command forensic tool. Create EBS snapshots of all attached volumes. Replace the instance's security groups with a no-rule isolation security group. Stop the instance.

explanation: D is correct. Termination protection and standby status guard the instance against automated replacement before evidence is collected; memory must be captured while the instance is running and can still reach the Systems Manager endpoints; snapshots then preserve the disk state; full network isolation follows once the agent-based collection is complete; and stopping the instance last takes it out of service for offline analysis. A is wrong because stopping the instance before the memory capture destroys the volatile memory that must be preserved. B is wrong because terminating the instance destroys its memory and, with volumes that delete on termination, its disks, and the replacement instance contains no evidence at all. C is wrong because replacing the security groups with a no-rule group before the capture cuts the instance's outbound path through the NAT gateway to Systems Manager, so the Run Command memory acquisition cannot execute.

stem: A GuardDuty Lambda Protection finding, Backdoor:Lambda/C&CActivity.B, shows that a production AWS Lambda function is communicating with a known command-and-control server. The security team traces the behavior to a malicious third-party dependency that shipped in the most recent deployment. The function is invoked by an Amazon SQS event source mapping and also directly by internal services through the AWS SDK. The team must immediately stop the function from executing any more attacker code through any invocation path, and must preserve the artifacts that the forensic investigation will need. The function's execution role is shared with several other production functions that must remain unaffected. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Set the function's reserved concurrency to zero so that every invocation from any event source is throttled while the function's code and configuration remain unchanged.
Delete the function's SQS event source mapping so the queue stops invoking the function, and ask the internal services to pause their direct SDK invocations.
Delete the Lambda function immediately and redeploy it from source control after the application team removes the malicious dependency from the package.
Detach all permissions policies from the function's execution role so that any attacker code that continues to run cannot make successful AWS API calls.
Download the function's deployment package and configuration, and preserve its CloudWatch Logs log group and recent traces as evidence for the forensic investigation.

explanation: A and E are correct. Setting reserved concurrency to zero throttles every new execution regardless of whether the trigger is the SQS event source mapping or a direct SDK call, which halts attacker code through all invocation paths without altering the function, and preserving the deployment package, configuration, and logs retains the artifacts the investigation needs. B is wrong because it covers only the SQS path and depends on other teams pausing their calls, so direct invocations can still execute attacker code. C is wrong because deleting the function destroys the compromised artifact that the forensic team must analyze. D is wrong because the execution role is shared, so stripping its policies breaks several unaffected production functions, and code that is still running could continue its non-AWS network activity anyway.

stem: A company runs several hundred Amazon EC2 instances across three AWS member accounts in one organization, and GuardDuty is administered from a delegated administrator account where all member findings are aggregated. The security team wants any instance that generates a Backdoor:EC2/C&CActivity.B finding to be quarantined automatically within minutes: the instance's security groups must be replaced with a pre-created isolation security group, and the instance must be tagged for investigation. The team does not want analysts in the approval path for this finding type, wants the LEAST operational overhead, and will not build custom polling against the GuardDuty APIs. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a CloudWatch alarm on GuardDuty's finding-count metric for that finding type and configure the alarm to invoke a Lambda function that locates and quarantines the affected instances.

Create an EventBridge rule in the delegated administrator account that matches the finding type and invokes a Systems Manager Automation runbook to replace the instance's security groups and apply the tag.

Deploy a Lambda function on a five-minute schedule that calls the GuardDuty ListFindings API in every member account, filters the results for the finding type, and then quarantines each affected instance.
Enable Security Hub CSPM automation rules that match the finding type and automatically update the finding's workflow status and severity so that the isolation is recorded for the security team.

explanation: B is correct. GuardDuty findings from all member accounts are delivered to EventBridge in the delegated administrator account, so a rule matching the finding type fires within minutes of detection, and a Systems Manager Automation runbook performs the security group replacement and tagging as a managed, auditable action with no polling and no custom scheduler. A is wrong because GuardDuty does not publish a per-finding-type CloudWatch metric suited to this, and an alarm carries no finding detail, so the function could not determine which instance to quarantine. C is wrong because scheduled polling of every member account adds latency and operational overhead and duplicates what EventBridge already delivers natively. D is wrong because Security Hub CSPM automation rules can only modify fields on a finding, such as workflow status or severity; they cannot replace security groups or tag instances.

stem: A security operations team triages all of its findings in AWS Security Hub CSPM in a central security account. For a subset of findings, such as exposed access keys on EC2 instances, the team has an approved remediation Lambda function, but company policy requires that a human analyst review each finding before remediation runs because the action is disruptive to workloads. Analysts want to trigger the approved remediation for one or more selected findings directly from the Security Hub CSPM console with a single action after their review, and the team wants to avoid building a separate approval portal. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a Security Hub CSPM custom action; analysts send reviewed findings to the action, and an EventBridge rule matching the custom action's ARN invokes the remediation Lambda function.
Create an EventBridge rule that matches all Security Hub CSPM findings of that type as they are imported and invokes the remediation Lambda function as soon as each finding arrives.

Create a Security Hub CSPM automation rule that matches the finding type and updates the finding's workflow status to RESOLVED, and configure the rule to invoke the remediation Lambda function afterward.
Configure an SSM Incident Manager response plan that is triggered by the findings and lists the remediation Lambda function as a runbook step for the on-call responder to execute.

explanation: A is correct. Custom actions exist for exactly this workflow: an analyst selects one or more findings in the Security Hub CSPM console and sends them to the custom action, which emits an event carrying the action's ARN to EventBridge, where a rule routes the findings to the approved Lambda function, so remediation runs only after human review and with a single console action. B is wrong because a rule on imported findings fires automatically for every match, which violates the requirement that an analyst review each finding first. C is wrong because automation rules run automatically at ingestion and can only modify finding fields; they cannot act as an analyst-triggered control or invoke Lambda functions. D is wrong because Incident Manager engages responders and tracks incidents; it does not provide a one-click action on selected findings inside the Security Hub CSPM console.
