stem: A detective control alerts a security engineer that a bucket policy on an Amazon S3 bucket was modified twenty minutes ago to allow anonymous read access, and CloudTrail attributes the change to a developer role that shows other signs of compromise. Company policy prohibits public access to any bucket in this account, now or in the future. While the compromised role is being investigated, the engineer must ensure as quickly as possible that no bucket in the account, including buckets the attacker might target next, can serve public reads, regardless of the bucket policies or ACLs that are applied. Which action meets these requirements?

options.text: Run IAM Access Analyzer on the account and review its findings to enumerate every bucket that is currently accessible from outside the account's zone of trust.
Remove the anonymous-read statement from the affected bucket's policy and create a CloudTrail-based alarm that notifies the team if any other bucket policy in the account is changed.
Enable Amazon S3 Block Public Access at the account level with all four settings on, which overrides bucket policies and ACLs that would otherwise grant public access.
Attach a service control policy to the account that denies s3:PutBucketPolicy and s3:PutBucketAcl so the compromised role cannot make any additional buckets public.

explanation: C is correct. Account-level Block Public Access applies to every existing and future bucket in the account, and its settings override bucket policies and ACLs that grant public access, so the exposed bucket stops serving anonymous reads immediately and no bucket the attacker touches next can be made public; a single API call meets the containment requirement fastest. A is wrong because Access Analyzer identifies public access but does not remove or prevent it. B is wrong because editing one bucket policy leaves every other bucket unprotected until a human responds to an alarm, which does not prevent public reads in the meantime. D is wrong because an SCP that blocks future policy changes does not remove the public access that already exists on the compromised bucket, and it would also block the responders' own remediation changes.

stem: An attacker used stolen credentials to run a mass delete against a business-critical Amazon S3 bucket that has versioning enabled. The application now returns 404 errors for thousands of objects, and the bucket serves the company's order-processing application, which must return to normal operation today. CloudTrail shows that the credentials invoked only the s3:DeleteObject action; the credentials did not have permission for s3:DeleteObjectVersion or s3:PutLifecycleConfiguration, and no lifecycle rules expire noncurrent versions. The stolen credentials have already been deactivated. The security engineer must restore the deleted objects in place as quickly as possible and with the least data movement. Which recovery action meets these requirements?

options.text: Issue delete requests for the delete markers that the mass delete created; removing a delete marker makes the most recent noncurrent version of each object current again.
Copy the most recent noncurrent version of every affected object into a newly created bucket, and then update the application configuration to read from the new bucket.
Run an S3 Batch Operations job that applies a legal hold to the affected objects so that S3 automatically reinstates the most recent version of each one.
Suspend versioning on the bucket and use the RestoreObject API to roll every affected object back to the last version that existed before the attack began.

explanation: A is correct. Because the credentials could only call s3:DeleteObject on a versioned bucket, every deletion simply added a delete marker on top of intact object versions; deleting those markers restores the objects in place with no data movement, which is the fastest recovery. B is wrong because copying versions to a new bucket moves the entire data set and requires an application configuration change, both of which the requirements exclude. C is wrong because a legal hold only prevents a locked version from being deleted; it does not remove delete markers or reinstate objects. D is wrong because suspending versioning does not undo delete markers, and RestoreObject retrieves archived objects from S3 Glacier storage classes; it is not a rollback mechanism.

stem: A company suffered an S3 ransomware incident in which an attacker who obtained administrator-level credentials in a workload account deleted objects and overwrote others with encrypted copies. During the post-incident review, the security team is asked to ensure that the company's most critical S3 data remains recoverable even if an attacker again obtains full administrator credentials in the workload account. The team accepts that an administrator-level attacker may tamper with any resource inside the compromised account itself, and recovery time objectives allow restores to take several hours. Which combination of controls ensures the data can be recovered after such a compromise? (Choose two.)

options.text: Encrypt the critical buckets with SSE-KMS by using a customer managed key that has automatic key rotation enabled.
Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a default retention period on the buckets that hold the critical data.
Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level so that no bucket in the workload account can be exposed publicly.
Apply lifecycle rules that transition noncurrent object versions to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days to preserve history at low cost.
Replicate the critical objects to a bucket in a separate backup account whose policies prevent workload-account principals from modifying or deleting the replicas.

explanation: B and E are correct. Object Lock in compliance mode prevents any principal in the account, including administrators and the root user, from deleting or overwriting protected versions until the retention period expires, and replication into a separately controlled backup account places recovery copies entirely outside the blast radius of a workload-account compromise. A is wrong because encryption and key rotation protect confidentiality; they do not stop a principal with delete permissions from destroying the objects. C is wrong because Block Public Access prevents public exposure; it offers no protection against deletion by an authenticated administrator. D is wrong because lifecycle transitions only change the storage class of versions; an administrator-level attacker can still delete the versions or remove the lifecycle configuration itself.

stem: A security engineer is investigating exposed IAM user credentials in an account where sensitive objects in an Amazon S3 bucket are encrypted with server-side encryption using a customer managed AWS KMS key. CloudTrail data events were never enabled for the bucket, but the account has a single management-event trail that has been logging to S3 for the past year. Leadership asks for definitive evidence of whether the exposed credentials were used to decrypt any of the bucket's objects during the 48-hour exposure window, which ended yesterday. The engineer must rely only on telemetry that already exists for the exposure window. Which investigation approach can provide this evidence?

options.text: Review CloudWatch usage metrics for the KMS key over the exposure window and correlate spikes in decrypt activity with the times the exposed credentials were known to be active in the account.

Search the existing trail's management events for Decrypt calls on the key where the userIdentity matches the exposed credentials, and use each event's encryption context to confirm the bucket's objects were involved.
Enable CloudTrail data events for the bucket now, and review the resulting GetObject events for requests that the exposed credentials issued during the 48-hour exposure window.
Review the AWS Config configuration timeline for the KMS key and the bucket to identify configuration changes and access activity attributable to the exposed credentials.

explanation: B is correct. AWS KMS records Decrypt as a CloudTrail management event, so the calls are already present in the existing trail for the entire window; filtering by the key and the compromised userIdentity, and inspecting the encryption context, which for S3 identifies the object or bucket ARN involved, gives definitive evidence of whether the bucket's objects were decrypted. A is wrong because aggregate usage metrics cannot attribute calls to a specific principal; correlation of spikes is circumstantial, not proof. C is wrong because data events are recorded only from the moment they are enabled; enabling them now cannot reveal GetObject activity from a window that ended yesterday. D is wrong because AWS Config records configuration changes to resources, not data-plane usage such as decrypt operations.

stem: During a compromise of an administrator's credentials, CloudTrail shows that the attacker called CreateGrant several times on a customer managed AWS KMS key that encrypts the company's production Amazon EBS volumes and Amazon RDS databases. The grants name principals that the security team does not recognize. The production workloads depend on the key for every volume attach and database restart, so the key must remain usable throughout the response, and the compromised administrator credentials have already been deactivated. The security engineer must remove the attacker's ability to use the key while causing no disruption to the production services that legitimately depend on it. Which response meets these requirements?

options.text: Schedule the KMS key for deletion with a seven-day waiting period, create a replacement key, and re-encrypt the production volumes and databases under the new key before the deletion completes.
Disable the KMS key until the investigation ends so that no principal, including the unrecognized grantees, can use it for any cryptographic operation.
Enable automatic annual rotation on the KMS key so that new key material is generated and the material available to the attacker's grantees becomes unusable.
List the key's grants, revoke every grant created by the compromised credentials, and audit the key policy to remove any unrecognized principals while leaving legitimate service grants intact.

explanation: D is correct. Grants are the mechanism the attacker used, so revoking the grants that the compromised credentials created removes the unauthorized access path, and auditing the key policy catches any other persistence, while the grants that AWS services legitimately hold for the volumes and databases remain intact, so production is unaffected. A is wrong because scheduling deletion endangers all data encrypted under the key and forces a disruptive re-encryption of production storage. B is wrong because disabling the key blocks every EBS volume attach and RDS restart that depends on it, which violates the no-disruption requirement. C is wrong because rotation generates new material for future encryption operations but does not revoke grants; the attacker's grantees could continue using the key after rotation.

stem: A security engineer at a company that operates a single standalone AWS account, which does not belong to an AWS Organization, receives an alert that the account's root user signed in to the AWS Management Console from an unfamiliar country. The root user has no multi-factor authentication device registered, and the sign-in used the correct password on the first attempt, which suggests the password is known to the attacker. The company still controls the email address that is registered to the account. The engineer must regain exclusive control of the root user before taking any other response steps. Which action should the engineer take FIRST?

options.text: Open a support case with AWS and request that all API and console activity in the account be suspended until the security team completes its investigation of the suspicious sign-ins.
Create an AWS Organizations service control policy that denies all actions for the root user and attach it to the account before the attacker signs in again.
Use the registered account email address to perform a root password reset, sign in, register a multi-factor authentication device for the root user, and delete any root access keys.
Contact AWS through the account's designated emergency security contact and ask AWS to rotate the root user's password and issue new credentials on the company's behalf.

explanation: C is correct. Because the company still controls the registered email address, resetting the root password through the account recovery flow locks the attacker out, registering MFA prevents the attacker from returning with a stolen password, and deleting root access keys removes the remaining root credential path; together these steps regain exclusive control of the root user. A is wrong because AWS Support does not suspend a customer's account activity as an incident response service, and waiting on a case leaves the attacker in control. B is wrong because the account is standalone; SCPs require AWS Organizations membership and cannot be created for this account. D is wrong because AWS does not rotate or reissue root credentials on a customer's behalf; recovery is performed by the customer through the verified email flow.

stem: A security team manages 60 AWS accounts through AWS Organizations with all features enabled, and centralized root access management is enabled for the organization. GuardDuty findings and CloudTrail events confirm that credentials in one member account are compromised and that the attacker is actively creating IAM principals and resources in that account. The team must immediately contain all attacker activity in the member account at the organization level, must ensure the attacker cannot regain entry by recovering the member account's root user password, and must leave the incident response team's designated forensics role usable inside the account. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Attach a resource control policy to the compromised account that denies every action so that principals in the account can no longer access any resources.
Remove the compromised account from the organization so that the attacker cannot use it to reach the other accounts, and investigate it as a standalone account.
Assume the OrganizationAccountAccessRole in the member account and delete the IAM users, roles, and access keys that the attacker created before applying any organization-wide controls.
Attach a quarantine SCP to the compromised account that denies all actions except those performed by the incident response team's designated forensics role.
Confirm through centralized root access management that the member account's root credentials are removed, which prevents password recovery for the account's root user.

explanation: D and E are correct. A quarantine SCP attached to the single account is the organization-level containment control: it denies every action for every principal in the account, including any principals the attacker created, while the exception preserves the forensics role's access. Centralized root access management removes member-account root credentials, and confirming that state guarantees the attacker cannot use the root password recovery flow to regain entry. A is wrong because resource control policies govern access to resources for a supported set of services; they cannot deny all of a member account's actions and do not function as a full account quarantine. B is wrong because removing the account from the organization strips away SCPs and centralized controls entirely, giving the attacker more freedom rather than less. C is wrong because deleting attacker artifacts before containment is eradication out of order; the attacker still holds working credentials and can recreate everything that is removed.

stem: A company maintains a dedicated forensics AWS account that is isolated from its workload accounts. During an investigation, a security engineer creates snapshots of the EBS volumes that are attached to a compromised EC2 instance in a workload account. The volumes are encrypted with the AWS managed key for Amazon EBS (aws/ebs). When the engineer attempts to share the snapshots with the forensics account by modifying the snapshot permissions, the operation is not available for these snapshots. The forensic analysts must be able to create volumes from the evidence in the forensics account. Which solution allows the snapshots to be analyzed in the forensics account?

options.text: Copy each snapshot and re-encrypt the copy with a customer managed KMS key, share the copies with the forensics account, and update the key policy so that account can use the key.
Modify the permissions on the original snapshots to add the forensics account ID as an authorized account, and instruct the analysts to create volumes from the shared snapshots in their own account.
Create unencrypted copies of the snapshots, share them with the forensics account, and instruct the analysts to enable encryption by default before restoring the evidence volumes.
Update the key policy on the aws/ebs AWS managed key in the workload account to allow the forensics account to use the key for decrypting the shared snapshots.

explanation: A is correct. Snapshots encrypted with the AWS managed aws/ebs key cannot be shared with other accounts, so the evidence must be copied with re-encryption under a customer managed key; the copies can then be shared with the forensics account, and a key policy statement allows that account to use the key to create volumes from them. B is wrong because sharing is exactly the operation that is unavailable for snapshots encrypted with an AWS managed key; adding the account ID to the originals is not possible. C is wrong because an encrypted snapshot cannot be copied to an unencrypted snapshot, and stripping encryption from evidence would be inappropriate even if it were possible. D is wrong because the key policy of an AWS managed key is controlled by AWS and cannot be edited to grant cross-account access.

stem: After a significant intrusion, a company's legal team informs the security engineer that memory images, disk images exported from EBS snapshots, and collected log files may be presented in court. The artifacts total several terabytes and will be retained for five years. The evidence must be stored so that the company can prove the artifacts have not been altered since collection, so that no principal in the account, including administrators, can modify or delete them during the retention period, and so that every access to the evidence is recorded for the chain-of-custody record. Which storage approach MOST completely meets these requirements?

options.text: Store the artifacts in a versioned S3 bucket, enable MFA delete so that versions cannot be removed without the root user's MFA device, and restrict access with a bucket policy.

Record a cryptographic hash of each artifact at collection, store the artifacts in an S3 bucket that uses Object Lock in compliance mode with a set retention period, and enable CloudTrail data events on the bucket.
Retain the artifacts as EBS snapshots in the security account, tag every snapshot with its case identifier, and use an IAM policy to block snapshot deletion by non-security principals.
Encrypt each artifact with a customer managed KMS key whose key policy grants usage only to the forensics team, and store the artifacts in a private S3 bucket with versioning.

explanation: B is correct. Collection-time hashes let the company prove artifacts are unchanged, Object Lock in compliance mode prevents every principal, including administrators and the root user, from overwriting or deleting the protected objects until the retention period ends, and CloudTrail data events record each access to the evidence for the chain-of-custody record. A is wrong because MFA delete only places version deletion behind the root user's MFA device; the root user can still delete evidence, so the no-principal requirement is unmet and nothing proves integrity. C is wrong because IAM policies can be changed by administrators, after which snapshots can be deleted, and there is no tamper-proof integrity record. D is wrong because encryption protects confidentiality; it does not prevent deletion by privileged principals or demonstrate that artifacts are unaltered.

stem: A company is formalizing its incident response capability after a tabletop exercise revealed that analysts had no safe place to examine compromised workloads. The security team must design an environment for analyzing evidence from compromised EC2 instances, which arrives as EBS snapshots shared from the workload accounts. The company uses AWS Organizations with a security reference architecture that includes a security tooling account. The analysis of potentially malware-infected volumes must not be able to contaminate production networks even if the malware attempts to spread, the environment must be reproducible and available within minutes of an incident being declared, and access must be limited to the forensics team. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a forensic subnet inside each production VPC with a restrictive security group, and have analysts restore the shared snapshots to analysis instances inside that subnet during an investigation.
Use Session Manager to connect directly to each compromised instance and run the analysis tooling in place, avoiding any need to move evidence between the accounts.

Maintain a dedicated forensics account with an isolated VPC that has no internet gateway and no connectivity to other networks, and provision analysis workstations and tooling on demand from infrastructure-as-code templates.
Restore the evidence volumes in the organization's security tooling account alongside the delegated administrator services, and let analysts reach the analysis workstations across the corporate VPN.

explanation: C is correct. A dedicated forensics account keeps the analysis blast radius away from production credentials and networks, an isolated VPC with no internet gateway and no peering or VPN attachments leaves restored malware with no path to spread, and infrastructure-as-code templates make the environment reproducible and available within minutes while IAM in the dedicated account restricts access to the forensics team. A is wrong because a subnet inside a production VPC shares that VPC's route tables and account administrators, so contamination of and interference from production remain possible. B is wrong because analyzing a compromised instance in place alters the evidence, risks tipping off the attacker, and runs trusted tooling on an untrusted host. D is wrong because the security tooling account runs the organization's delegated administrator services that must be protected, and connecting the workstations to the corporate VPN gives restored malware a network path, violating the isolation requirement.

stem: A security engineer must reconstruct every API action taken with a specific access key ID across all 40 accounts in an AWS Organization over the past six months. The organization has an organization trail that has been delivering management events for all accounts to a central Amazon S3 bucket in a log archive account for more than a year, and the engineer has read access to that bucket. The investigation budget is limited, so the solution must be the MOST cost-effective and must avoid copying or ingesting the log data into another service before querying it. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Define an Athena table over the organization trail's S3 location with partition projection for account, Region, and date, and run SQL queries that filter events on the access key ID.
Create a CloudTrail Lake event data store, import the six months of trail files from the S3 bucket, and run CloudTrail Lake SQL queries against the imported events for the access key.
Deploy an OpenSearch Service domain, ingest the six months of CloudTrail objects with an ingestion pipeline, and use dashboard queries to isolate the access key's activity.
Use the CloudTrail console's event history in each of the 40 accounts, filter by the access key identifier, and export the matching events to CSV files for consolidation.

explanation: A is correct. Athena queries the trail files where they already sit in the log archive bucket, partition projection avoids maintaining partition metadata while limiting each query to the relevant accounts and dates, and the cost is per-query data scanning with no ingestion, which satisfies both the cost constraint and the no-copy constraint. B is wrong because importing into CloudTrail Lake copies the data into an event data store and incurs ingestion and retention charges, violating the constraint against ingesting the data elsewhere. C is wrong because an OpenSearch domain adds cluster costs and a full ingestion pipeline for what is a one-time investigation. D is wrong because the console event history covers only the most recent 90 days per account, so a six-month investigation cannot be completed there.

stem: A security engineer deactivated an IAM user's exposed access key after the key was found in a public code repository. Two days later, GuardDuty generates Persistence:IAMUser/AnomalousBehavior findings for the account. A CloudTrail review shows that, during the original exposure window, the exposed key was used to call CreateUser, CreateAccessKey, CreateLoginProfile, and AttachUserPolicy. The engineer realizes that deactivating the exposed key addressed only the attacker's initial access. The account's other pre-existing credentials show no signs of exposure, and the affected IAM user's own permissions have already been reviewed by the security team. Which action should the engineer take next to eradicate the attacker's access?

options.text: Rotate the affected IAM user's remaining credentials once more, enforce MFA on the user, and continue monitoring the new GuardDuty findings for further signs of anomalous behavior in the account.
Search CloudTrail for every write operation the exposed key performed during the exposure window, and remove the IAM users, access keys, login profiles, and policy attachments it created.
Enable IAM Access Analyzer unused access findings for the account and remove any credentials that the analyzer reports as unused after the configured review period ends.
Deploy an AWS Config rule that flags IAM users with directly attached policies and configure its automatic remediation to detach the noncompliant policies that it finds.

explanation: B is correct. The CloudTrail evidence shows the attacker used the initial access to create additional principals and credentials, so eradication requires enumerating everything the exposed key changed during the window and deleting the attacker-created users, keys, login profiles, and policy attachments; the new GuardDuty findings indicate this backdoor access is still in use. A is wrong because the original user's credentials were already contained; rotating them again does not touch the separate principals the attacker created. C is wrong because the attacker's backdoor credentials are actively in use, so unused-access analysis would not flag them, and waiting out a review period leaves the attacker inside. D is wrong because a Config rule about directly attached policies is a general hygiene control; it neither identifies nor removes the specific users and keys the attacker created.

stem: Developers report that a nightly build automation job suddenly began failing with AccessDenied errors overnight. A security engineer investigates the IAM user that the job uses and finds that a policy named AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV3 is now attached to the user, and that the user's access key appears in a public GitHub repository that was indexed by search engines yesterday. The developers ask the engineer to detach the policy immediately so that the nightly builds can resume. The account's CloudTrail trail is enabled, and no other security alerts have fired so far. What should the engineer conclude, and how should the engineer respond?

options.text: GuardDuty attached the policy as an automated remediation after a finding; the engineer should detach it as soon as the related GuardDuty finding has been archived in the management console.
An attacker attached the policy to lock legitimate automation out of the account; the engineer should detach it immediately and reset the IAM user's console password.
AWS attached the policy because the account exceeded service quotas during the build; the engineer should request a quota increase and detach the policy to restore the nightly builds.

AWS attached the quarantine policy after detecting the exposed key; the engineer should keep it attached, deactivate and rotate the key, review CloudTrail for misuse, and detach only after remediation.

explanation: D is correct. AWS attaches the AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine policies to an IAM user when it detects the user's access key exposed publicly, and the policy denies high-risk actions to limit the damage an attacker can do; the correct response is to treat the key as compromised, deactivate and replace it, investigate CloudTrail activity from the exposure window, and remove the policy only once remediation is complete. A is wrong because GuardDuty generates findings; it does not attach quarantine policies to IAM users. B is wrong because the policy is a protective control applied by AWS, not attacker activity, and detaching it before rotating the key restores the attacker's full access. C is wrong because quota issues never result in an IAM quarantine policy, and detaching it without rotating the key reopens the exposure.

stem: GuardDuty generates an UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS finding: temporary credentials issued to the IAM role attached to a public-facing web server's instance profile are being used from an IP address outside AWS. The application team suspects that a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw in the web application allowed the attacker to read credentials from the instance metadata service, which currently allows IMDSv1. The web server must continue serving traffic during the response, and a code fix for the SSRF flaw will take the application team several days to deliver. Which combination of actions revokes the attacker's access and prevents the same theft from recurring? (Choose two.)

options.text: Remove the IAM role from the instance profile so the credentials the attacker exfiltrated stop being honored by AWS as soon as the association is gone.
Create a new access key pair for the role, distribute it to the web server, and deactivate the key pair the attacker exfiltrated from the metadata service.
Attach a policy to the role that denies all actions for sessions issued before the current time, allowing the instance to retrieve fresh, unaffected credentials automatically.
Require IMDSv2 on the instance and set the metadata response hop limit to 1, blocking metadata retrieval through the application-layer SSRF request path.
Add deny entries for the attacker's IP address to the network ACL on the web server's subnet to block further use of the stolen credentials.

explanation: C and D are correct. The revocation policy immediately denies every session issued before its timestamp, which cuts off the exfiltrated credentials while the instance transparently obtains new, working credentials from its instance profile; enforcing IMDSv2 with a hop limit of 1 defeats the SSRF vector, because the required token exchange cannot be completed through forwarded application-layer requests, protecting the instance until the code fix ships. A is wrong because removing the role breaks the running application, and credentials that were already issued remain valid until they expire even after the association is removed. B is wrong because IAM roles do not have access key pairs to rotate; role credentials are generated automatically by AWS. E is wrong because the stolen credentials work from any internet address, so blocking a single IP address revokes nothing.

stem: A security team suspects that compromised EC2 instances in a private subnet are exfiltrating data to an external endpoint over a nonstandard protocol. To confirm the incident's scope, the team must capture and inspect full packet payloads from the suspect instances during the ongoing activity, and analysts must not install any software or agent on the compromised instances, because doing so could alert the attacker and alter evidence. The suspect instances run on current-generation Nitro-based instance types and must remain in service while the evidence is gathered. The capture must be analyzed in an isolated forensic environment inside the same VPC. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable VPC Flow Logs on the suspect instances' network interfaces with all available fields and deliver the logs to an S3 bucket for the analysts to inspect.
Enable GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring on the instances so the security agent records the processes and network activity that are responsible for the suspicious connections.
Configure VPC Traffic Mirroring sessions on the suspect instances' network interfaces that send mirrored traffic to a target appliance running packet-analysis tools in an isolated forensic subnet.
Enable Route 53 Resolver query logging for the VPC and analyze the logged lookups to identify the destination domains that the instances are contacting.

explanation: C is correct. Traffic Mirroring copies full packets from the suspect network interfaces to a mirror target without touching the instances themselves, so analysts receive complete payloads in an isolated forensic subnet while the attacker sees no change on the compromised hosts. A is wrong because flow logs record metadata such as addresses, ports, and byte counts; they never contain packet payloads, so the protocol and the exfiltrated content cannot be analyzed. B is wrong because Runtime Monitoring requires deploying the security agent onto the compromised instances, which the requirements forbid, and it reports behavioral telemetry rather than full packet captures. D is wrong because Resolver query logging shows only DNS lookups, which cannot confirm what data left over a nonstandard protocol.

stem: A security engineer is hardening a public subnet that hosts internet-facing EC2 web servers. The engineer replaces the subnet's default network ACL with a custom network ACL that has an inbound rule allowing TCP port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and an outbound rule allowing TCP port 443 to 0.0.0.0/0, with all other traffic denied in both directions. The instances' security group allows inbound TCP port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and all outbound traffic. After the change, external clients report that HTTPS connections to the web servers hang and time out. The engineer confirms that client requests are reaching the instances and that the application is healthy. Which change restores connectivity while keeping the network ACL restrictive?

options.text: Add an outbound network ACL rule that allows TCP ports 1024-65535 to 0.0.0.0/0, because the servers' responses return to the clients on ephemeral ports.
Add an inbound network ACL rule that allows TCP ports 1024-65535 from 0.0.0.0/0 so that the clients' ephemeral source ports are accepted into the subnet.
Add an outbound rule to the instances' security group that allows TCP ports 1024-65535, because security groups must explicitly permit response traffic back to clients.
Change the outbound network ACL rule to allow TCP port 80 in addition to port 443 so that redirect responses can also reach the requesting clients.

explanation: A is correct. Network ACLs are stateless, so response packets are evaluated independently of the inbound request. Clients connect from ephemeral source ports in the 1024-65535 range, and the servers' responses are addressed back to those ports, which the current outbound rule (443 only) denies. B is wrong because inbound requests already arrive on destination port 443 and are allowed; the failure is in the outbound direction, not inbound. C is wrong because security groups are stateful and automatically allow return traffic for established connections, and this group already allows all outbound traffic anyway. D is wrong because responses to an HTTPS request travel back to the client's ephemeral port, not to port 80 or 443, so adding port 80 does not restore connectivity.

stem: An internet-facing application runs on EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer that has client IP preservation enabled. The security team identifies a single source IP address that is continuously scanning the application and attempting brute-force logins against its authentication endpoint. The team must block all traffic from this IP address before it reaches the instances, must continue to serve every other client without interruption, and does not want to modify the application or introduce additional services into the architecture. The instances run in subnets that use the default network ACL, and their security group allows inbound TCP port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Which action meets these requirements?

options.text: Add a deny rule to the instances' security group that blocks all traffic from the attacker's IP address while keeping the existing allow rules in place for every other client.
Add an inbound deny entry for the attacker's IP address to the subnets' network ACL, using a rule number lower than the entry that allows the traffic.
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the Network Load Balancer and add an IP set match rule that blocks requests from the attacker's IP address.
Remove the rule allowing TCP port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 from the security group and add individual allow rules for each known legitimate client range.

explanation: B is correct. Network ACLs support explicit deny entries and evaluate rules in ascending rule-number order, so a low-numbered deny for the attacker's IP address drops that traffic at the subnet boundary while every other client continues to match the existing allow entries. A is wrong because security groups only support allow rules; there is no deny rule to add. C is wrong because AWS WAF cannot be associated with a Network Load Balancer; it attaches to resources such as CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers, and API Gateway stages. D is wrong because a public application cannot enumerate every legitimate client range, so this change would cut off unknown legitimate users, violating the requirement to serve all other clients.

stem: A retail company's public web application is served through an Amazon CloudFront distribution that has an AWS WAF web ACL attached. A promotional signup form on the site is being flooded with automated submissions. Analysis shows that the abusive requests originate from thousands of rotating residential IP addresses, and that many legitimate customers share IP addresses because they connect through carrier-grade NAT. The business requires that real customers can still submit the form, even if they must complete an additional verification step, that automated submissions are stopped, and that the control applies only to the signup path rather than the whole site. What should the security engineer configure in AWS WAF?

options.text: Create a rate-based rule that blocks any source IP address exceeding a low request threshold, with a scope-down statement that limits the rule to the signup path.
Create a geographic match rule in the web ACL that blocks the countries currently generating the highest volume of automated submissions to the promotional signup form.
Create a rule with a URI-path match statement for the signup path and set the rule action to CAPTCHA so clients submitting there must solve a challenge first.
Create an IP set match rule that blocks the observed bot addresses, refreshed by a scheduled Lambda function that parses the WAF logs.

explanation: C is correct. The CAPTCHA action challenges every client that requests the signup path: automated submitters cannot solve the puzzle while real customers complete it and proceed, which matches the business requirement that humans may continue after an extra step, and the URI-path match statement confines the control to the signup path. A is wrong because customers behind carrier-grade NAT share source addresses, so a low IP-based threshold would block groups of legitimate users, while the attackers' rotating addresses stay under any per-IP threshold. B is wrong because blocking whole countries cuts off legitimate customers and the rotating residential addresses span many geographies. D is wrong because the bot addresses rotate continuously, so an IP set is stale the moment it is written and requires constant custom maintenance.

stem: A security engineer manages an AWS WAF web ACL that protects a developer portal behind an Application Load Balancer. The web ACL includes the AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet rule group with all rules using their default actions. After a new feature allows users to paste code snippets into a form, the portal begins returning 403 errors for legitimate submissions. The WAF logs show that a single rule inside the managed rule group is responsible for blocking these requests, while the other rules in the group continue to catch genuinely malicious traffic. The engineer must stop the false positives while keeping every other protection in the managed rule group fully enforced. Which action meets these requirements?

options.text: Remove AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet from the web ACL and replace it with a set of custom rules that reproduce only the protections the portal needs.
Set the override action of the entire managed rule group to Count so that its rules record matches in the logs without blocking any requests.
Add a higher-priority custom allow rule that matches the form's URI path so that requests to that path skip evaluation by the managed rule group.
Override only the specific rule that generates the blocks to Count within the managed rule group, leaving the remaining rules in the group enforced.

explanation: D is correct. AWS WAF lets you override the action of individual rules inside a managed rule group; setting just the offending rule to Count stops its false-positive blocks while every other rule in the group keeps its blocking behavior, which is exactly the stated requirement. A is wrong because rebuilding the managed protections as custom rules discards AWS-maintained rule updates and adds large, ongoing maintenance effort. B is wrong because overriding the whole group to Count disables enforcement of every rule in it, removing the protections that are still catching real attacks. C is wrong because an allow rule that short-circuits evaluation for the form's path exempts that path from all inspection, leaving it open to genuine injection attacks.

stem: A consumer web application behind an Application Load Balancer with an AWS WAF web ACL is experiencing credential-stuffing attacks. Distributed clients submit large volumes of stolen username and password pairs to the application's /login endpoint, and some of the submitted pairs come from publicly known credential breaches. The security team must throttle high-volume sources that target the login endpoint specifically, and must also detect and block login attempts that use credentials known to be compromised. Traffic to the rest of the site must remain unaffected by the new controls. Which combination of AWS WAF configurations meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Associate the AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList rule group with the web ACL so that requests from IP addresses flagged by Amazon threat intelligence are blocked across the site.
Enable AWS Shield Advanced on the Application Load Balancer so that the Shield Response Team applies mitigations when login traffic exceeds its normal baseline.
Create a geographic match rule that blocks countries where the company has no legitimate user base to reduce the automated login volume across the application.
Create a rate-based rule with a scope-down statement matching POST requests to the /login path so only clients exceeding the threshold on that endpoint are blocked.
Add the AWSManagedRulesATPRuleSet rule group configured with the login path and credential field locations so requests using compromised credential pairs are blocked.

explanation: D and E are correct. A rate-based rule with a scope-down statement counts and throttles only the sources hammering POST /login, leaving the rest of the site untouched, and the account takeover prevention (ATP) managed rule group inspects the configured username and password fields against AWS's stolen-credential database, blocking attempts that use breached pairs. A is wrong because the IP reputation list applies site-wide, does not target the login path, and does nothing about breached credentials. B is wrong because Shield Advanced addresses DDoS availability events, not authentication abuse with valid-looking requests. C is wrong because geographic blocking is a site-wide blunt control that neither throttles per-endpoint volume nor identifies compromised credentials.

stem: A financial services company runs workloads in private subnets that must initiate outbound HTTPS connections only to an approved list of vendor domains. Compliance requires the control to be enforced in the network path itself, so that a compromised instance that bypasses the VPC DNS resolver and connects directly to a destination IP address is still prevented from reaching unapproved endpoints. The security team also requires that every denied connection attempt is logged for investigation. All egress traffic from the private subnets already flows through a dedicated inspection subnet before reaching a NAT gateway, and the team can add inspection components to that path. Which solution enforces these requirements?

options.text: Deploy AWS Network Firewall in the egress path with a stateful rule group that allow-lists the approved domains through TLS SNI inspection, denies all other outbound traffic, and sends alerts to firewall logs.

Associate a Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule group with the VPC that permits DNS queries only for the approved vendor domains, blocks resolution of every other domain name, and logs each blocked query.
Configure the workloads' security groups with outbound rules that reference the approved vendor domain names so that only connections matching those domains are permitted to leave.
Create network ACL outbound allow entries for the IP address ranges that each vendor publishes and deny all other outbound traffic from the private subnets.

explanation: A is correct. AWS Network Firewall sits in the packet path, so its stateful domain allow-list, evaluated against the TLS SNI of each outbound session, is enforced even when an instance skips DNS and connects straight to an IP address; non-matching traffic is dropped by the default-deny rule and logged through the firewall's alert logs. B is wrong because DNS Firewall controls only name resolution; a process that connects directly to an IP address never issues a query, so the stated bypass defeats it. C is wrong because security group rules cannot reference domain names, only CIDR blocks, prefix lists, and security group IDs. D is wrong because vendor IP ranges change frequently, network ACLs are capped at a small number of entries, and stateless ACLs provide no domain awareness or connection logging.

stem: A security team suspects that malware on several EC2 instances is using outbound HTTPS connections to popular, legitimately categorized domains to blend command-and-control traffic into normal activity. The team already routes all egress traffic through AWS Network Firewall and enforces domain-based filtering, but the malicious payloads travel inside TLS sessions to domains that the existing filter allows. The team must now inspect the decrypted payloads of outbound TLS sessions against intrusion-prevention signatures before the traffic leaves the network. The instances can be configured to trust an internal certificate authority, and the workloads must keep functioning normally. Which approach meets the requirement?

options.text: Enable detailed flow logging on the firewall and analyze the captured flow records with Amazon Athena to identify command-and-control patterns inside the outbound traffic.

Add a TLS inspection configuration to the Network Firewall that references a CA certificate in AWS Certificate Manager so the firewall decrypts outbound sessions, evaluates stateful signatures, and re-encrypts the traffic.
Attach an AWS WAF web ACL that uses managed rule groups to the VPC's egress path so that the bodies of outbound HTTPS requests are inspected for malicious content before they leave the network.
Enable stateless rule inspection on the firewall for TCP port 443 with packet payload match conditions to detect malicious byte patterns inside the encrypted packets.

explanation: B is correct. A TLS inspection configuration lets Network Firewall act as an in-path proxy: using the CA certificate from ACM it terminates the outbound TLS session, runs the decrypted stream through its stateful intrusion-prevention rules, then re-encrypts toward the destination, and the instances' trust in the internal CA keeps applications working. A is wrong because flow logs contain connection metadata such as addresses, ports, and byte counts, never payload content. C is wrong because AWS WAF associates with resources like CloudFront, ALBs, and API Gateway to inspect inbound web requests; it cannot be inserted into a VPC's egress path. D is wrong because the payload bytes of a TLS session are encrypted, so stateless pattern matching on port 443 packets cannot see the malicious content.

stem: A security engineer is adding AWS Network Firewall to an existing VPC that has an internet gateway, public subnets that host NAT gateways and an Application Load Balancer, and private subnets with application instances across two Availability Zones. The requirement is that all traffic flowing between the internet gateway and the public subnets is inspected by the firewall in both directions, and the application architecture must not change. The design must remain functional if one Availability Zone becomes unavailable. The engineer has already created the firewall policy and rule groups and now needs to complete the network integration. Which set of changes completes the deployment?

options.text: Create the firewall endpoints inside the existing public subnets and update the instances' security groups so that their traffic is directed to the firewall endpoints for inspection.
Attach the VPC to a transit gateway with appliance mode enabled and move the firewall into a separate inspection VPC that all internet-bound traffic must traverse.

Create a dedicated firewall subnet in each Availability Zone, point the public subnets' default routes at the firewall endpoints, and associate an internet gateway ingress route table that sends the public subnet CIDRs to the endpoints.

Deploy the firewall endpoints into the existing private subnets and update the private subnets' route tables so that all traffic destined for the internet gateway is forced through the firewall endpoints before it can reach the public subnets.

explanation: C is correct. The distributed deployment model places firewall endpoints in small dedicated subnets in each Availability Zone for resilience, sends outbound traffic there via the public subnets' default routes, and uses internet gateway ingress routing to force inbound traffic for the public subnet CIDRs through the same endpoints, achieving bidirectional inspection with route changes only. A is wrong because firewall endpoints must live in their own subnets whose route tables differ from the workloads', and security groups cannot redirect traffic to an endpoint. B is wrong because a centralized transit gateway inspection VPC is a multi-VPC pattern that re-architects this single VPC unnecessarily and does not inspect traffic between this VPC's internet gateway and its public subnets. D is wrong because the traffic to inspect flows between the internet gateway and the public subnets; placing endpoints behind the private route tables leaves the load balancer's internet traffic uninspected.

stem: During a threat-hunting exercise, a security team discovers that malware inside several VPCs attempts to resolve domain names associated with DNS tunneling and data exfiltration, along with domains linked to botnet command-and-control infrastructure. The affected workloads use the default VPC resolver at the .2 address for all DNS lookups. The team must block resolution of these known-malicious domain categories across many VPCs, must continue to allow all other DNS queries, and must receive alerts when a blocked query occurs. The team prefers AWS managed threat intelligence over maintaining its own domain lists and wants minimal operational overhead. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy AWS Network Firewall endpoints in every VPC with stateless rules that drop all UDP and TCP traffic on port 53 that leaves each VPC, and monitor the dropped connection attempts through the firewall's flow logs.
Enable Amazon GuardDuty in every account so that DNS queries to known-malicious domains generate findings, and notify the security team through EventBridge when findings appear.
Add outbound network ACL deny entries for the IP ranges behind the malicious domains on every subnet, and update the entries whenever the threat intelligence feed changes.
Associate Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule groups that use the AWS managed domain lists with each VPC, set the rule action to block, and alert on blocked queries from the DNS Firewall logs.

explanation: D is correct. Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall filters queries at the VPC resolver itself, which is exactly where these workloads resolve names; the AWS managed domain lists cover malware, botnet command and control, and DNS tunneling domains without the team curating anything, the block action stops resolution while other queries pass, and query logging of blocked hits drives alerting. A is wrong because queries to the .2 resolver are answered inside the VPC and never traverse the firewall, and dropping all port 53 egress would break any legitimate external resolution without blocking the actual exfiltration path. B is wrong because GuardDuty is a detection service; it raises findings but cannot block a DNS query. C is wrong because domains map to constantly changing IP ranges, network ACL entries are limited in number, and blocking resolved IPs does not stop the DNS-based exfiltration itself.

stem: A company processes regulated data on EC2 instances in a VPC that reaches Amazon S3 through a gateway VPC endpoint. The security team must establish a two-way perimeter. First, identities operating inside the VPC must be unable to send data to S3 buckets that are owned outside the company's AWS Organizations organization. Second, the company's data buckets must reject any request that does not arrive through the VPC endpoint, with a documented exception for one administrative role that is used from the corporate network. The security team wants the two controls to operate independently so that a failure of either one does not collapse the whole perimeter. Which combination of controls meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Attach an endpoint policy to the gateway endpoint that allows S3 actions only when the aws:ResourceOrgID condition key matches the company's organization ID.
Attach a security group to the gateway endpoint that permits HTTPS traffic only between the application subnets and the Amazon S3 prefix list for the Region.
Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level so that data in the buckets cannot be shared outside the organization by any principal in the account.
Add bucket policies to the data buckets that deny requests when aws:sourceVpce does not match the endpoint ID, with a condition that exempts the administrative role.
Enable Amazon Macie in the account so that sensitive objects that are copied to buckets outside the organization generate findings for the security team to review.

explanation: A and D are correct. The endpoint policy governs everything that leaves the VPC toward S3, and the aws:ResourceOrgID condition confines those requests to buckets owned inside the organization, blocking exfiltration to attacker-owned buckets. The bucket-policy deny on aws:sourceVpce makes the data buckets unreachable except through the endpoint, and the exemption clause preserves the documented administrative access from the corporate network. B is wrong because gateway endpoints do not support security groups; they are route-table targets, not network interfaces. C is wrong because Block Public Access prevents anonymous and public access, not authenticated uploads to an external account's bucket or access that bypasses the endpoint. E is wrong because Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data in the company's own buckets; it is detective, cannot see external buckets, and blocks nothing.

stem: An application that runs in private subnets processes objects stored in Amazon S3 buckets in the same Region. The VPC currently sends S3 traffic through a NAT gateway, and a recent architecture review requires that traffic to Amazon S3 no longer traverse the internet or any NAT device. The solution must not introduce hourly charges or per-gigabyte data processing charges for the S3 connectivity itself, and the security team wants the option to later restrict which buckets are reachable by attaching a policy to the connection point. The application's request volume to Amazon S3 is high and steady throughout the day. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, add the endpoint's prefix list route to the private subnets' route tables, and attach an endpoint policy to control which buckets are reachable.
Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 with private DNS enabled so that the application's S3 traffic uses elastic network interfaces inside the private subnets.
Keep the existing NAT gateway path and attach a network ACL to the private subnets that allows outbound HTTPS traffic only to the IP ranges in the Amazon S3 prefix list published for the Region.
Enable Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration on the buckets so that the application's traffic rides the AWS edge network instead of the public internet path through the NAT gateway.

explanation: A is correct. A gateway endpoint keeps S3 traffic on the AWS network via a route-table prefix list entry, has no hourly or data processing charge, and supports an endpoint policy that can later restrict the reachable buckets, satisfying every stated constraint. B is wrong because interface endpoints work but bill per endpoint-hour and per gigabyte processed, violating the cost constraint when a free gateway endpoint suffices. C is wrong because traffic still flows through the NAT gateway, which the review prohibits, and the NAT data processing charges remain. D is wrong because Transfer Acceleration changes the edge path for uploads and downloads but the traffic still leaves through the NAT gateway and the public S3 endpoint, and it adds per-gigabyte acceleration fees.

stem: A company routes all AWS Secrets Manager API calls from its VPC through an interface VPC endpoint. During a design review, the security team identifies an exfiltration risk: if an attacker achieves code execution on an instance in the VPC, the attacker could configure credentials from an unrelated AWS account that the attacker controls and call Secrets Manager through the endpoint to move data into that account. The team must ensure that only IAM principals belonging to the company's AWS Organizations organization can make API calls through the endpoint. The solution must not require changes to application code or to individual secret resource policies. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Modify the security group attached to the endpoint's network interfaces so that only the application subnets' CIDR ranges are allowed to send HTTPS traffic to the endpoint.
Attach an endpoint policy to the interface endpoint that denies all Secrets Manager actions unless the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key matches the company's organization ID.
Add a resource policy to every secret in the account that grants access to the company's IAM roles and explicitly denies requests made by any other principal.
Disable private DNS on the interface endpoint so that callers must use endpoint-specific DNS names, which prevents unknown credentials from resolving the service hostname.

explanation: B is correct. An endpoint policy is evaluated for every request that transits the endpoint regardless of which account's credentials sign it, so a deny conditioned on aws:PrincipalOrgID stops principals outside the organization, including the attacker's foreign-account credentials, without touching application code or secret policies. A is wrong because the attacker is already executing code inside the application subnets, so a CIDR-based security group rule permits exactly the traffic that must be stopped. C is wrong because the attacker calls Secrets Manager against resources in the attacker's own account; policies on the company's secrets are never evaluated for that request, and the option also violates the constraint against editing secret policies. D is wrong because DNS naming is not an access control; the attacker can simply use the endpoint-specific hostname or the endpoint's IP addresses.

stem: A software-as-a-service provider hosts a REST API on EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer in its production VPC. Dozens of enterprise customers want to call the API from their own VPCs without sending traffic over the public internet. Many customer VPCs use CIDR ranges that overlap with the provider's address space. The provider must approve each customer individually before connectivity is established, must restrict access to specific customer AWS accounts, and must ensure that customers cannot reach any other resource inside the provider's VPC. The provider expects to onboard additional customers every month and wants onboarding to stay simple. Which solution should the provider implement?

options.text: Establish a separate VPC peering connection with each customer VPC and use restrictive route table entries and security groups to limit which of the provider's internal addresses each customer is able to reach.
Attach the provider and customer VPCs to a shared transit gateway through AWS Resource Access Manager and advertise only the API subnet's route to the customer attachments.
Create a VPC endpoint service backed by the Network Load Balancer with acceptance required, add the customers' AWS principals to the allow list, and have each customer create an interface endpoint.
Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection from each customer VPC to the provider VPC and publish the API through the tunnels with routes restricted to the API subnet.

explanation: C is correct. AWS PrivateLink is built for this pattern: the endpoint service exposes only the Network Load Balancer, so customers can reach nothing else in the provider VPC; overlapping CIDRs do not matter because no routing between the VPCs occurs; the principal allow list restricts which AWS accounts may connect; and acceptance-required gives per-customer approval. A is wrong because VPC peering cannot be established between VPCs with overlapping CIDR ranges and exposes the network rather than a single service. B is wrong because a transit gateway also requires non-overlapping routes and connects networks, giving customers broader reachability than one API. D is wrong because Site-to-Site VPN tunnels traverse the public internet, conflict with overlapping address space, and create per-customer operational burden.

stem: A company exposes a partner-facing API through an existing Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener. Partners connect from their own data centers over the internet. A new contract requires that every partner request present a client certificate issued by the company's private certificate authority in AWS Private CA, that any request without a valid and currently unrevoked client certificate is rejected before it reaches the application targets, and that the application code is not modified to perform certificate validation. The company wants to keep the existing load balancer rather than introduce a new entry point. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable mutual TLS on the HTTPS listener in passthrough mode so that the load balancer forwards the client certificate in headers to the targets for validation.
Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer TLS listener and terminate the mutual TLS handshake on the application instances themselves.

Add an AWS WAF web ACL to the existing load balancer with a rule statement that inspects each request and blocks any request that does not carry the partner's client certificate thumbprint in a custom header.

Enable mutual TLS on the HTTPS listener in verify mode with a trust store that contains the private CA bundle and a certificate revocation list so invalid certificates are rejected at the load balancer.

explanation: D is correct. ALB mutual TLS in verify mode authenticates the client certificate against the trust store's CA bundle during the handshake and consults the attached certificate revocation list, so requests with missing, invalid, or revoked certificates are rejected at the load balancer with no application changes. A is wrong because passthrough mode performs no validation at the load balancer; it merely forwards certificate data in headers and leaves verification to the application, which the contract forbids. B is wrong because it discards the existing entry point and pushes the mTLS handshake onto the application instances, which is exactly the code-level validation the requirement excludes. C is wrong because headers are attacker-controlled input; AWS WAF cannot participate in the TLS handshake, so a spoofed thumbprint header defeats the check.

stem: A company serves a web application through an Amazon CloudFront distribution that has an AWS WAF web ACL attached. The origin is an internet-facing Application Load Balancer. A security review finds that attackers who discover the load balancer's public DNS name can send requests to it directly, bypassing CloudFront and every WAF protection. The security team must ensure that the load balancer processes only requests that arrived through the company's own CloudFront distribution, and the controls must not depend on manually tracking published IP address ranges. The team also wants layered controls rather than a single point of enforcement, and the load balancer must remain internet-facing. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create network ACL deny entries on the load balancer's subnets for all sources except the CloudFront ranges in the ip-ranges.json document, updating the entries when the ranges change.
Update the load balancer's security group so that inbound HTTPS is allowed only from the AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront origin-facing servers.
Enable origin access control (OAC) on the CloudFront origin so that the distribution signs its origin requests and the load balancer rejects traffic that is not signed.
Configure CloudFront to add a custom header with a secret value to origin requests, and reject requests without that header using a listener rule or a WAF rule on the load balancer.
Require CloudFront signed URLs on the distribution's cache behaviors so that requests sent directly to the load balancer fail the signature validation.

explanation: B and D are correct. The AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront origin-facing servers is maintained by AWS, so a security group rule referencing it restricts the load balancer to CloudFront's infrastructure at the network layer with no manual IP tracking, and the secret custom header proves the request came through the company's own distribution rather than any CloudFront tenant, enforced by a listener or WAF rule. A is wrong because network ACLs cannot reference managed prefix lists and hand-maintained IP entries violate the no-manual-tracking requirement. C is wrong because OAC signs requests to origins such as S3 and Lambda function URLs; it is not available for Application Load Balancer origins. E is wrong because signed URLs are validated by CloudFront at the edge, so a request sent straight to the load balancer never encounters that check.

stem: A compliance audit of an internet-facing Application Load Balancer finds that clients can successfully negotiate TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 sessions with the load balancer's HTTPS listener. Company policy requires that the load balancer accept only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 connections and only cipher suites that provide forward secrecy. The fix must be applied at the point where TLS is terminated. The targets receive plain HTTP from the load balancer over the private network and must not be modified, and the certificate configuration must remain unchanged. The change must not interrupt service for clients that already use modern TLS versions. What should the security engineer do?

options.text: Update the HTTPS listener to use a predefined security policy such as ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 that limits negotiation to TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 with forward-secrecy cipher suites.
Attach an AWS WAF web ACL to the load balancer with a rule that inspects each request's TLS version attribute and blocks values lower than TLS 1.2.
Configure the target group's protocol settings to require TLS 1.2 or later so that the load balancer refuses older protocol versions offered by connecting clients.
Modify the load balancer's security group so that inbound connections on port 443 are accepted only from clients that support modern TLS protocol versions.

explanation: A is correct. The listener's security policy is exactly the control that governs which TLS protocol versions and cipher suites the load balancer will negotiate; selecting a TLS 1.3/1.2 policy with forward-secrecy suites enforces the requirement at the termination point without touching targets or certificates. B is wrong because AWS WAF evaluates requests after the TLS handshake has already completed and has no rule statement for rejecting handshake protocol versions. C is wrong because target group settings govern the connection between the load balancer and its targets, which here is plain HTTP on the private side, not the client-facing handshake. D is wrong because security groups filter on addresses, ports, and protocols at layers 3 and 4 and cannot inspect or act on TLS version negotiation.

stem: A company serves a static website from an Amazon S3 bucket through an Amazon CloudFront distribution that has an AWS WAF web ACL attached. A penetration test reveals that the site's content can be fetched directly from S3 URLs, which bypasses CloudFront and all of the WAF protections. The company is also migrating the bucket's objects to SSE-KMS encryption with a customer managed key, and the chosen solution must continue to work after that migration. The company must ensure that the content can be retrieved only through the CloudFront distribution, and it wants to prevent any future objects from being exposed publicly. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a CloudFront origin access identity (OAI), grant it read access in the bucket policy, and remove all other principals' access to the bucket's objects.

Configure an origin access control (OAC) on the distribution, update the bucket policy to allow the CloudFront service principal only when aws:SourceArn matches the distribution, and enable S3 Block Public Access.

Add a bucket policy condition that allows the s3:GetObject action only when the aws:Referer header of the request matches a long secret value that the CloudFront distribution is configured to add to its origin requests.
Require CloudFront signed URLs for all cache behaviors on the distribution so that requests made directly to the S3 bucket fail the URL signature validation.

explanation: B is correct. Origin access control signs origin requests with SigV4, supports objects encrypted with SSE-KMS customer managed keys, and combines with a bucket policy that admits only the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal scoped by aws:SourceArn to this distribution; Block Public Access then guarantees no direct path remains. A is wrong because the legacy origin access identity does not support SigV4 signing for SSE-KMS-encrypted objects, so it breaks after the encryption migration. C is wrong because the Referer header is client-supplied and trivially spoofed, so anyone who learns the value regains direct access. D is wrong because signed URLs are enforced by CloudFront at the edge; a request that goes straight to the S3 URL never passes through CloudFront, so the bucket itself stays exposed unless its own policy is locked down.

stem: A company's security standard requires that every EC2 instance launched anywhere in its AWS Organizations organization enforces IMDSv2 so that instance metadata can be retrieved only with session tokens. The company has already configured Region-level instance metadata defaults to require IMDSv2 in its major accounts, but engineers can still pass metadata options at launch time that re-enable IMDSv1 on a new instance. The security team must guarantee that no new instance can launch with IMDSv1 available, regardless of which account, tool, launch template, or console workflow is used. Existing noncompliant instances are being handled by a separate remediation effort. Which solution meets this requirement?

options.text: Update the organization's approved AMIs so that the IMDSv2 requirement is embedded in each image, and direct all teams to launch instances only from the approved AMIs.
Create an AWS Config organization rule that flags instances with IMDSv1 enabled and pair it with an automatic remediation action that modifies the instance metadata options.
Attach a service control policy that denies ec2:RunInstances whenever the ec2:MetadataHttpTokens condition key does not equal required, so noncompliant launch requests fail.
Configure the instance metadata defaults to require IMDSv2 in every remaining Region and account so that all newly launched instances inherit the token requirement.

explanation: C is correct. A service control policy is a preventive guardrail evaluated on every launch request in every member account; denying ec2:RunInstances unless ec2:MetadataHttpTokens equals required makes an IMDSv1-permitting launch fail no matter which tool, template, or console path issued it. A is wrong because an AMI's metadata configuration is only a starting point; a launch-time metadata-options parameter overrides it, which is the exact gap described. B is wrong because AWS Config is detective: the instance launches with IMDSv1 enabled and stays exposed until the remediation runs, so the guarantee of never launching noncompliant is not met. D is wrong because the stem states that Region-level defaults are already being bypassed by explicit launch parameters; extending defaults to more Regions does not remove that override.

stem: A payments company must decrypt and process card-network signing keys on EC2 instances. Security requirements state that plaintext key material may exist only inside an isolated compute environment that has no persistent storage, no interactive administrator access, and no external network connectivity, and that even administrators with root access on the host instance must be unable to read the key material from memory. AWS KMS must release the data key only after cryptographically verifying the identity of the isolated environment that requests it. The company wants to keep the workload on EC2 rather than adopt a different compute service. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Run the decryption workload on an EC2 Dedicated Host so the hardware is not shared with other customers, and restrict interactive access to a minimal administrator group.
Run the workload in a container with a hardened seccomp profile and a read-only file system, and scope the task's IAM role to permit only the single KMS decrypt action.
Store the key material on an encrypted EBS volume protected by a customer managed KMS key and require IMDSv2 so instance credentials cannot be stolen through SSRF.
Process the keys inside an AWS Nitro Enclave and add a kms:RecipientAttestation condition to the KMS key policy so that Decrypt succeeds only for the enclave's attested image measurements.

explanation: D is correct. A Nitro Enclave is a hardened, isolated environment carved from the parent instance with no persistent storage, no interactive access, and no external networking, and its memory is inaccessible even to root on the parent. Cryptographic attestation lets the KMS key policy's kms:RecipientAttestation condition release the data key only to an enclave whose measured image matches, satisfying the verification requirement. A is wrong because a Dedicated Host isolates hardware from other AWS customers, not key material from the company's own root administrators. B is wrong because seccomp and read-only file systems restrict system calls and writes, but a root user on the host can still inspect the container's process memory. C is wrong because EBS encryption protects data at rest; once decrypted for processing, the plaintext sits in ordinary instance memory readable by privileged users.

stem: An internal audit finds that many running EC2 instances in a production account still allow IMDSv1, and that the Auto Scaling groups managing the fleet use launch templates that leave instance metadata options at their original values. The security team must require IMDSv2 session tokens on the currently running instances without terminating or replacing them, and must also ensure that every instance the Auto Scaling groups launch in the future requires IMDSv2 from the moment it boots. The account contains several hundred affected instances, so the per-instance work must be scriptable. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Update the instances' security groups to block outbound traffic to 169.254.169.254 so that the metadata service can be reached only by clients presenting session tokens.
Uninstall the metadata service package from the running instances' operating systems and rebuild the Auto Scaling groups' AMI without the package included.
Run modify-instance-metadata-options against each running instance to set HttpTokens to required, driving the change with a script or Systems Manager Automation.
Set HttpPutResponseHopLimit to 0 in the launch templates so that IMDSv1 requests can no longer receive responses from the instance metadata service.
Create a new launch template version that sets HttpTokens to required in the metadata options, and update the Auto Scaling groups to use the new version.
