explanation: C and E are correct. The modify-instance-metadata-options API changes HttpTokens to required on a running instance with no restart or replacement, and it scripts cleanly across hundreds of instances; a new launch template version with HttpTokens set to required, adopted by the Auto Scaling groups, makes every future instance enforce IMDSv2 at boot. A is wrong because instance metadata traffic to the link-local address is handled by the instance itself and is not evaluated by security groups, so no such filtering occurs. B is wrong because the metadata service is provided by the EC2 platform, not an operating system package, and removing access entirely would break IAM role credential delivery. D is wrong because 0 is not a valid hop limit and the hop limit controls how far responses travel, not which protocol version is accepted.

stem: A company operates several hundred EC2 instances across two Regions running Amazon Linux and Windows Server. Security policy requires that operating system patches classified as critical are installed within seven days of release, that patching runs only during an approved weekly change window, and that the security team can produce per-instance compliance evidence for auditors on demand. All of the instances are already managed nodes in AWS Systems Manager. The team wants the approach with the least ongoing operational effort and does not want to build or maintain custom patching scripts. The instances must stay in service during patching whenever possible. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Create Patch Manager patch baselines that auto-approve critical patches, register the instances with maintenance windows that run the patch task weekly, and use Patch Manager compliance reporting as the audit evidence.

Use Amazon Inspector to continuously scan the instances for missing operating system patches, and have the operations team apply each of the reported patches manually on every instance during the weekly change window.
Create an EventBridge scheduled rule that invokes a Lambda function to run operating-system-specific update commands on each instance through Run Command documents the team maintains.
Rebuild the fleet's AMIs every week with EC2 Image Builder pipelines that include the latest patches, and replace all of the running instances after each successful build.

explanation: A is correct. Patch baselines with auto-approval rules pick up critical patches within the required timeline without human curation, maintenance windows confine execution to the approved weekly change window, and Patch Manager records per-instance compliance state that answers the audit requirement, all as managed features with minimal effort. B is wrong because Amazon Inspector identifies missing patches but does not install them, and manual patching of several hundred instances every week is the opposite of low operational effort. C is wrong because it recreates what Patch Manager already provides using custom scripts the team must maintain, which the requirements exclude, and it produces no built-in compliance reporting. D is wrong because weekly AMI rebuilds and full fleet replacement is a heavyweight pipeline for OS patching and still needs separate evidence of per-instance compliance.

stem: A company wants to retire the corporate VPN that employees currently use to reach internal web applications hosted behind internal Application Load Balancers in AWS. The replacement must evaluate every HTTP request against policies that combine the user's identity and group claims from the corporate OIDC identity provider with the security posture of the user's device as reported by the company's device management service. The applications must not be published to the internet as ordinary public endpoints, and every access decision must be logged for audit. The security team also wants to avoid managing VPN client software on employee devices. Which approach should the security engineer choose?

options.text: Deploy AWS Client VPN with certificate-based mutual authentication and a client posture script that runs when each employee establishes a connection to the VPN endpoint.

Deploy AWS Verified Access with the OIDC identity provider as an identity trust provider and the device management service as a device trust provider, attaching access policies to an endpoint for each application.

Publish each internal application through an internet-facing Application Load Balancer that uses OIDC authentication actions on its listener rules so that users must first sign in with the corporate identity provider before any request reaches the application.
Provide employees with Amazon WorkSpaces virtual desktops restricted by IP access control groups, and have them reach the internal applications only from within those desktops.

explanation: B is correct. AWS Verified Access is built for VPN-less access to internal applications: it evaluates each request against Cedar policies that combine claims from an OIDC identity trust provider with posture data from a device trust provider, fronts the internal load balancers without publishing them as ordinary public endpoints, and logs every access decision for audit. A is wrong because Client VPN still grants network-level access after the initial connection; a one-time posture script at connect time is not per-request evaluation. C is wrong because it exposes the applications directly to the internet and OIDC authentication actions cannot evaluate device posture. D is wrong because WorkSpaces adds a whole virtual desktop layer, controls access by source IP rather than per-request identity-plus-device policy, and does not retire complexity so much as relocate it.

stem: A three-tier application runs in a single VPC: web servers in public subnets, application servers in an Auto Scaling group in private subnets, and an Amazon RDS for MySQL database in isolated subnets. The database must accept connections on port 3306 only from the application servers. The application tier scales in and out many times per day, so its instances' private IP addresses change constantly. The security team wants the restriction enforced at the instance level, wants it to keep working through scaling events without any custom automation, and wants no broader network ranges granted access than necessary. Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure the database security group to allow inbound connections on port 3306 from the full CIDR ranges of all of the private subnets in which the application servers are currently launched.
Add network ACL entries on the database subnets that allow port 3306 from the current private IP addresses of the application servers in the Auto Scaling group.
Configure the database security group to allow port 3306 with the application tier's security group ID as the source, and attach that group in the Auto Scaling group's launch template.
Use a Lambda function triggered by Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks to update the database security group with each new application server's private IP address as it launches.

explanation: C is correct. A security group rule that names another security group as its source matches any instance that carries the referenced group, so every application server admitted by the launch template is authorized automatically, membership tracks scaling events with zero automation, and nothing outside the application tier gains access. A is wrong because subnet CIDR ranges admit every current and future resource placed in those subnets, which is broader than the application servers alone. B is wrong because network ACLs are subnet-level, stateless controls, and hardcoded instance IP entries go stale at the next scaling event. D is wrong because it meets the goal only by building custom automation that the team explicitly does not want, and it introduces failure modes such as races between instance launch and rule insertion.

stem: A company has standardized on a third-party next-generation firewall appliance for deep packet inspection. The security team must place a horizontally scalable fleet of these virtual appliances inline for traffic entering and leaving multiple spoke VPCs. Each network session must always be processed by the same appliance so that stateful inspection works, appliances must scale out behind a single entry point, and inspection must be inserted transparently through route table changes only, with no reconfiguration of the workloads themselves. The vendor publishes its appliance as an Amazon Machine Image, and the security team will manage the appliance software and policies with the vendor's own tools. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the appliance fleet behind an internal Network Load Balancer and configure every workload in the spoke VPCs to use the load balancer's private IP addresses as its default gateway for all outbound and inter-VPC traffic.
Use AWS Network Firewall endpoints in each spoke VPC and import the vendor's inspection signatures into stateful rule groups to replicate the appliance's behavior.
Peer each spoke VPC with a central security VPC that contains the appliance fleet, adding routes that send the spokes' traffic across the peering connections to the appliances.

Deploy the appliance fleet behind a Gateway Load Balancer in a security VPC and add Gateway Load Balancer endpoints to the spoke VPCs' route tables so traffic reaches the appliances transparently with flow stickiness.

explanation: D is correct. Gateway Load Balancer is purpose-built for inline virtual appliances: it presents a single entry point through Gateway Load Balancer endpoints that act as route table targets, encapsulates traffic in GENEVE so the insertion is transparent to workloads, hashes flows so both directions of a session reach the same appliance, and scales the appliance fleet horizontally. A is wrong because a Network Load Balancer address cannot be a route target or default gateway, so transparent bump-in-the-wire insertion is not possible. B is wrong because the requirement is to run the vendor's own appliance; AWS Network Firewall is a different inspection engine and cannot simply import a proprietary appliance's capabilities. C is wrong because VPC peering is not transitive and does not support routing traffic through a middlebox in the peered VPC toward another destination.

stem: An online media company runs a public web application on an Application Load Balancer behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an AWS WAF web ACL. During a recent layer 7 DDoS attack, the operations team struggled to design effective mitigations on its own, and the attack caused a large, unexpected increase in the AWS bill because the protected resources scaled out to absorb the traffic. Leadership asks a security engineer to obtain capabilities beyond what the company already receives from AWS Shield Standard, and wants them in place before the next major online event. The company has an AWS Business Support plan. Which actions should the engineer take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced, protect the CloudFront distribution and the Application Load Balancer, and use the Shield Response Team for mitigation assistance during future attacks.
Rely on AWS Shield Standard's always-on detection, which automatically escalates layer 7 events to the Shield Response Team for mitigation on the company's behalf at no additional cost.
Purchase AWS Enterprise Support, which includes direct engagement from the Shield Response Team during DDoS events without any additional protection subscription.
Request DDoS-related service credits under AWS Shield Standard, which reimburses the scaling charges of resources covered by its always-on network and transport layer protections.
After onboarding to Shield Advanced, use its cost protection to request service credits for usage spikes that protected resources incur as a result of DDoS attacks.

explanation: A and E are correct. Subscribing to Shield Advanced and protecting the CloudFront distribution and the load balancer gives the company access to the Shield Response Team, which the existing Business Support plan lets the team engage for mitigation assistance during attacks, closing the expertise gap. Cost protection is a separate Shield Advanced benefit: once the resources are protected, the company can request service credits for the scaling charges that DDoS attacks cause; note that AWS requires the associated web ACL to carry a rate-based rule in Block mode as a prerequisite for such credit requests, but that rule alone confers no credit entitlement without the subscription. B is wrong because Shield Standard provides automatic network and transport layer mitigation only and includes no Shield Response Team involvement. C is wrong because a support plan by itself does not provide Shield Response Team engagement for DDoS mitigation; that requires a Shield Advanced subscription. D is wrong because Shield Standard includes no cost-protection or service-credit benefit; DDoS-related credits apply only to resources protected under a Shield Advanced subscription.

stem: Developers occasionally need interactive SSH sessions on EC2 instances that run in private subnets without public IP addresses. The company has decommissioned its bastion hosts and refuses to operate any always-running access infrastructure. The instances run a minimal operating system image on which the AWS Systems Manager agent is not installed and cannot be added, although the standard SSH daemon is running. Developers already authenticate to AWS with federated IAM roles. Connections must be authorized and audited through IAM, and the solution must work without adding internet connectivity to the private subnets. Sessions are infrequent, so any per-use cost is acceptable. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint in the VPC and have the developers open SSH sessions through the endpoint, authorizing who may connect with IAM policies.
Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with interface VPC endpoints so that the developers can start interactive shell sessions from the AWS console without any inbound access.
Launch a hardened bastion instance in a public subnet with security group rules that permit SSH only from the corporate network's registered IP address ranges.
Deploy AWS Client VPN attached to the VPC so that the developers can connect directly to the instances' private IP addresses across the VPN tunnel.

explanation: A is correct. An EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint provides identity-aware TCP tunneling into the VPC with no agent on the instance, no public IP addresses, no internet path, and no always-running compute to maintain; IAM policies authorize who may open tunnels and CloudTrail records the connection attempts, while the existing SSH daemon serves the session. B is wrong because Session Manager depends on the Systems Manager agent, which the stem says cannot be installed on these images. C is wrong because the company has explicitly decommissioned bastion hosts and refuses always-running access infrastructure, which a bastion instance is. D is wrong because a Client VPN endpoint is continuously billed standing infrastructure and grants network-level access, with connection authorization far less granular than per-instance IAM control.

stem: A company inspects east-west traffic between spoke VPCs by routing it through a central inspection VPC attached to a transit gateway. The inspection VPC contains stateful third-party firewall appliances behind a Gateway Load Balancer deployed across two Availability Zones. After cutover, the security team observes that some TCP sessions between spokes in different Availability Zones fail intermittently. Packet captures show that the forward and return packets of the same flow arrive at appliances in different Availability Zones, so the stateful appliances discard the half of the flow for which they hold no connection state. The fix must not introduce additional cross-Availability-Zone data transfer between the load balancer and the appliances. What should the team change to resolve the drops?

options.text: Enable cross-zone load balancing on the Gateway Load Balancer so that appliances in either Availability Zone can receive and match both directions of every inspected flow.
Enable appliance mode on the transit gateway attachment for the inspection VPC so that both directions of a flow are consistently forwarded through the same Availability Zone.
Add static routes in each spoke VPC that pin traffic to the inspection subnet in its own Availability Zone so that flows remain zone-local from end to end.
Replace the stateful rules on the firewall appliances with stateless rules so that packets are evaluated individually and unmatched flow halves are no longer discarded.

explanation: B is correct. By default a transit gateway sends traffic to an attachment in the same Availability Zone where it entered, so the forward and return legs of a cross-zone flow can enter the inspection VPC in different zones; appliance mode makes the transit gateway hash each flow to a single zone for its lifetime, so both directions reach the same appliance and its connection state matches. A is wrong because cross-zone load balancing works by forwarding traffic to appliances in other Availability Zones, which introduces exactly the cross-zone data transfer between the load balancer and the appliances that the requirement excludes, and it leaves the transit gateway's zone selection untouched. C is wrong because a spoke's route table points at the transit gateway, not at the inspection VPC's subnets, and the return path from the other spoke cannot be pinned from the sender's side. D is wrong because abandoning stateful inspection removes the security capability the architecture exists to provide rather than fixing the routing asymmetry.

stem: Auditors require that every interactive shell session administrators open on the company's EC2 instances is fully recorded, including the commands typed and the output returned, that the recordings are encrypted with a customer managed AWS KMS key, and that the records are retained centrally for five years. Administrators already connect exclusively through AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, inbound SSH is disabled across the fleet, and the instances have the IAM permissions the agent needs. The solution must capture the session content itself, not merely the fact that a session occurred. The fleet spans several accounts that forward records to a central archive. Which configuration meets the auditors' requirements?

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail management event logging for all of the accounts and retain the resulting StartSession and TerminateSession event history for five years in a central S3 bucket encrypted with the customer managed KMS key.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the instances' subnets and archive the log files to an S3 bucket with a five-year lifecycle policy and KMS encryption applied.

Update the Session Manager preferences to write session activity logs to a central S3 bucket or CloudWatch Logs destination encrypted with the customer managed KMS key, and retain the destination data for five years.
Create an EventBridge rule that captures Session Manager state-change notifications and stores the events in an encrypted DynamoDB table for the retention period.

explanation: C is correct. Session Manager's logging preferences stream the full content of each session, the commands entered and the output returned, to an S3 bucket or CloudWatch Logs group, both of which can be encrypted with the customer managed KMS key and retained centrally for the mandated five years. A is wrong because CloudTrail records the StartSession and TerminateSession API calls, which prove a session happened but contain none of the keystrokes or output the auditors demand. B is wrong because VPC Flow Logs capture connection metadata such as addresses, ports, and byte counts, never terminal content. D is wrong because state-change notifications are lifecycle events about sessions beginning and ending, so a DynamoDB archive of them also fails the content requirement.

stem: A company must eliminate inbound SSH access to its Linux EC2 instances. The instances run in private subnets that have no internet connectivity of any kind, and the VPC must stay that way. The security team requires that administrators connect through IAM-authenticated sessions, that security groups contain no inbound rules at all for port 22, and that traffic between the instances and the management service never leaves the AWS network. The instances already run the AWS Systems Manager agent and an appropriate instance profile has been prepared for attachment. The team also wants the rollout to happen without instance downtime. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Restrict the instances' security groups so that inbound SSH is permitted only from the corporate network's public IP address ranges instead of from 0.0.0.0/0.
Attach the instance profile with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore permissions to the instances, remove every inbound SSH rule from their security groups, and use Session Manager for shell access.
Create interface VPC endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages in the instances' subnets so the agent communicates with Systems Manager privately.
Add a NAT gateway to the VPC so that the Systems Manager agent can reach its regional service endpoints over the internet for session traffic.
Create an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint in the VPC and allow inbound port 22 from the endpoint's security group in each instance's security group.

explanation: B and C are correct. The instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore lets the agent register with Systems Manager so administrators open IAM-authenticated Session Manager shells, and because the agent makes only outbound connections, every inbound SSH rule can be deleted. The interface endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages carry that agent traffic privately inside the VPC, satisfying the rule that it never leaves the AWS network from an internet-less VPC. A is wrong because narrowing the source range still leaves an inbound port 22 rule, which the requirements prohibit outright. D is wrong because a NAT gateway routes the agent's traffic across the internet and adds the internet connectivity the VPC must not have. E is wrong because EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint delivers SSH to the instance's port 22, which requires an inbound rule referencing the endpoint, again violating the no-inbound-SSH constraint.

stem: A security engineer is investigating an AWS Lambda function that returns AccessDenied errors whenever it attempts to read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket named security-artifacts-bucket. The function's execution role has an identity policy that allows s3:GetObject on the bucket and all of its objects. The bucket policy contains a single statement that allows the s3:GetObject action, names the function's execution role ARN as the principal, and sets the Resource element to "arn:aws:s3:::security-artifacts-bucket". The bucket uses default server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3), and the function and bucket are in the same AWS account. Which change to the bucket policy will resolve the errors?

options.text: Change the Principal element to the Lambda service principal, lambda.amazonaws.com, so that the Lambda service is granted access to the bucket.
Change the Action element to s3:ListBucket so that the statement covers read operations that the function performs against the bucket.
Change the Resource element to "arn:aws:s3:::security-artifacts-bucket/*" so that the statement applies to the objects in the bucket.
Add the Lambda function's ARN as a second entry in the Resource element so that the statement covers both the bucket and the function.

explanation: C is correct. s3:GetObject is an object-level action, so it must be granted on object ARNs of the form arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/*. A Resource element that names only the bucket ARN matches bucket-level actions, so the current statement authorizes nothing that GetObject requests can use. A is wrong because the function accesses S3 with its execution role's credentials; granting the lambda.amazonaws.com service principal does not authorize the role and would broaden access to the entire service rather than this function. B is wrong because s3:ListBucket is a bucket-level action that authorizes listing, not reading object contents. D is wrong because Resource entries in an S3 bucket policy must be S3 ARNs; a Lambda function ARN is not a valid resource in a bucket policy.

stem: A company is building a web application that must authenticate external users across multiple microservices that run on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). The solution must use temporary credentials and must minimize the management overhead of maintaining user databases. A security engineer is defining the order of implementation steps. Which sequence of steps implements a secure authentication strategy that meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure an Amazon Cognito user pool for user authentication. Create an Amazon Cognito application client for the web application. Implement an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with AWS Lambda authorizers that validate tokens before forwarding requests to the microservices. Set up an IAM role for each microservice and grant each role appropriate permissions.

Set up AWS IAM Identity Center to give users access to the microservices. Create an Amazon DynamoDB table to store user credentials for each microservice. Implement an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with AWS Lambda authorizers that validate tokens. Set up an IAM role for each microservice and grant each role appropriate permissions.

Create an Amazon DynamoDB table to store user credentials for each microservice. Create an Amazon Cognito application client for the web application. Set up an IAM role for each microservice and grant each role appropriate permissions. Implement an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with AWS Lambda authorizers that validate tokens.

Configure an Amazon Cognito user pool for user authentication. Set up an IAM role for each microservice and grant each role appropriate permissions. Create an Amazon DynamoDB table to store user credentials for each microservice. Implement an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with AWS Lambda authorizers that validate tokens.

explanation: A is correct. An Amazon Cognito user pool provides managed authentication for external users with no user database to operate, an application client lets the web application interact with the pool, Lambda authorizers on an API Gateway HTTP API validate the pool's tokens before requests reach the microservices, and per-microservice IAM roles supply temporary credentials with least-privilege permissions. B is wrong because IAM Identity Center is for workforce access, not external application users, and a DynamoDB credential table reintroduces the user-database management the requirements exclude. C is wrong because it also builds a self-managed credential store in DynamoDB, which adds overhead and risk compared with Cognito-managed authentication. D is wrong because it includes the unnecessary DynamoDB credential table and defers token validation until after roles are wired, leaving the services without an authentication gate.

stem: An AWS account administrator created an IAM group for the company's developers and attached a managed policy that is designed to require multi-factor authentication (MFA). The policy contains a Deny statement for all actions with a condition of Bool aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: false, along with a NotAction exemption that allows users to manage and enable their own MFA devices. After the policy is applied, developers who authenticate to the AWS Management Console with MFA can work normally, but the same users report that every Amazon EC2 command that they run with the AWS CLI by using their long-term access keys fails with an authorization error. What should the administrator do to resolve this problem while still enforcing MFA?

options.text: Change the condition in the Deny statement so that it tests whether aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true instead of false.
Instruct users to run the aws sts get-session-token CLI command with the --serial-number and --token-code parameters, and to use the returned temporary credentials for subsequent API and CLI calls.
Implement federated API and CLI access with SAML 2.0, and configure the identity provider to enforce multi-factor authentication for every sign-in.

Create a role that enforces MFA in its trust policy, instruct users to run sts assume-role with the --serial-number and --token-code parameters, and add sts:AssumeRole to the NotAction element of the Deny statement.

explanation: B is correct. Requests signed with long-term access keys carry no MFA context, so the aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent key is absent and the Deny statement blocks them. Calling sts get-session-token with the MFA device serial number and a current token code returns temporary credentials whose sessions include aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent set to true, so subsequent CLI calls pass the condition. A is wrong because denying when the key is true would block exactly the MFA-authenticated sessions and allow non-MFA access. C is wrong because migrating all API access to SAML federation is a re-architecture of the company's identity model, which is unnecessary to fix CLI access for existing IAM users. D is wrong because adding sts:AssumeRole to the NotAction exemption lets any principal without MFA assume roles, creating a bypass that undermines the MFA requirement.

stem: A security engineer needs to configure AWS IAM Identity Center to use the company's external SAML 2.0 identity provider (IdP) as its identity source, and must set up automatic provisioning so that users and groups synchronize from the IdP. Which sequence of steps meets these requirements?

options.text: Obtain the SAML metadata from IAM Identity Center. Obtain the SAML metadata from the external IdP. Configure the external IdP as the identity source in IAM Identity Center by exchanging the metadata between the two systems. Enable automatic provisioning in the IAM Identity Center settings. Enable automatic provisioning in the external IdP by using the provisioning endpoint and access token.

Configure the external IdP as the identity source in IAM Identity Center. Enable automatic provisioning in the external IdP. Obtain the SAML metadata from IAM Identity Center. Obtain the SAML metadata from the external IdP. Enable automatic provisioning in the IAM Identity Center settings.

Create an IAM role that has a trust policy that specifies the IdP's API endpoint. Obtain the SAML metadata from the external IdP. Configure the external IdP as the identity source in IAM Identity Center. Enable automatic provisioning in the IAM Identity Center settings. Enable automatic provisioning in the external IdP.

Enable automatic provisioning in the external IdP. Enable automatic provisioning in the IAM Identity Center settings. Obtain the SAML metadata from the external IdP. Obtain the SAML metadata from IAM Identity Center. Configure the external IdP as the identity source in IAM Identity Center.

explanation: A is correct. Changing the identity source to an external IdP is a metadata exchange: the engineer collects the SAML metadata that each side presents, uploads the IdP's metadata into IAM Identity Center while giving the Identity Center metadata to the IdP, and only then enables SCIM automatic provisioning, first in Identity Center, which generates the SCIM endpoint and access token, and then in the IdP, which consumes them. B is wrong because it configures the identity source before the metadata that the configuration requires has been obtained, and it enables provisioning in the IdP before the SCIM endpoint exists. C is wrong because IAM Identity Center federation is configured in Identity Center itself; no IAM role trust policy pointing at an IdP API endpoint is involved. D is wrong because provisioning cannot be enabled in the IdP first, since the SCIM endpoint and token are produced by IAM Identity Center, and the metadata exchange must precede everything.

stem: A security engineer at a financial services company receives a report that members of the data-engineering IAM group can no longer download objects from an Amazon S3 bucket named finance-exports, even though a recent change was expected to grant them access. The group has a customer managed policy that allows s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::finance-exports/*, and the bucket policy also allows s3:GetObject for the same principals on the object ARNs. A second policy attached to the group, named corporate-guardrails, contains a statement with Effect: Deny for s3:* on all resources with a condition of NotIpAddress on aws:SourceIp that lists the corporate VPN CIDR ranges. The affected engineers are working from a newly opened office whose egress IP range has not yet been added to that policy. Why does Amazon S3 deny the requests?

options.text: The identity-based allow and the bucket policy allow conflict with each other, so Amazon S3 falls back to an implicit deny until one of the two overlapping allow statements is removed.
The Deny statement in corporate-guardrails matches the requests from the new office, and an explicit deny in any applicable policy overrides every allow in identity-based and resource-based policies.
IAM evaluates the most recently attached policy first, so corporate-guardrails takes precedence over the older allow policy until the allow policy is detached and re-attached to the group.
The s3:GetObject action also requires s3:ListBucket permission on the bucket ARN itself, and neither the identity-based policy nor the bucket policy grants that bucket-level action.

explanation: B is correct. The engineers' new office IP is outside the CIDR list in the NotIpAddress condition, so the Deny statement matches their requests, and IAM policy evaluation always resolves an explicit deny above any allow, regardless of which policy contains the allow. A is wrong because overlapping allows never conflict; permissions from identity-based and resource-based policies are combined as a union within an account. C is wrong because policy evaluation has no ordering by attachment time; all applicable statements are evaluated together. D is wrong because s3:GetObject does not depend on s3:ListBucket; listing is a separate bucket-level operation, and its absence would not block object downloads that were previously working.

stem: During a quarterly permissions review, a security engineer discovers that an IAM role named audit-reader in account 111122223333 can successfully call s3:GetObject on objects in a bucket named compliance-evidence that is owned by the same account, even though none of the role's attached identity-based policies mention Amazon S3 at all. The bucket policy contains a statement with Effect: Allow, the audit-reader role ARN as the Principal, the s3:GetObject action, and arn:aws:s3:::compliance-evidence/* as the Resource. No permissions boundary is set on the role, and no service control policy or resource control policy applies to the account. The audit team asks the engineer to explain why the access succeeds. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Within a single account, a request is allowed if either an identity-based policy or a resource-based policy allows it, so the bucket policy statement naming the role is sufficient on its own.

Amazon S3 grants read access to all principals in the bucket owner's account by default, and this default remains in effect until S3 Block Public Access is enabled on the bucket and the bucket's access control lists are disabled.
The role's trust policy implicitly grants the S3 permissions that appear in the bucket policy, because trust policies and resource-based policies are evaluated as a single combined document.
IAM evaluates bucket policies before identity-based policies and stops at the first matching allow statement, so the identity-based policies were never consulted for these requests.

explanation: A is correct. For a request where the principal and the resource are in the same account, the identity-based and resource-based policies are evaluated as a union, so an allow in either one authorizes the request as long as nothing denies it; the bucket policy naming the role ARN is therefore sufficient by itself. B is wrong because S3 has no account-wide default read grant; without an applicable allow, same-account principals are implicitly denied. C is wrong because a role's trust policy controls only who can assume the role; it grants no data-access permissions and is not merged with bucket policies. D is wrong because evaluation is not ordered with early termination on allows; all policies are considered, and only an explicit deny short-circuits the outcome.

stem: A data pipeline role named etl-runner in a development account, 222233334444, must read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket named prod-datasets that is owned by a production account, 111122223333. The production team has already added a bucket policy statement that allows s3:GetObject for the etl-runner role ARN on arn:aws:s3:::prod-datasets/*. The bucket uses SSE-S3 encryption, S3 Block Public Access remains enabled, and no service control policy, resource control policy, or permissions boundary applies to either account. When the pipeline runs, every GetObject call fails with an AccessDenied error. The etl-runner role currently has identity-based policies that cover only Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon CloudWatch Logs. What should the security engineer do to fix the failure?

options.text: Change the bucket policy Principal from the etl-runner role ARN to the development account root ARN so that the grant delegates access to the entire account.
Disable S3 Block Public Access on the prod-datasets bucket so that the cross-account allow statement in the bucket policy can take effect for the role.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket and update the pipeline to use the accelerated endpoint, which supports cross-account request signing.
Attach an identity-based policy to the etl-runner role in the development account that allows s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::prod-datasets/*.

explanation: D is correct. Cross-account access requires an allow on both sides: the resource owner's bucket policy must allow the external principal, and the principal's own account must allow the action through an identity-based policy. The bucket side is done, but the role has no S3 permissions, so its own account denies the call. A is wrong because delegating to the account root still requires an identity-based allow on the role, so the failure would persist while the grant becomes broader than needed. B is wrong because Block Public Access affects public and anonymous access controls, not a specific cross-account principal named in the bucket policy. C is wrong because Transfer Acceleration changes the transfer endpoint for performance and has no effect on authorization.

stem: A platform team provisions IAM roles for developers through a pipeline that attaches a permissions boundary named developer-boundary to every role it creates. The boundary allows only Amazon S3, Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and AWS CodeBuild actions. A developer's role has an identity-based policy that allows dynamodb:* on all resources, but every attempt by the role to create a DynamoDB table fails with an AccessDenied error. The company's security standard states that the permissions boundary framework must remain attached to all developer roles. No service control policy or resource control policy restricts DynamoDB in the account, and CloudTrail confirms the deny originates from IAM policy evaluation. Which action gives the role working DynamoDB access while meeting the standard?

options.text: Attach the AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess AWS managed policy to the role in addition to its existing identity-based policy so that the allow is granted twice.
Detach the developer-boundary policy from this specific role and rely on its identity-based policy, since boundaries are optional for roles that need database access.
Add the required DynamoDB actions to the developer-boundary managed policy, because effective permissions are the intersection of the boundary and the identity-based policies.
Add the role to an IAM group that has DynamoDB permissions, because group memberships are evaluated outside the scope of a permissions boundary.

explanation: C is correct. A permissions boundary caps what identity-based policies can grant: the effective permissions are the intersection of the two, so an action missing from the boundary is denied no matter what the identity-based policy allows. Updating developer-boundary to include the DynamoDB actions restores access while the boundary framework stays attached. A is wrong because adding more identity-based allows cannot exceed the boundary; the intersection still excludes DynamoDB. B is wrong because detaching the boundary violates the stated security standard that boundaries remain on all developer roles. D is wrong because IAM groups can contain only IAM users, not roles, so this configuration is not possible at all.

stem: A company runs 120 AWS accounts in a single organization in AWS Organizations. After an external penetration test showed that a developer could grant a personal AWS account access to an internal Amazon S3 bucket by editing the bucket policy, the security team must guarantee that no S3 bucket in any member account can be accessed by principals outside the organization, even when an application team misconfigures its own bucket policy. The control must be preventive rather than detective, must apply automatically to existing and future accounts, and must be manageable from the organization's management or delegated administrator account. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Attach a resource control policy (RCP) to the organization root that denies s3:* when the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key does not match the organization's ID.
Attach a service control policy (SCP) to the organization root that denies s3:* for any principal whose aws:PrincipalOrgID does not match the organization's ID.
Create an organization-wide IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer and configure automated archiving for findings that involve principals inside the organization.
Require every application team to include a deny statement for external principals in each bucket policy, and audit compliance with an AWS Config conformance pack.

explanation: A is correct. RCPs are organization-managed policies that cap the permissions available on resources in member accounts, so a root-attached RCP denying s3:* for principals outside the organization overrides any bucket policy a team writes, applies to existing and future accounts, and is preventive and centrally managed. B is wrong because SCPs bound only the principals inside the organization; they place no restriction on an external account's principals accessing a member account's bucket. C is wrong because Access Analyzer is a detective control that reports external access after it becomes possible rather than preventing it. D is wrong because per-bucket deny statements depend on every team's diligence, and a Config conformance pack only detects noncompliant policies after the fact.

stem: A company manages 60 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations and has already connected its external identity provider to AWS IAM Identity Center as the identity source. The security team must give the database team read-only access in all production accounts, the platform team administrative access in sandbox accounts, and the finance team billing access in the management account. Account teams open roughly four new accounts every month, and the security team wants new access assignments to require minimal per-account work, with all role provisioning handled centrally rather than by logging in to each member account. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST ongoing administrative effort?

options.text: Create IAM SAML identity providers and federation roles in every member account, and map each team's identity provider group to the matching role in each account individually.
Create IAM users for each team member in every account they need, group the users by team, and enforce a strong password and MFA policy across the accounts.

Create a single permission set with administrator access, assign every team's group to all accounts with it, and rely on team managers to instruct members which services they are allowed to use in each account environment.

Create a permission set in IAM Identity Center for each access level, then assign each team's directory group to the appropriate accounts; Identity Center provisions and updates the corresponding roles in each account automatically.

explanation: D is correct. Permission sets are defined once in IAM Identity Center and, when a group is assigned to an account, Identity Center creates and maintains the underlying roles in that account automatically, so onboarding a new account is a central assignment rather than per-account role engineering. A is wrong because building SAML providers and federation roles in every account by hand recreates what Identity Center automates and multiplies work with each new account. B is wrong because per-account IAM users are long-term credentials that contradict centralized workforce federation and create heavy lifecycle overhead. C is wrong because one administrator permission set for everyone abandons least privilege; instructions from managers are not an access control.

stem: A company's workforce signs in to AWS through IAM Identity Center, which is connected to an external SAML identity provider. An employee reports that a laptop was stolen while the employee had an active AWS access portal browser session and cached AWS CLI single sign-on tokens. The identity team disabled the employee's account at the identity provider within minutes, but a security engineer testing with a copy of the cached tokens confirms that role credentials for the employee's assigned accounts can still be issued. The security team must stop the stolen laptop from obtaining any further credentials as quickly as possible, without disrupting other employees who use the same permission sets. What should the security engineer do?

options.text: Rotate the employee's IAM access keys in every assigned account, because the cached CLI tokens are derived from long-term access keys that remain valid until they are rotated.

In the IAM Identity Center console, revoke the employee's active access portal sessions, because sessions that were established before the identity provider disablement remain usable until they expire or are revoked.
Detach the permission set's managed policies from the AWSReservedSSO roles in each of the employee's assigned accounts until the incident is closed, then reattach them.

Take no further action, because disabling the user at the external identity provider immediately invalidates the AWS access portal session and every cached single sign-on token that was issued to the employee.

explanation: B is correct. The access portal session and the CLI's cached tokens are issued by IAM Identity Center itself, so disabling the user at the external identity provider blocks new sign-ins but does not invalidate sessions that already exist; revoking the employee's active sessions in the Identity Center console stops the stolen tokens from being exchanged for further role credentials while leaving every other user untouched. A is wrong because Identity Center users have no IAM access keys; the cached tokens are Identity Center session artifacts, not derivatives of long-term keys. C is wrong because detaching policies from the AWSReservedSSO roles cuts off every employee who uses those permission sets, which the requirement forbids, and Identity Center manages those roles itself. D is wrong because identity provider disablement takes effect at the next authentication, so the existing portal session and cached tokens keep working until they expire or are revoked.

stem: A mobile application has several million consumer users who sign in through an Amazon Cognito user pool. The application must let each signed-in user upload profile images directly from the device to an Amazon S3 bucket by calling the S3 API, and each user must be able to write only under a prefix that is unique to that user. The engineering team refuses to operate any server-side proxy or URL-signing backend for uploads, and the security team requires temporary AWS credentials that are scoped per user. The images average several megabytes, and upload volume peaks during evenings and weekends across many geographic regions. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create one IAM user for the application, embed its access key in the mobile app build, and restrict the key with an IAM policy that limits uploads to the application's bucket.
Create an IAM role for each application user at registration time and store the role ARN in the user's profile so the app can assume it after sign-in.

Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool that exchanges user pool tokens for temporary credentials for an authenticated IAM role whose policy scopes s3:PutObject to a prefix containing the ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} policy variable.
Run an AWS Lambda function behind Amazon API Gateway that verifies the user pool token and returns S3 pre-signed PUT URLs restricted to the caller's prefix.

explanation: C is correct. A Cognito identity pool exchanges the user pool's tokens for temporary, automatically expiring AWS credentials, and the authenticated role's policy can use the ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} variable so each user's session can write only under that user's own prefix, all without any server-side component. A is wrong because an embedded long-term access key is shared by every install, is extractable from the app package, and cannot scope access per user. B is wrong because creating a role per user does not scale to millions of users and the app would still need credentials to call sts:AssumeRole. D is wrong because a Lambda-and-API-Gateway signing service is exactly the server-side backend the team refuses to operate, and pre-signed URLs are not per-user AWS credentials.

stem: A platform team operates a credential-vending service that assumes a single IAM role named batch-runner and hands the resulting temporary credentials to hundreds of short-lived internal batch jobs. The batch-runner role's identity-based policy allows read and write access to every team bucket so that the service can serve any job. A security review requires that each vended credential set be usable only against the one Amazon S3 bucket and prefix that the requesting job declares, and the platform team refuses to create and maintain a separate IAM role for every job type. Jobs are created and retired daily by many different teams. Which change enforces the per-job restriction?

options.text: Create a separate IAM role for each job type with a policy scoped to that job's bucket and prefix, and have the vending service choose the matching role at request time based on the job's declared identity and workload metadata.
Attach a permissions boundary to the batch-runner role that lists every team bucket, so each session inherits a boundary that limits it to the declared prefix.
Attach a service control policy to the account that restricts s3:* to the requesting job's bucket by matching the job name in the aws:ResourceAccount condition key.

Have the vending service pass an inline session policy in each sts:AssumeRole call that allows only the declared bucket and prefix, so the session's effective permissions become the intersection of the role policy and the session policy.

explanation: D is correct. Session policies are supplied at AssumeRole time and cap that specific session: the effective permissions are the intersection of the role's identity-based policies and the session policy, so each vended credential set can be narrowed to one bucket and prefix while a single role serves every job. A is wrong because it meets the restriction only by creating a role per job type, which the team explicitly refuses to maintain. B is wrong because a permissions boundary is a static property of the role that applies identically to all sessions; it cannot vary per job request. C is wrong because SCPs apply account-wide guardrails, cannot vary per session, and aws:ResourceAccount matches account IDs, not job names or prefixes.

stem: After a near miss in which an Amazon SQS queue was briefly readable by an unknown external account, a company's security team must continuously identify every Amazon S3 bucket, AWS KMS key, SQS queue, IAM role, and Secrets Manager secret across its AWS organization that is accessible to principals outside the organization. The team wants findings generated automatically as resource policies change, wants the organization boundary treated as the trust boundary, and does not want to write or maintain any custom analysis code. The findings must cover sharing that already exists as well as sharing that is introduced later, and the team will route them to its ticketing system for triage. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer with the organization as the zone of trust in each active Region, and triage the findings it generates for resources shared outside the organization.

Deploy an AWS Config aggregator with custom Lambda-backed rules that parse each supported resource policy, flag statements whose principals are not organization members, and route each noncompliant result to the security team's ticketing system for review.
Schedule Amazon Athena queries over the organization's CloudTrail logs to list cross-account API calls, and treat any caller account outside the organization as a finding.
Enable AWS Trusted Advisor and subscribe to its security checks for publicly accessible S3 buckets and snapshots, forwarding check results to the security team weekly.

explanation: A is correct. An external access analyzer with the organization as its zone of trust uses automated reasoning over resource policies for exactly these resource types, continuously generates findings when a policy allows access from outside the organization, and requires no custom code. B is wrong because Lambda-backed Config rules require the team to write and maintain policy-parsing code, which the requirements exclude. C is wrong because CloudTrail shows access that already happened; it cannot reveal a policy that permits external access that has not yet been exercised. D is wrong because Trusted Advisor covers a narrow set of public-exposure checks, does not evaluate against an organization trust boundary, and does not cover KMS keys, SQS queues, IAM roles, and secrets comprehensively.

stem: During a cloud migration, a team attached the AdministratorAccess managed policy to an application role as a temporary measure. The migration is complete, and the security team must now replace that policy with a least-privilege policy that reflects only the actions and services the application has actually used during the past 90 days. The application makes calls to a mix of Amazon S3, Amazon DynamoDB, and AWS Step Functions APIs, and its exact action usage is not documented anywhere. CloudTrail has been recording management events for the account throughout the period. Which approach produces the replacement policy with the LEAST manual effort?

options.text: Open the role's last-accessed information in the IAM console, note which services show recent activity, and attach the AWS managed ReadOnlyAccess policy plus full-access policies for those services.
Query the CloudTrail logs with Amazon Athena to list every eventName the role invoked, then hand-write an identity-based policy that enumerates the matching IAM actions.
Use IAM Access Analyzer policy generation to analyze the role's CloudTrail activity for the period, review the generated policy draft, and attach the refined policy in place of AdministratorAccess.
Replace AdministratorAccess with the PowerUserAccess managed policy, which removes IAM administration actions while preserving the service access the application already uses.

explanation: C is correct. Access Analyzer policy generation reads the role's CloudTrail activity and produces a policy scoped to the services and actions actually used, leaving the engineer only a review-and-refine step, which is the least manual path to least privilege. A is wrong because last-accessed information is service-level, and attaching full-access policies per service grants far more than the actions used. B is wrong because Athena gives the raw event list but the engineer must still translate events into actions and author the policy by hand. D is wrong because PowerUserAccess still grants nearly every service action in the account and is not a least-privilege policy for this application.

stem: A security organization must run a program to shrink its identity attack surface across all 85 accounts in its AWS organization. The program's first deliverable is a continuously updated, organization-wide view of IAM roles that have not been used for months, access keys and passwords that are stale, and permissions that principals hold but never exercise, so that owners can be asked to remove them. The security-tooling account must host the view, the management account must not run tooling, and the team wants a managed capability rather than scheduled scripts. Progress against the program will be reported to the CISO every month. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Generate an IAM credential report in every member account on a schedule, copy the reports to the security-tooling account, and build a consolidated stale-credential dashboard from the CSV files.

Register the security-tooling account as the delegated administrator for IAM Access Analyzer and create an organization-level unused access analyzer, then work the unused-role, unused-credential, and unused-permission findings from its dashboard.
Deploy the iam-user-unused-credentials-check AWS Config managed rule through an organization conformance pack and aggregate the compliance results into the security-tooling account.
Enable Amazon GuardDuty with a delegated administrator in the security-tooling account and monitor its IAM finding types for principals whose credentials show no recent activity.

explanation: B is correct. The unused access analyzer is a managed Access Analyzer capability that reports unused roles, unused access keys and passwords, and unused permissions across the organization, and delegated administration lets the security-tooling account own the analyzer and dashboard without running tooling in the management account. A is wrong because credential reports cover credential age and use per account but say nothing about unused permissions, and the copy-and-consolidate pipeline is exactly the scripted tooling the team wants to avoid. C is wrong because that Config rule evaluates only IAM user credentials, missing unused roles and unexercised permissions. D is wrong because GuardDuty detects threats and anomalous credential use; it does not inventory dormant access.

stem: A manufacturing company runs batch workloads on physical servers in its own data center that must call Amazon S3 and AWS KMS APIs several times per hour. The security policy prohibits storing long-term AWS access keys anywhere on the servers. Each server already holds an X.509 certificate issued by the company's private certificate authority, and the certificates are rotated by existing PKI automation. The company wants the servers to obtain temporary AWS credentials by proving their identity with these existing certificates. The servers cannot be migrated to AWS in the foreseeable future, and network connectivity to AWS is provided through an existing private connection. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an IAM user per server, store each access key in an on-premises vault, and rotate the keys automatically every 30 days using the vault's existing rotation workflow and the company's change management process.
Register the servers as AWS Systems Manager hybrid-activated managed instances and let the activation's IAM role provide credentials for the batch workloads' API calls.
Configure an Amazon Cognito identity pool with developer-authenticated identities and have each server exchange a signed token from an internal service for temporary credentials.

Set up IAM Roles Anywhere with a trust anchor referencing the private CA, create a profile listing the allowed roles, and use the credential helper to exchange each server's certificate for temporary credentials.

explanation: D is correct. IAM Roles Anywhere is built for on-premises workloads with existing PKI: the trust anchor establishes trust in the private CA, the profile scopes which roles can be obtained, and the credential helper exchanges each server's X.509 certificate for temporary role credentials, so no long-term keys ever reach the servers. A is wrong because vaulted, rotated access keys are still long-term credentials on premises, which the policy prohibits. B is wrong because hybrid activation exists to let Systems Manager manage the instances and does not use the company's certificates as the workload identity proof the requirements specify. C is wrong because developer-authenticated identities target application end users and would require the company to build and operate a custom token-issuing service instead of using its PKI.

stem: As part of an account hygiene initiative, a security engineer is removing IAM roles that are no longer needed from a legacy account. The account stopped using Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling last year, and the engineer attempts to delete the role named AWSServiceRoleForAutoScaling from the IAM console. The deletion fails with an error stating that the role is currently in use, and the engineer also notices that the console offers no way to edit the role's trust policy or detach its attached policy. An auditor insists the role must be removed before the account is certified. What should the engineer do to remove the role?

options.text: Find and delete the remaining Auto Scaling resources that still depend on the role, then retry the deletion, which the owning service verifies and completes once nothing uses the role.
Edit the role's trust policy with the AWS CLI to remove the autoscaling.amazonaws.com service principal, which releases the service's lock so the role can be deleted.
Detach the role's managed policy with the AWS CLI first, because a service-linked role cannot be deleted while any permissions policy remains attached to it.
Open a support case, because service-linked roles are owned by AWS and can be removed from a customer account only by the service team on request.

explanation: A is correct. Service-linked role deletion is gated by the owning service: it checks for resources that still depend on the role, and the deletion succeeds only after those resources, such as remaining Auto Scaling groups, are cleaned up, so the engineer must remove the dependent resources and retry. B is wrong because the trust policy of a service-linked role is defined by the service and cannot be modified by the customer through any interface, including the CLI. C is wrong because the attached policy of a service-linked role is likewise service-managed and cannot be detached, and detachment is not the deletion prerequisite. D is wrong because customers can delete service-linked roles themselves after dependency cleanup; no support case is required.

stem: A company's platform engineers federate from an external identity provider into a shared operations role to administer production accounts. During a recent incident review, the team could not determine which engineer had modified a security group, because CloudTrail showed only the shared assumed-role identity, and engineers had supplied arbitrary values for the role session name. The security team now requires that every session carry the engineer's corporate identity in a field that the engineer cannot change after it is set, that appears in CloudTrail for every action, and that survives when the session assumes further roles. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add a trust policy condition requiring sts:RoleSessionName to equal the engineer's username so the session name field in CloudTrail always identifies the person.
Issue each engineer a personal IAM user with MFA for production work so that CloudTrail records a distinct user ARN instead of a shared assumed-role identity for every administrative action.

Configure the identity provider to set the engineer's corporate identity as the source identity during federation, and permit sts:SetSourceIdentity in the relevant trust policies so the value is fixed at assumption and persists through role chaining.
Enable CloudTrail Insights on the management event trail so that unusual administrative actions are attributed to the engineer who performed them.

explanation: C is correct. Source identity is set once when the IdP-federated session is created, cannot be changed by the engineer for the life of the session, is recorded in CloudTrail events, and persists across subsequent role assumptions, which satisfies every stated requirement. A is wrong because the role session name only labels the first session; when that session assumes another role a new session name is chosen, so attribution does not survive role chaining the way the requirement demands. B is wrong because reverting to personal IAM users abandons federation and reintroduces long-term credentials rather than fixing session attribution. D is wrong because CloudTrail Insights surfaces unusual activity volumes; it adds no identity information to individual events.

stem: A compliance team performs a quarterly review of a standalone AWS account that still contains IAM users for a legacy application team. For each review, auditors require a single document that covers every IAM user in the account and shows whether a console password is enabled, when the password was last used, whether MFA is enabled, the age of each access key, and when each access key was last used. The security engineer wants to produce this evidence with the LEAST effort each quarter and without deploying any new infrastructure into the account. The account contains about 200 IAM users that the legacy team still maintains. What should the engineer do?

options.text: Open the Access Advisor tab for each IAM user in the console and export the service last-accessed data for the auditors to combine into a single document.
Generate the IAM credential report for the account each quarter and give the auditors the resulting CSV, which lists every user with password, MFA, and access key status and last-used details.
Write a script that calls ListUsers, GetLoginProfile, ListMFADevices, ListAccessKeys, and GetAccessKeyLastUsed, then merges the responses into a spreadsheet for the auditors.
Enable an AWS Config recorder for IAM resources and have the auditors review the configuration snapshot of each IAM user resource for the quarter.

explanation: B is correct. The credential report is a built-in, account-wide CSV that already contains exactly the requested fields, password status and last use, MFA status, and access key age and last use, for every IAM user, so one generate-and-download step per quarter satisfies the audit with no new infrastructure. A is wrong because Access Advisor shows which services an entity accessed, not credential status, and requires per-user manual work. C is wrong because a multi-API script reproduces what the credential report provides natively and adds code to maintain, which is more effort. D is wrong because Config records configuration state of IAM resources but does not capture last-used timestamps for passwords and access keys.

stem: A research company hosts hundreds of project teams in a shared AWS account. Each team's Amazon EC2 instances and AWS Secrets Manager secrets are tagged with a project tag at creation through mandatory infrastructure pipelines. The identity team currently writes a new IAM policy for every project that enumerates the project's resource ARNs, and policy authoring has become the bottleneck for onboarding. The security team wants engineers to manage only resources whose project tag matches the project value on the engineer's own session, and wants onboarding a new project to require no IAM policy changes at all. Which strategy meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a customer managed policy per project that lists the project's resource ARNs, and attach the matching policies to each team's role when the team is onboarded.
Add resource-based policies to each team's secrets and use VPC endpoint policies for EC2 so that each project's resources admit only that project's engineers.
Move each project into its own organizational unit and control access with service control policies that allow actions only on the project's tagged resources.

Adopt ABAC: tag each engineer's role or session with a project value, and write shared policies whose conditions require aws:ResourceTag/project to equal ${aws:PrincipalTag/project} for the managed actions.

explanation: D is correct. With attribute-based access control, one shared policy compares the resource's project tag with the principal's project tag at request time, so a new project needs only correctly tagged sessions and resources, and no IAM policy is created or edited during onboarding. A is wrong because a policy per project is exactly the authoring bottleneck the team must eliminate. B is wrong because EC2 instances do not support resource-based policies and VPC endpoint policies filter endpoint traffic rather than expressing per-project management permissions. C is wrong because SCPs never grant access and reorganizing OUs per project inside a single shared account is not even possible, since OUs contain accounts, not projects.

stem: An automation platform authenticates to AWS by assuming a role named orchestrator in a hub account, and then uses the orchestrator session's credentials to call sts:AssumeRole for a role named worker in each spoke account. The worker role's maximum session duration is configured as 12 hours, and the orchestrator role's maximum session duration is also 12 hours. When the platform requests worker sessions with a DurationSeconds value of 43200, the AssumeRole call is rejected with an error stating that the requested duration exceeds the allowed maximum, yet a security engineer testing from an IAM user can obtain a 12-hour worker session successfully. What explains the rejection?

options.text: The platform is performing role chaining: when a role session's credentials are used to assume another role, the new session is capped at 1 hour regardless of the target role's configured maximum session duration.

The worker role's maximum session duration must also be raised in each spoke account's IAM settings, because the console default of 1 hour overrides the role-level configuration for cross-account callers until each spoke account raises the setting.
The platform is calling a Regional STS endpoint, and Regional endpoints cap sessions at 1 hour, while the global STS endpoint that the engineer used honors the full 12-hour maximum.
A permissions boundary on the orchestrator role is limiting the duration, because boundaries constrain session duration in addition to the actions available to a session.

explanation: A is correct. Assuming a role by using another role session's credentials is role chaining, and chained sessions are capped at 1 hour no matter what maximum session duration is configured on the target role, which is why the same request succeeds for the IAM user, whose call is not chained. B is wrong because maximum session duration is a property of each role that the stem says is already 12 hours, and there is no account-level override for cross-account callers. C is wrong because Regional and global STS endpoints apply the same session duration rules. D is wrong because permissions boundaries constrain which actions a session can perform and have no effect on session duration.

stem: A company migrated its GitHub Actions deployment pipeline from stored access keys to an IAM role that is assumed through the token.actions.githubusercontent.com OIDC provider. A penetration tester then demonstrated that a workflow in an unrelated public GitHub repository could assume the deployment role, because the role's trust policy validates only that the token's aud claim equals sts.amazonaws.com. The security team requires that only workflows that run in the company repository octo-org/deploy-app on the main branch can assume the role, while the pipeline continues to use OIDC with no stored secrets. The review board rated the finding critical because the role can deploy to production. What should the security engineer do?

options.text: Replace the OIDC integration with an IAM user whose access keys are stored as encrypted GitHub Actions secrets that only the octo-org/deploy-app repository can read.
Add an sts:ExternalId condition to the trust policy and configure the workflow to send a secret external ID value with each AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity request.
Add a condition on aws:SourceIp to the trust policy that permits only the published IP address ranges used by GitHub-hosted action runners.

Keep the existing aud condition and add a StringEquals condition on token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub in the trust policy that requires the value repo:octo-org/deploy-app:ref:refs/heads/main for every assumption request.

explanation: D is correct. The sub claim of a GitHub Actions OIDC token encodes the repository and ref that the workflow runs from, so a trust policy condition requiring repo:octo-org/deploy-app:ref:refs/heads/main restricts assumption to main-branch workflows of that one repository while preserving the secretless OIDC flow. A is wrong because returning to stored access keys reintroduces the long-term secrets the migration eliminated. B is wrong because sts:ExternalId applies to AssumeRole calls made by AWS principals; AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity does not support an external ID parameter. C is wrong because GitHub-hosted runner IP ranges are shared by every GitHub customer, so an IP condition would still admit the attacker's repository and would break whenever the ranges change.

stem: During an internal penetration test, a tester who held a developer role in a shared account launched an Amazon EC2 instance and attached an instance profile that belonged to an administrative deployment role, then read the role's credentials from the instance metadata service and gained administrative access. The developer role's identity-based policy allows ec2:RunInstances broadly and allows iam:PassRole with a Resource of "*". Developers legitimately need to keep launching instances with a set of approved application roles that all live under the IAM path /app-roles/. The shared account also hosts workloads that belong to several other teams. Which remediation prevents the escalation while preserving the developers' workflow?

options.text: Remove ec2:RunInstances from the developer role's policy and require developers to submit instance launch requests to the platform team through a ticketing queue.

Change the iam:PassRole statement's Resource to arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/app-roles/* and add a condition requiring iam:PassedToService to equal ec2.amazonaws.com, so that only approved application roles can be passed.
Require IMDSv2 with a session hop limit of 1 on all instances that developers launch so that instance role credentials cannot be read from the metadata service.
Remove iam:PassRole from the developer role's policy entirely and instruct developers to launch instances without an instance profile attached.

explanation: B is correct. Scoping iam:PassRole to the /app-roles/ path stops developers from passing the administrative deployment role to an instance while still allowing all approved application roles, and the iam:PassedToService condition prevents the same permission from passing roles to other services. A is wrong because removing ec2:RunInstances breaks the legitimate launch workflow the remediation must preserve. C is wrong because IMDSv2 defends against metadata-stealing attacks such as SSRF from outside the instance; a user who launches the instance can still run code on it and read the credentials legitimately. D is wrong because removing iam:PassRole prevents attaching any instance profile, so applications on new instances lose their approved roles.

stem: A company stores shared build artifacts in a central Amazon S3 bucket in a tooling account. Every account in the company's AWS organization must be able to read the artifacts, and the AWS Control Tower Account Factory creates several new member accounts each month. The bucket policy currently contains an allow statement whose Principal element lists 47 account root ARNs, and onboarding tickets show the list is repeatedly forgotten when accounts are created, which breaks new teams' builds. The security team wants read access to extend to new member accounts automatically, with the LEAST operational overhead and without opening the bucket to accounts outside the organization. What should the team do?

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function triggered by CreateAccount events from AWS Organizations that appends each new account ID to the bucket policy's Principal list automatically.
Create an S3 access point for each member account with a policy that grants that account read access, and have Account Factory provision the access point during account creation.
Replace the 47-entry principal list with a single statement that allows the read actions for any principal, with a condition requiring aws:PrincipalOrgID to equal the organization's ID.
Keep the account list in the bucket policy and add an AWS Config rule that flags the policy as noncompliant whenever a new organization account is missing from the list.

explanation: C is correct. The aws:PrincipalOrgID condition confines the allow to principals whose account belongs to the organization, so every existing and future member account gets read access through one static statement, nothing is exposed outside the organization, and no per-account maintenance remains. A is wrong because event-driven policy rewriting is custom automation that must be operated and debugged, and a policy that grows by account ID will eventually hit bucket policy size limits. B is wrong because provisioning and maintaining an access point per account multiplies configuration work rather than reducing it. D is wrong because a Config rule only reports the missing entries; someone still has to update the list for every new account.

stem: A company keeps a break-glass administrative role in each production account.
