Senior engineers hold IAM users in a central identity account and assume the break-glass role cross-account with the AWS CLI when an emergency requires it. A security review found that an engineer whose laptop was stolen had long-term access keys configured, and the thief could have assumed the production administrative role with those keys alone. The security team requires that any assumption of the break-glass role must prove possession of an MFA device at the moment the role is assumed, without affecting the service roles that operate normally in the production accounts. What should the security engineer do?

options.text: Add a Condition with Bool aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent set to true to the break-glass role's trust policy so that AssumeRole succeeds only for callers whose request is signed with MFA-authenticated credentials.
Require MFA at AWS Management Console sign-in for all IAM users in the identity account so that every engineer authenticates with a second factor before working.
Attach a service control policy to the production accounts that denies every action when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false so that non-MFA sessions can do nothing.
Enable MFA delete on the production accounts' CloudTrail S3 buckets so that a thief with stolen keys cannot cover their tracks after assuming the role.

explanation: A is correct. Putting the aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition in the break-glass role's trust policy makes the MFA check part of the AssumeRole authorization itself, so stolen long-term keys alone can no longer obtain the role, and only this role's assumption path is affected. B is wrong because console sign-in MFA does not constrain CLI calls signed with access keys, which is exactly the stolen-laptop path. C is wrong because service roles and other automated sessions carry no MFA context, so an account-wide SCP keyed on MFA would deny the legitimate service activity the requirement says must be unaffected. D is wrong because MFA delete protects log objects from deletion and does nothing to stop the role assumption.

stem: A legacy payment reconciliation application authenticates with an IAM user's access key that is configured in the application's deployment environment. The application cannot yet be migrated to IAM roles, and the company's security standard requires the access key to be rotated every 90 days. The application runs continuously, and the operations team has been told that the previous rotation attempt caused a two-hour outage because the old key was removed before the new one was in place. The security engineer must design a rotation procedure that keeps the application running throughout the rotation and confirms the old key is genuinely out of use before it is destroyed. Which steps should be part of the procedure? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a second access key for the IAM user, deploy the new key to the application's environment, and confirm the application authenticates successfully with the new key.
Delete the existing access key first and immediately create a replacement that reuses the same access key ID so that the application configuration does not need to change.
Create a new IAM user with a fresh access key for each rotation cycle and repoint the application at the new user before removing the previous user.
Configure the application to call sts:GetSessionToken at startup so that the existing long-term access key no longer falls under the rotation requirement.
After the application switches to the new key, check the old key's last-used timestamp to verify it is idle, deactivate the old key, and delete it after a monitoring period with no errors.

explanation: A and E are correct. An IAM user can hold two access keys at once, so creating the second key and cutting the application over first means the old credential stays valid during the transition, and checking last-used information before deactivating, then deleting, the old key proves nothing still depends on it, which prevents a repeat outage. B is wrong because access key IDs cannot be reused; deleting the key first is exactly the sequence that caused the previous outage. C is wrong because swapping entire IAM users each quarter multiplies lifecycle work and changes the principal ARN that policies reference. D is wrong because GetSessionToken credentials are still derived from the long-term key, which continues to exist and still requires rotation.

stem: A company federates its workforce into AWS through a SAML 2.0 identity provider and a small set of shared IAM roles. The data platform team must now grant analysts access to Amazon S3 analytics resources based on the department attribute that is already maintained for every user in the corporate directory, and the security team has rejected a design that would create a separate IAM role for every department because departments are reorganized several times a year. The chosen design must carry each analyst's department from the directory into the AWS session and enforce it in authorization decisions. Which combination of actions implements this design? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create one IAM role per department and configure the identity provider to map each directory group to its department's role at federation time.

Configure the identity provider to emit the department value in the SAML assertion as the https://aws.amazon.com/SAML/Attributes/PrincipalTag:department attribute, and allow the sts:TagSession action in the shared role's trust policy.
Tag each shared federation role with a department tag so that every session inherits the department of the role it assumes.
Store the department-to-resource mapping in an Amazon DynamoDB table and query it from an AWS Lambda function that approves or denies each S3 request.
Write the shared role's identity-based policies with conditions that compare aws:PrincipalTag/department with the department tag on the target S3 resources.

explanation: B and E are correct. Emitting the directory attribute as a PrincipalTag SAML attribute passes the department as a session tag when the analyst federates, the trust policy must allow sts:TagSession for the tagged session to be created, and policies that compare aws:PrincipalTag/department to the resource's department tag turn that session attribute into the authorization decision. A is wrong because a role per department is the design the security team rejected and reorganizations would force constant role churn. C is wrong because a static tag on a shared role gives every user of that role the same department regardless of who they are. D is wrong because IAM does not consult external Lambda lookups during S3 authorization; that logic cannot intercept API-level access decisions.

stem: A company is onboarding a third-party monitoring SaaS that runs from the vendor's own AWS account and needs read-only telemetry access to the company's production account. The vendor's documentation asks the company to create an IAM role that the vendor's platform will assume. The company's security team is specifically concerned about the confused-deputy scenario, in which another customer of the same vendor tricks the vendor's platform into assuming the company's role, and about the trust policy admitting any principal beyond the vendor's designated integration workload. The vendor's platform serves thousands of customers from the same AWS account. Which combination of trust policy controls addresses these concerns? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add a Condition with Bool aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent set to true so that the vendor's platform must present an MFA token code with every AssumeRole call it makes.
Share the role's ARN with the vendor only through an encrypted channel and treat the ARN as a secret so other customers of the vendor cannot discover it.
Add a Condition that requires the sts:ExternalId value to equal the unique identifier that the vendor's platform generates for the company's integration.
Set a Condition on aws:PrincipalOrgID that matches the vendor's AWS organization ID so that assumption requests from any other organization are rejected.
Set the trust policy's Principal element to the specific IAM role in the vendor's account that serves the company's integration, rather than the vendor's account root or a wildcard.

explanation: C and E are correct. The external ID is the standard confused-deputy defense: the vendor's platform sends the company-specific value only when acting on behalf of the company, so another customer cannot cause the vendor to satisfy the condition, and pinning the Principal to the vendor's specific integration role narrows who can even attempt the assumption. A is wrong because an automated SaaS platform has no MFA device; this condition would simply break the integration. B is wrong because role ARNs follow predictable formats and are not secrets; confidentiality of the ARN provides no authorization control. D is wrong because restricting to the vendor's organization still admits the whole vendor platform acting for any of its customers, which is precisely the confused-deputy case the control must prevent.

stem: A security engineer is reviewing an Amazon SNS topic that receives S3 event notifications for a sensitive ingest workflow. The topic's resource policy contains a statement with Effect: Allow, a Principal of the s3.amazonaws.com service principal, and the sns:Publish action on the topic's ARN, with no conditions. The engineer is concerned that, because the statement trusts the S3 service itself, an S3 bucket owned by a completely different AWS account could be configured to publish notifications into the company's topic. The engineer must constrain the statement so that only the company's designated ingest bucket can use the service to publish. Which changes should the engineer make to the statement? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add a Condition requiring aws:PrincipalOrgID to match the company's organization ID so that requests made through the S3 service principal from other organizations are rejected.
Replace the s3.amazonaws.com service principal in the Principal element with the ARN of the ingest bucket so that only that bucket is trusted to publish.
Attach an identity-based policy to the ingest bucket that allows sns:Publish on the topic so that the publish permission is granted from the bucket's side as well.
Add a Condition requiring aws:SourceAccount to equal the AWS account ID that owns the ingest bucket.
Add a Condition requiring aws:SourceArn to equal the ARN of the designated ingest bucket.

explanation: D and E are correct. When a service principal makes a request on behalf of a resource, aws:SourceAccount and aws:SourceArn identify the account and the specific resource that triggered the call, so requiring the company's account ID and the exact bucket ARN ensures only the designated ingest bucket can publish through the S3 service, which is the standard cross-service confused-deputy mitigation; because an S3 bucket ARN contains no account ID, aws:SourceArn alone cannot constrain the owning account, so AWS requires both keys together. A is wrong because service-principal requests do not carry a customer organization context, so an aws:PrincipalOrgID condition would not match and would break the integration rather than scope it. B is wrong because a bucket ARN is a resource identifier, not a principal, and cannot appear in the Principal element. C is wrong because S3 buckets have no identity-based policies; permissions on the topic side are what govern publishing.

stem: A platform organization wants application developers to create and manage the IAM roles that their own microservices use, because routing every role request through the security team has become a delivery bottleneck. The security team will allow this self-service only if it can guarantee, preventively rather than through after-the-fact review, that no role a developer creates can ever hold permissions beyond a ceiling that the security team defines, no matter which policies the developer attaches to the role. Developers must still be able to create roles and attach policies freely within that ceiling. Which combination of actions establishes this guarantee? (Choose two.)

options.text: Attach a service control policy to the developers' accounts that denies iam:CreateRole and iam:AttachRolePolicy for all developer principals in those accounts.
Create a customer managed policy that defines the security team's maximum allowed permissions, to serve as the permissions boundary for every role that developers create.
Require developers to use only inline policies on the roles they create so that the roles' permissions cannot be shared with or attached to any other principal.
Grant the developers iam:CreateRole and iam:AttachRolePolicy only with a condition that requires the iam:PermissionsBoundary value to equal the approved boundary policy's ARN.
Enable IAM Access Analyzer unused access findings for the developers' accounts and have the security team remove over-privileged roles as findings are raised.

explanation: B and D are correct. The boundary policy defines the ceiling, and conditioning the developers' iam:CreateRole and iam:AttachRolePolicy permissions on iam:PermissionsBoundary equaling that policy's ARN means a role simply cannot be created or modified unless the boundary is attached, after which every role's effective permissions are capped at the intersection with the ceiling. A is wrong because denying role creation outright removes the self-service capability the organization is trying to enable. C is wrong because inline-only policies change where policy documents live, not how much permission they can grant. E is wrong because unused access findings are detective and arrive after creation, while the requirement is an up-front guarantee.

stem: Following a credential-stuffing incident traced to a leaked access key, a company's CISO has mandated the elimination of long-term credentials for all human access across the organization's AWS accounts. Employees currently sign in through a mix of IAM users and ad hoc federation, and some teams still create new IAM users when onboarding staff. The security team must move all workforce sign-in to a model that issues only temporary credentials, and must also prevent teams from quietly recreating long-term human credentials in member accounts in the future. The organization uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. Which combination of actions accomplishes this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Adopt a 30-day access key rotation standard for all IAM users and enforce it with an AWS Config rule that flags keys older than the standard allows.
Move every IAM user's access keys into AWS Secrets Manager and enable automatic rotation so the keys are replaced without human involvement.
Migrate workforce sign-in to AWS IAM Identity Center connected to the corporate identity provider, with permission sets granting each group short-lived role sessions in the accounts they need.
Require MFA on all existing IAM users and disable console passwords for accounts that have not signed in during the past 90 days.
Attach a service control policy to the member account organizational units that denies iam:CreateUser and iam:CreateAccessKey, with an exception path for approved break-glass principals.

explanation: C and E are correct. Identity Center federation replaces IAM user sign-in with short-lived role credentials sourced from the corporate directory, which satisfies the temporary-credentials mandate, and the SCP prevents member account teams from creating new IAM users or access keys going forward, closing the recreation loophole preventively. A is wrong because rotated access keys are still long-term credentials, which the mandate eliminates rather than manages. B is wrong for the same reason; storing and rotating keys in Secrets Manager changes their storage location, not their long-term nature. D is wrong because MFA and password hygiene harden IAM users but keep the long-term credential model the CISO has prohibited.

stem: A security engineer is troubleshooting an application that runs on Amazon EC2 and reads objects from an Amazon S3 bucket that uses SSE-KMS with a customer managed AWS KMS key. The application's instance profile role has an attached IAM policy that allows kms:Decrypt on the key's ARN, yet every read fails with an AccessDenied error that references AWS KMS. The key was created by an infrastructure-as-code pipeline, and its key policy contains only one statement, which designates the pipeline's deployment role as the key administrator. The key and the role are in the same AWS account, and no service control policies or permissions boundaries apply to the role. Which action will resolve the errors?

options.text: Update the key policy to add a statement that allows the application's instance profile role to perform kms:Decrypt on the key.
Attach the AWSKeyManagementServicePowerUser AWS managed policy to the instance profile role so that the role receives broader KMS usage permissions.
Use the application role to call the CreateGrant API operation on the key, creating a grant that authorizes the role itself to decrypt.
Create a permissions boundary that allows kms:Decrypt on the key's ARN and attach the boundary to the instance profile role.

explanation: A is correct. Access to a KMS key always starts at the key policy: unless the key policy names the caller directly or contains the default statement that delegates authorization to IAM policies in the account, an IAM allow by itself has no effect. This key policy contains only an administrator statement, so the role must be added to the key policy. B is wrong because a managed policy is still an identity-based policy, and the key policy does not delegate to IAM policies, so the AccessDenied error persists. C is wrong because a principal can create a grant only if it already holds kms:CreateGrant authorization on the key, which this role lacks. D is wrong because a permissions boundary only limits what a role's policies may allow; it never grants additional access.

stem: A SaaS provider runs a multi-tenant document-processing platform in which short-lived worker tasks are launched thousands of times per hour. Each task must be able to decrypt exactly one tenant's data with that tenant's customer managed AWS KMS key for the duration of one job, and the permission must be revocable within seconds of job completion. The security team has ruled out editing key policies on a per-job basis because the key policy document has a size limit and policy updates are subject to eventual consistency. The mechanism must be fully programmatic, and a task must be able to use its new permission immediately after it is issued. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Update the tenant key's policy at job start to add the task role, and remove that statement from the key policy as soon as the job completes.
Create a KMS grant for the task role on the tenant key at job start, pass the returned grant token with the first requests, and call RetireGrant when the job completes.
Attach an inline IAM policy that allows kms:Decrypt on the tenant key to the task role at job start, and delete the inline policy from the role when the job completes.
Add a kms:ViaService condition to each tenant key's policy so that only requests that arrive through the document-processing platform's service endpoints can decrypt.

explanation: B is correct. Grants are the KMS mechanism designed for temporary, programmatic permission delegation: they are created and retired through API calls, the grant token lets the grantee use the permission immediately without waiting for the grant to propagate, and RetireGrant removes the permission as soon as the job ends. A is wrong because the team has already ruled out per-job key policy edits, which hit the policy size limit and are subject to eventual consistency. C is wrong because IAM policy changes also propagate with eventual consistency, so neither immediate use nor seconds-level revocation is guaranteed, and the key policy would still have to delegate to IAM. D is wrong because kms:ViaService matches only requests made through integrated AWS services, not the provider's own application code, and it is not a per-job revocable permission.

stem: A financial services company stores regulated documents in Amazon S3 buckets in eu-central-1 that use SSE-KMS with a dedicated customer managed key. An internal audit found that several administrator roles hold broad kms:* permissions through identity-based policies. The security team must guarantee that the dedicated key can be used for cryptographic operations only when the request comes through Amazon S3 in eu-central-1 on behalf of an authorized principal; direct kms:Decrypt calls from an administrator's workstation must fail. The control must be enforced on the key itself so that it cannot be bypassed by IAM policies created in the future, and the administrators' existing IAM policies must not be modified. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Attach a service control policy to the account that denies kms:Decrypt and kms:Encrypt whenever the aws:RequestedRegion value is not eu-central-1.
Create a VPC interface endpoint for AWS KMS and configure an endpoint policy that allows cryptographic operations only when they originate from Amazon S3.
Scope the cryptographic permission statements in the key policy with a condition that requires kms:ViaService to equal s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com.
Add an aws:CalledVia condition that lists Amazon S3 to each administrator's identity-based policy so that only service-initiated calls are allowed.

explanation: C is correct. The kms:ViaService condition key restricts a key policy statement so that it matches only requests that an integrated AWS service, here Amazon S3 in eu-central-1, makes to KMS on behalf of a principal. Because the condition lives in the key policy, a direct Decrypt call from a workstation fails no matter what IAM policies the caller holds, and no future IAM policy can bypass it. A is wrong because a Region-based SCP still permits direct KMS calls made in eu-central-1, so it does not require that requests flow through S3. B is wrong because an endpoint policy governs only traffic that traverses that specific endpoint; direct calls from workstations over other paths are unaffected. D is wrong because it requires modifying the administrators' IAM policies, which the requirements forbid, and Amazon S3 does not populate the aws:CalledVia context key.

stem: A multi-tenant application stores each tenant's records as ciphertext attributes in a shared Amazon DynamoDB table. The application encrypts and decrypts the attributes by calling AWS KMS directly with a single shared customer managed key, and every cryptographic call supplies an encryption context of TenantId with the tenant's identifier. Each tenant is served by a dedicated IAM role. Compliance now requires cryptographic enforcement of tenant isolation: even if a tenant's role somehow reads another tenant's ciphertext from the table, that role must be unable to decrypt it. The company must keep using the single existing key because per-tenant keys would exceed the key-management scope agreed with its auditors. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable fine-grained access control on the table with a dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition so that each tenant role can read only the items in its own partition.
Create a separate DynamoDB table for each tenant and scope each tenant role's DynamoDB permissions to only its own table's ARN.
Add a kms:ViaService condition to the key policy so that the shared key can be used only through DynamoDB in the workload's Region.
In the key policy, scope each tenant role's kms:Decrypt permission with a kms:EncryptionContext:TenantId condition that must equal that tenant's own identifier.

explanation: D is correct. KMS validates the encryption context supplied on Decrypt against the context bound to the ciphertext, and the kms:EncryptionContext:TenantId condition makes each tenant role's decrypt permission valid only for ciphertext whose context carries that tenant's identifier. Even with another tenant's ciphertext in hand, the role's Decrypt call fails the key policy condition, which is cryptographic-boundary enforcement on the single shared key. A is wrong because dynamodb:LeadingKeys controls which items can be read, not what can be decrypted; ciphertext obtained through any other path would still decrypt. B is wrong because per-tenant tables are an access-control change, not a cryptographic one, and any role that obtains ciphertext could still decrypt it with the shared key. C is wrong because the application calls KMS directly, so a kms:ViaService restriction to DynamoDB would break the application and still would not distinguish one tenant from another.

stem: A data-lake bucket in account A stores objects encrypted with SSE-KMS under a customer managed key that also resides in account A. An analytics role in account B must read the objects. The bucket policy in account A already allows the account B role to perform s3:GetObject on the bucket and its objects, and the role can list the bucket successfully. However, every GetObject call fails with an AccessDenied error that references AWS KMS. The key policy in account A currently contains only the default statement that delegates authorization to IAM policies within account A. Which change will allow the analytics role to read the objects?

options.text: Add a key policy statement in account A that allows the account B role to perform kms:Decrypt, and attach an IAM policy to the role in account B that allows kms:Decrypt on the key's ARN.
Attach an IAM policy to the role in account B that allows kms:Decrypt on the key's ARN; the key policy needs no change because the bucket policy already grants cross-account access to the objects.

Add a key policy statement in account A that allows the account B role to perform kms:Decrypt; nothing is needed in account B because a key policy statement alone fully authorizes an external principal.

Update the bucket policy in account A to also allow the kms:Decrypt action for the account B role, because Amazon S3 forwards its bucket policy permissions to AWS KMS when it decrypts the objects that it returns to the caller.

explanation: A is correct. Cross-account use of a KMS key requires permission from both sides: the key policy in the key's account must allow the external principal, and an IAM policy in the caller's account must allow the same KMS actions on the key. S3 uses the caller's credentials for the KMS Decrypt, so both pieces are needed. B is wrong because the key policy delegates only to IAM policies within account A; without a key policy statement for the account B principal, the IAM allow in account B authorizes nothing. C is wrong because, unlike same-account access, cross-account access is not complete with the key policy alone; the caller's own account must also delegate the permission through an IAM policy. D is wrong because kms:Decrypt is not an S3 action and cannot be granted in a bucket policy; S3 does not forward bucket permissions to KMS.

stem: A security engineer must harden an Amazon S3 bucket that receives regulated telemetry from hundreds of internal producer applications. Two controls are mandated. First, any request that arrives over unencrypted HTTP must be rejected. Second, every uploaded object must be encrypted with one specific customer managed AWS KMS key; uploads that specify a different KMS key or a different server-side encryption type must be rejected rather than accepted with different protection. All producers set explicit server-side-encryption headers on their uploads, but some name a different KMS key or a different encryption type, so the enforcement must be implemented in the bucket's own policy rather than in client configuration. Which combination of bucket policy statements meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: A Deny statement covering all S3 actions on the bucket and its objects with a condition of Bool aws:SecureTransport equal to false.
An Allow statement for s3:PutObject with a condition that s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption equals aws:kms, so that only KMS-encrypted uploads receive permission.
A Deny statement covering all S3 actions on the bucket and its objects with a condition of Bool aws:SecureTransport equal to true.
A Deny statement for s3:PutObject with a condition that aws:PrincipalOrgID does not match the company's organization identifier.
A Deny statement for s3:PutObject with a condition that s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id does not equal the required key's ARN.

explanation: A and E are correct. A denies every request whose aws:SecureTransport value is false, which is exactly the set of plaintext HTTP requests, and an explicit deny cannot be overridden by any allow. E denies any upload whose s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id value is not the required key's ARN, so uploads that name a different key, or that do not resolve to the required key at all, are rejected at request time. B is wrong because an Allow statement never rejects anything; principals with other allows could still upload objects with different encryption, and it also fails to pin the specific key. C is wrong because its logic is inverted; it would deny exactly the TLS traffic that must be permitted. D is wrong because an organization-membership perimeter addresses neither of the two mandated controls.

stem: A company imported its own key material from an on-premises HSM into a symmetric AWS KMS key with origin EXTERNAL two years ago, satisfying a policy that all cryptographic material must originate in hardware the company controls. The same policy requires the encryption material to be rotated every 12 months. A security engineer tried to enable automatic key rotation on the key from the console, but the operation failed. All applications reference the key through an alias rather than a key ID, and the company will generate the replacement material in the same on-premises HSM. The engineer must implement rotation while ensuring that data encrypted under the old material remains decryptable. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Open an AWS Support case to enable automatic rotation for the key, because rotation of imported key material requires an account-level opt-in from AWS before the feature becomes available in the account.

Generate new material in the on-premises HSM, import it into the existing key as pending rotation material, and call RotateKeyOnDemand so the key rotates in place while earlier material remains available for decryption.
Create a new KMS key with origin EXTERNAL, import the newly generated key material into it, and repoint the alias to the new key while retaining the old key for decryption.
Convert the existing key into a multi-Region primary key and create a replica, because each replica receives freshly generated key material that satisfies the rotation requirement.

explanation: B is correct. AWS KMS supports on-demand rotation for keys with imported material: the engineer imports the newly generated material into the same key, where it waits in the PENDING_ROTATION state, and then calls RotateKeyOnDemand. The key ID, ARN, and alias never change, and KMS retains every earlier version of the imported material as long as it has not expired or been removed with DeleteImportedKeyMaterial, so ciphertext encrypted before the rotation still decrypts transparently. A is wrong because no support opt-in exists; automatic annual rotation is genuinely unsupported for the EXTERNAL origin, and on-demand rotation is the only rotation KMS offers for it. C is wrong because creating a replacement key and re-pointing the alias is the legacy workaround: it still works, but it proliferates keys and churns the ARN behind the alias, operational overhead that rotating the existing key in place eliminates. D is wrong because an existing single-Region key cannot be converted to multi-Region, and replica keys deliberately share the same key material as the primary, so nothing would rotate.

stem: A healthcare company is designing disaster recovery for a new application that will encrypt patient records client-side with the AWS Encryption SDK before writing them to Amazon S3, with cross-Region replication carrying the objects to a recovery Region. The recovery objective requires the standby stack in the second Region to decrypt records without making any cross-Region calls to AWS KMS in the primary Region, because the plan must tolerate a complete primary-Region outage. Re-encrypting the existing ciphertext during a failover is not acceptable, because the dataset is expected to reach hundreds of terabytes. The application has not launched yet, so the team can choose its key architecture now. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an independent customer managed key in each Region and configure the standby stack to decrypt the replicated ciphertext with the recovery Region's own key.
Create a single-Region key in the primary Region and rely on S3 replication to re-encrypt each replica object under a destination key in the recovery Region.
Create a multi-Region primary key in the primary Region, replicate it into the recovery Region, and configure each stack to call only its local Region's key.
Create a single-Region key in the primary Region and grant the standby stack cross-Region access so that it can call the primary Region's KMS endpoint during a failover.

explanation: C is correct. Multi-Region key pairs share the same key material and key ID, so ciphertext produced under the primary key decrypts under the replica key in the recovery Region. Each stack calls only its local KMS endpoint, no re-encryption is ever needed, and a full primary-Region outage does not affect the standby's ability to decrypt. A is wrong because two independent keys have unrelated key material; ciphertext encrypted under the primary Region's key can never be decrypted by the other key. B is wrong because the records are encrypted client-side, so S3 replication moves opaque ciphertext; destination re-encryption applies only to server-side encryption and cannot rewrap Encryption SDK output. D is wrong because it depends on the primary Region's KMS endpoint being reachable, which is exactly what the plan assumes is unavailable.

stem: A media company must encrypt video master files, each between 1 GB and 40 GB in size, before uploading them to an archival system that is not an AWS service. Security policy requires that the encryption keys be protected by a customer managed AWS KMS key and that no plaintext key material be persisted anywhere. Engineers first attempted to call the KMS Encrypt API operation directly on the files, but every call was rejected because of the operation's payload limit. The solution must minimize the number of KMS API calls per file and must keep all bulk cryptographic work local to the processing instances rather than inside AWS KMS. Which approach should the company use?

options.text: Call GenerateDataKey once per file, encrypt the file locally with the returned plaintext data key, discard that plaintext key from memory, and store the encrypted data key alongside the file.
Split each file into 4 KB segments and call the KMS Encrypt API operation on each segment, storing the ordered ciphertext segments so that the file can be reassembled after decryption.
Create an asymmetric RSA KMS key and call the Encrypt API operation on each whole file with the public key, because asymmetric keys are not subject to the symmetric payload limit.
Request a service quota increase to raise the maximum Encrypt payload size so that each file can be encrypted with a single Encrypt call against the customer managed key.

explanation: A is correct. This is envelope encryption: GenerateDataKey returns a plaintext data key and a copy encrypted under the customer managed key, the bulk encryption happens locally in one pass, the plaintext key is discarded, and only the KMS-wrapped data key is stored. Each file costs a single KMS call, and no plaintext key material persists. B is wrong because a 40 GB file would require millions of Encrypt calls, with enormous cost and latency, and KMS would perform all the cryptographic work the requirements say must stay local. C is wrong because RSA encryption payloads are limited to less than the key size, a few hundred bytes, so asymmetric keys are even more constrained, not less. D is wrong because the roughly 4 KB Encrypt payload limit is a fixed property of the API, not an adjustable service quota.

stem: After an acquisition, a security team discovers that a newly absorbed production account contains hundreds of unencrypted Amazon EBS volumes attached to running instances, and that new unencrypted volumes keep appearing because dozens of teams launch instances from a mix of launch templates, CloudFormation stacks, and third-party CI/CD tools that the security team cannot modify. The team must ensure that every newly created volume in the account's active Regions is encrypted with the company's customer managed KMS key without causing any launch or volume-creation request to fail, and the team must also bring the existing unencrypted volumes into compliance. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Modify each existing unencrypted volume's encryption attribute so that the volume is converted to an encrypted volume in place with the customer managed key and without detaching it.
Enable EBS encryption by default in every Region that the account uses, and set the customer managed key as the default encryption key in each Region.
Deploy the AWS Config encrypted-volumes managed rule with an automatic remediation action that converts noncompliant volumes to encrypted volumes in place.
Attach a service control policy that denies ec2:RunInstances and ec2:CreateVolume whenever the request does not set the volume encryption flag to true.
Snapshot each unencrypted volume, copy the snapshot with encryption under the customer managed key, create replacement volumes from the encrypted copies, and swap the attachments.

explanation: B and E are correct. B makes encryption automatic at creation time: with encryption by default enabled, every new volume and snapshot restore in the Region is encrypted under the configured key regardless of what the launch template, stack, or tool specifies, and requests succeed rather than fail. E is the only way to encrypt existing data, because EBS encryption cannot be turned on for a volume after creation; the snapshot-copy-restore-swap sequence produces encrypted replacements. A is wrong because no in-place encryption attribute exists for EBS volumes. C is wrong for the same reason; a remediation action cannot convert a volume in place, so the rule can only detect. D is wrong because an SCP rejects noncompliant requests, causing exactly the launch failures the requirements prohibit, and it does nothing for the existing volumes.

stem: A payments platform encrypts several thousand small messages per second in an AWS Lambda function by using the AWS Encryption SDK with a customer managed KMS key. During traffic spikes, the function's GenerateDataKey calls are throttled and end-to-end latency rises sharply. The security team will allow a single data key to protect more than one message, but only within strict bounds: a reused key must never be used for longer than five minutes or for more than 1,000 messages. The solution must reduce the volume of KMS requests without changing the message format that downstream consumers already decrypt with the same SDK. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Request an increase to the account's KMS request-rate quota so that GenerateDataKey calls stop being throttled during the platform's traffic spikes.
Configure the Encryption SDK's data key caching with a caching cryptographic materials manager that enforces a maximum age of five minutes and a maximum of 1,000 messages per cached key.
Generate one data key when each Lambda execution environment initializes and reuse it for every message that the environment processes until the environment is recycled.
Replace the Encryption SDK in the function with direct kms:Encrypt calls for each individual message so that the function no longer needs to generate or manage any data keys at all.

explanation: B is correct. Data key caching in the AWS Encryption SDK exists precisely for this pattern: the caching cryptographic materials manager reuses a data key across messages while enforcing configured security thresholds for maximum age, maximum messages, and maximum bytes, which maps directly to the five-minute and 1,000-message bounds, and the output remains standard Encryption SDK format. A is wrong because a quota increase leaves one KMS call per message, so request volume is not reduced and costs keep scaling with traffic. C is wrong because a Lambda execution environment can live for hours and process unbounded messages, so the five-minute and 1,000-message limits would be violated. D is wrong because it makes one KMS call per message, worsening the throttling, and it changes the ciphertext format that downstream Encryption SDK consumers expect.

stem: An advertising analytics company writes hundreds of millions of small objects each day to an Amazon S3 bucket that uses SSE-KMS with a customer managed key. A cost review shows that AWS KMS request charges generated by the bucket's encryption traffic now exceed the storage cost itself. Security requirements state that objects must remain encrypted under the existing customer managed key so that key usage stays auditable in AWS CloudTrail and access can still be revoked through the key policy. The change must not require any modification to the many producer and consumer applications that write and read the objects. Which change reduces the KMS request charges while meeting the requirements?

options.text: Change the bucket's default encryption to SSE-S3 so that Amazon S3 manages the encryption keys itself and object operations stop generating KMS requests.
Change the bucket's default encryption to the AWS managed key aws/s3 so that the bucket's encryption traffic is billed to the Amazon S3 service rather than to the account's own KMS usage.
Enable an S3 Bucket Key on the bucket so that S3 uses a short-lived bucket-level key derived from the customer managed key instead of calling KMS for each object.
Introduce client-side data key caching with the AWS Encryption SDK in every producer application so that data keys are reused across many uploaded objects.

explanation: C is correct. An S3 Bucket Key is a bucket-level key that S3 obtains from the customer managed key and then uses to generate per-object data keys locally, cutting KMS requests, and therefore request charges, dramatically while objects remain protected under the same customer managed key with CloudTrail-auditable usage and key policy revocation intact; no application changes are required. A is wrong because SSE-S3 removes the customer managed key entirely, losing both the key policy revocation control and per-key CloudTrail auditability. B is wrong because SSE-KMS with the aws/s3 managed key still makes billable KMS requests, and an AWS managed key has no customer-editable key policy. D is wrong because it requires modifying every producer application and changes the object format for consumers, which the requirements prohibit.

stem: A defense contractor must store sensitive artifacts in Amazon S3 under a control framework that mandates two independent layers of encryption at rest, each layer using distinct data keys, so that a defect in one cryptographic layer cannot expose plaintext. The upload pipeline is a packaged third-party product: the team can set request headers and bucket defaults, but it cannot embed custom encryption code into the product. The protecting keys must be managed in AWS KMS with usage auditable in CloudTrail, and the team wants both layers applied server side by Amazon S3 so that download behavior remains unchanged for existing consumers. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure the pipeline to upload with SSE-KMS and enable an S3 Bucket Key so that the bucket-level key and the per-object data key together form the two required layers.
Encrypt each artifact with the AWS Encryption SDK before upload and store the result with SSE-KMS so that a client-side layer and a server-side layer combine.
Upload the artifacts with SSE-C over TLS and enable SSE-S3 default encryption so that the customer-provided layer and the S3 managed layer apply together.
Set the bucket's default encryption to DSSE-KMS with a customer managed key so that S3 applies dual-layer server-side encryption with two distinct data keys per object.

explanation: D is correct. DSSE-KMS is dual-layer server-side encryption: Amazon S3 encrypts each object twice with two distinct data keys derived through the customer managed KMS key, satisfying the two-independent-layers mandate entirely server side, with normal GET behavior for consumers and KMS usage recorded in CloudTrail. A is wrong because an S3 Bucket Key is a cost optimization within single-layer SSE-KMS; the object is still encrypted once, so there is only one layer of object encryption. B is wrong because the packaged product cannot embed custom encryption code, so a client-side Encryption SDK layer is not implementable, and downloads would return ciphertext to consumers. C is wrong because SSE-C and SSE-S3 are mutually exclusive server-side options for an object, and SSE-C would force the team to manage and transmit raw keys outside KMS.

stem: A security team is decommissioning an application and wants to delete its dedicated customer managed AWS KMS key. Historical CloudTrail data shows no key usage for 60 days, but the team knows that other workloads may hold ciphertext, EBS snapshots, or backups that silently depend on the key, and that ciphertext encrypted under a deleted key is unrecoverable forever. The team wants to retire the key in the way that MOST safely surfaces any remaining dependency before the key material is destroyed, and it also wants an alert if any principal attempts to use the key during the retirement period. Which approach should the team take?

options.text: Disable the key, alarm on CloudTrail events that record attempted use of the disabled key, and schedule deletion with a 30-day waiting period only after a clean observation window.

Schedule the key for deletion with the minimum seven-day waiting period, because KMS blocks cryptographic use during the pending window and the deletion can still be canceled at any time before the window expires.
Delete the key's alias so that applications can no longer resolve it, watch for application errors for a month, and then schedule the key for deletion.
Remove every statement except the administrator statement from the key policy so that usage attempts fail with AccessDenied, and schedule deletion once no complaints arrive.

explanation: A is correct. Disabling a key is fully reversible and makes every use attempt fail in a way that CloudTrail records, so an alarm on those events surfaces hidden dependencies; only after a clean observation window does the team schedule deletion, and choosing the maximum 30-day waiting period preserves the longest possible recovery runway. B is wrong because jumping straight to deletion with the shortest window compresses the discovery period to seven days and puts a destruction deadline behind any dependency that surfaces late. C is wrong because deleting an alias does not stop use of the key: callers that reference the key ID, and services that recorded the key ID in resource metadata, keep working, so dependencies stay invisible. D is wrong because gutting the key policy risks locking out legitimate administration, and silence from users is a far weaker signal than alarmed CloudTrail evidence.

stem: A company must give its data-science account, account B, a copy of a production Amazon RDS for MySQL database that runs in account A. The production instance has storage encryption enabled with a customer managed AWS KMS key that resides in account A. A database engineer in account A plans to share a snapshot so that account B can restore its own instance, but the engineer's first attempt, which tried to share the most recent automated snapshot, was rejected by the console. The data must remain encrypted at every step of the process. Which combination of steps will make an encrypted snapshot usable in account B? (Choose two.)

options.text: Change the sharing settings of the automated snapshot to add account B directly, because automated snapshots support cross-account sharing once storage encryption is enabled.
Copy the snapshot and re-encrypt the copy with the default aws/rds managed key before sharing it, because AWS managed keys simplify cross-account restores.
Mark the encrypted snapshot as public so that account B can copy it, and then revert the snapshot to private after the copy has completed.
Create a manual copy of the snapshot that is encrypted with the customer managed key, and share that manual snapshot with account B.
Update the customer managed key's policy in account A to allow account B to use the key, including kms:Decrypt, kms:DescribeKey, and kms:CreateGrant.

explanation: D and E are correct. Automated snapshots cannot be shared, so the engineer must create a manual copy, and sharing that encrypted copy is only half the job: account B can copy or restore it only if the customer managed key's policy in account A grants account B use of the key, including the ability to create grants for the RDS service in account B. A is wrong because RDS does not allow sharing automated snapshots with other accounts under any encryption setting. B is wrong because snapshots encrypted with the default aws/rds AWS managed key can never be shared cross-account, and an AWS managed key's policy cannot be edited to allow it. C is wrong because encrypted snapshots cannot be made public, and public exposure would violate the requirement to keep the data protected.

stem: A company is migrating a customer-records service to Amazon DynamoDB and is selecting the table's encryption-at-rest configuration. The security requirements state that the security team must be able to restrict which principals can use the encryption key through a resource-based key policy, must see every use of the key attributed to the calling service context in AWS CloudTrail, and must be able to immediately disable the key if a compromise is suspected, rendering the table's data unreadable until the key is re-enabled. The application team refuses to add any client-side encryption code to the service. Which encryption configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Use the default AWS owned key for the table, and rely on CloudTrail data events for DynamoDB to provide the required audit trail of access.
Use a customer managed AWS KMS key for the table so that the key policy, CloudTrail key-usage logging, and the ability to disable the key remain under the team's control.
Use the AWS managed key aws/dynamodb for the table, which records every use of the key in CloudTrail and is rotated automatically by AWS every year without any customer management effort.
Keep the default AWS owned key for the table and add client-side encryption for the sensitive attributes with the AWS Database Encryption SDK.

explanation: B is correct. Only a customer managed key delivers all three controls: the team writes the key policy, every cryptographic use of the key appears in CloudTrail, and the team can disable the key at will, which makes the table's data unreadable until re-enabled. A is wrong because an AWS owned key belongs to a DynamoDB-managed key pool: it has no key policy the customer can see, its use is not logged to the customer's CloudTrail, and it cannot be disabled. C is wrong because although the aws/dynamodb managed key does log usage to CloudTrail, its key policy cannot be modified to restrict principals and the key cannot be disabled by the customer. D is wrong because it violates the no-client-side-code constraint and still leaves the table-level key outside the team's control.

stem: During an annual compliance audit, a security engineer proposes enabling automatic key rotation on a symmetric customer managed AWS KMS key that has protected several years of Amazon S3 objects through SSE-KMS. The auditors, who are accustomed to certificate renewals that require redeployment work, ask the engineer to document exactly what will happen to the existing ciphertext and to the applications that use the key when automatic rotation is enabled and the first yearly rotation occurs. The key was created with KMS-generated key material, every application references the key through its alias, and no key policies or grants will change as part of the proposal. What should the engineer document as the effect of the first rotation?

options.text: Amazon S3 re-encrypts every existing object under the new key material as soon as the rotation completes, which temporarily increases KMS request charges for large buckets.
Existing ciphertext becomes undecryptable until it is re-encrypted, so the team must run a batch re-encryption job across the buckets before the first rotation date arrives.
KMS generates new key material for future encryption operations while retaining all previous material, so existing ciphertext still decrypts and no application or data changes are needed.
The rotation creates a new key with a new key ID, and the alias moves to it automatically, so applications keep working but old objects need the previous key ID.

explanation: C is correct. Automatic rotation generates new backing key material once a year, but the key keeps its key ID, ARN, alias, policies, and grants; KMS retains every previous version of the material and transparently selects the correct one when decrypting, so existing ciphertext stays readable, nothing is re-encrypted, and applications continue unchanged. The same semantics apply to on-demand rotations triggered between yearly cycles. A is wrong because rotation never touches stored data; Amazon S3 does not re-encrypt objects when a key's material rotates. B is wrong because the retained previous material guarantees that old ciphertext keeps decrypting, so no re-encryption job is required. D is wrong because automatic rotation does not create a new key or change the key ID; creating a replacement key and repointing the alias describes manual rotation, which is one option for keys that automatic rotation does not support; keys with imported material can instead be rotated in place on demand.

stem: A European bank's regulator requires that the cryptographic keys protecting a new workload reside in single-tenant hardware security modules dedicated to the bank, with the bank retaining exclusive control over the HSM user accounts and the ability to zeroize the hardware. At the same time, the workload teams must keep using native integrations, specifically SSE-KMS on Amazon S3 and encrypted Amazon EBS volumes, through standard AWS KMS API operations. The key material must remain hosted inside AWS Regions, and the bank rejects any solution whose availability depends on its own on-premises data centers. The bank's internal auditors will review the HSM user configuration and zeroization procedures each year. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use standard customer managed keys in AWS KMS, because KMS stores key material in FIPS-validated HSMs and key policies give the bank full control over key usage.
Provision an AWS CloudHSM cluster and integrate the workloads with the cluster directly through the PKCS #11 and JCE client libraries instead of the AWS KMS API.
Create a KMS external key store backed by HSMs in the bank's own data centers, connected to AWS KMS through an external key store proxy.
Create an AWS CloudHSM key store for AWS KMS backed by a dedicated CloudHSM cluster, and create the workload's KMS keys inside that key store.

explanation: D is correct. A CloudHSM key store, the CloudHSM-backed custom key store, roots KMS keys in a single-tenant CloudHSM cluster that the bank exclusively controls, including HSM users and the ability to zeroize, while the keys remain ordinary KMS keys that S3 SSE-KMS and EBS encryption consume through standard KMS APIs, all hosted inside AWS Regions. A is wrong because standard KMS keys live in a multi-tenant HSM fleet operated by AWS; key policies control usage but do not give the bank dedicated hardware or the power to zeroize it. B is wrong because bypassing KMS for direct CloudHSM client integration abandons the required native SSE-KMS and EBS integrations. C is wrong because an external key store deliberately places key material outside AWS in the bank's data centers, violating both the in-AWS hosting requirement and the ban on on-premises availability dependencies.

stem: An engineering team integrates with a payment vendor whose API key must be rotated every 30 days under the vendor contract, and the vendor exposes a management API that can issue a new key and revoke the old one. Today the API key is hard-coded in application configuration files and redeployed manually at each rotation, which has already caused two outages. The security team requires that the credential be stored encrypted under a customer managed AWS KMS key, that applications fetch the current value at runtime instead of embedding it, and that rotation run automatically on schedule against the vendor's management API. The vendor is not one of the Secrets Manager integration partners, so no managed external secret type exists for it. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Store the API key as a SecureString parameter in Systems Manager Parameter Store and turn on the parameter's built-in automatic rotation schedule.
Store the API key in AWS Secrets Manager and enable managed rotation, which rotates credentials for third-party services without requiring any rotation function.
Store the API key in AWS Secrets Manager as a secret encrypted with the customer managed KMS key, and update the applications to fetch the secret at runtime.
Configure automatic rotation every 30 days with a custom AWS Lambda rotation function that calls the vendor's management API to issue a new key and revoke the old one.
Store the API key in a server-side encrypted Amazon DynamoDB table and schedule an EventBridge rule that starts a rotation workflow in AWS Step Functions to call the vendor's management API.

explanation: C and D are correct. Secrets Manager stores the credential encrypted under the chosen customer managed key and serves it to applications at runtime through GetSecretValue, and because the credential belongs to a third-party service, rotation is implemented with a custom Lambda rotation function that Secrets Manager invokes on the 30-day schedule to call the vendor's management API, update the secret, and revoke the old key. A is wrong because Parameter Store has no built-in rotation capability for SecureString parameters. B is wrong because Lambda-free managed rotation applies to supported AWS database credentials and to the managed external secrets of Secrets Manager integration partners; the stem states this vendor is not an integration partner, so a rotation function is still required. E is wrong because a DynamoDB table plus a hand-built Step Functions workflow re-creates what Secrets Manager provides, without versioned staging labels or a standard runtime retrieval interface, and adds unnecessary operational burden.

stem: An operations team runs a fleet of NGINX reverse proxies on Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises virtual machines, all serving the same public domain. TLS must terminate inside the NGINX processes themselves, so each proxy needs the certificate and its private key available on the local file system. The team wants certificates that public clients trust by default, wants issuance and lifecycle management handled through AWS Certificate Manager rather than a third-party certificate authority, and accepts the per-certificate fee that this model carries. The team asks a security engineer how ACM can supply certificates for this architecture today. What should the engineer recommend?

options.text: Request an exportable public certificate from ACM, then export the certificate with its encrypted private key and a passphrase for installation on each proxy.
Request a standard public certificate from ACM and use the console's download action to retrieve the private key for distribution to the proxy fleet.
Create an AWS Private CA, issue exportable certificates from it, and install the private CA's root certificate on each proxy so that the chain validates.
Provision the certificate on an Application Load Balancer tier instead, and configure each NGINX proxy to terminate TLS by referencing the load balancer's certificate ARN.

explanation: A is correct. ACM supports exportable public certificates, a paid option chosen at request time, which allows the certificate and its passphrase-encrypted private key to be exported and installed on workloads that terminate TLS themselves, including EC2 instances and on-premises machines, while ACM remains the issuing and management service. B is wrong because standard, non-exportable ACM public certificates never release their private keys; there is no download action for them. C is wrong because certificates chained to an AWS Private CA are not trusted by default in public clients, so visitors would see trust errors, and installing the root on each proxy fixes only the servers, not the browsers. D is wrong because a certificate ARN is usable only by integrated AWS services; an NGINX process cannot terminate TLS by referencing an ACM ARN, and the requirement is termination in NGINX itself.

stem: A company's public web application sits behind an Application Load Balancer. Last year an engineer purchased a one-year certificate from a third-party certificate authority and imported it into AWS Certificate Manager, and that certificate is now 30 days from expiry. The ACM console shows the certificate's renewal eligibility as ineligible. The security team wants all future expirations for this domain handled automatically, with no recurring manual steps and no annual purchase workflow, while keeping the same domain name on the same load balancer listener. The team controls the domain's public DNS zone in Amazon Route 53. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST ongoing operational effort?

options.text: Enable managed renewal on the imported certificate so that ACM contacts the issuing third-party certificate authority and renews the certificate before each expiration.
Request a new public certificate from ACM for the domain with DNS validation, create the validation CNAME record in Route 53, and associate the new certificate with the listener.
Create a scheduled AWS Lambda function that purchases a replacement certificate from the third-party certificate authority each year, imports it into ACM, and updates the listener.

Request a new public certificate from ACM with email validation so that renewal notices are sent to the domain's registered contacts for a one-click approval each time the certificate approaches expiration.

explanation: B is correct. An ACM-issued public certificate with DNS validation renews automatically for as long as the validation CNAME record remains in the zone and the certificate stays associated with a supported service such as the ALB, so after the one-time issuance there are no recurring steps and no purchases. A is wrong because imported certificates are never eligible for ACM managed renewal; ACM cannot renew certificates it did not issue, which is exactly why the console reports ineligibility. C is wrong because it institutionalizes the annual purchase workflow inside custom code that must itself be maintained, credentialed, and monitored. D is wrong because email-validated certificates depend on a person responding to validation mail before renewals complete, which is a recurring manual step that DNS validation eliminates.

stem: A compliance framework requires that traffic to an internal claims-processing application be encrypted in transit on every network hop, including the hop between the load balancer and the application instances inside the VPC. The application currently runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener, and the ALB forwards requests to the target group over HTTP on port 80. The security team must close the unencrypted hop while continuing to use the AWS WAF web ACL that is associated with the load balancer for layer 7 inspection of incoming requests. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer TCP listener that passes TLS through to the instances so that traffic is never decrypted at the load balancer.
Keep the configuration unchanged, because traffic between an Application Load Balancer and targets inside the same VPC is transparently encrypted by the underlying network fabric.
Install certificates on the application instances, configure the application to serve HTTPS, and change the target group protocol to HTTPS so that the ALB re-encrypts traffic to the targets.
Enable TLS session stickiness on the existing HTTP target group so that the ALB reuses each client's negotiated TLS session when it forwards requests to the targets.

explanation: C is correct. With an HTTPS target group and certificates on the instances, the ALB terminates the client TLS session, performs its layer 7 processing, and establishes a new TLS connection to each target, so every hop is encrypted while the WAF web ACL stays attached to the ALB and keeps inspecting requests. A is wrong because AWS WAF cannot be associated with a Network Load Balancer; TCP passthrough would close the hop but sacrifice the mandated layer 7 inspection. B is wrong because ALB-to-target traffic configured as HTTP is plaintext at the protocol layer; opportunistic encryption on some Nitro hardware paths is not a control the team configures, audits, or can claim for compliance. D is wrong because TLS session stickiness does not exist; stickiness controls target selection, and no setting extends a client's TLS session across an HTTP target group.

stem: A security engineer enabled cross-Region replication within one account from a source Amazon S3 bucket to a destination bucket, using a dedicated IAM role, to support disaster recovery. Objects in the source bucket are encrypted with SSE-KMS under customer managed key K1 in the source Region, and replicated objects must be stored encrypted under customer managed key K2 in the destination Region. After the rule was enabled, the engineer observed that objects encrypted with SSE-S3 replicate correctly, but none of the SSE-KMS objects replicate, and the replication configuration saved without any errors. Which combination of changes will make the SSE-KMS objects replicate? (Choose two.)

options.text: Update the replication rule so that it includes objects encrypted with SSE-KMS, and specify K2 as the replica encryption key for objects written to the destination.
Update the replication role's permissions so that the role can use K1 for kms:Decrypt in the source Region and K2 for kms:Encrypt in the destination Region.
Enable an S3 Bucket Key on the destination bucket so that the replication traffic no longer needs to make per-object requests to AWS KMS.
Change the source bucket's default encryption setting to SSE-S3 so that newly written objects no longer require KMS decryption during replication.
Add a bucket policy to the destination bucket that names the source bucket's ARN as the principal and allows it to perform the s3:ReplicateObject and s3:ReplicateDelete actions on the destination.

explanation: A and B are correct. S3 replication skips SSE-KMS objects unless the rule explicitly opts in to replicating KMS-encrypted objects and names a replica KMS key for the destination, which A configures. Replication then runs as the dedicated role, so that role must be able to decrypt source objects under K1 and encrypt replicas under K2, which B grants; without both, the KMS objects continue to be silently skipped. C is wrong because a Bucket Key only reduces the number of KMS requests for cost purposes; it does not enable replication of KMS-encrypted objects. D is wrong because it downgrades the required protection for new objects and does nothing for the existing SSE-KMS objects that must replicate. E is wrong because a bucket cannot be a principal in a policy, and same-account replication needs no destination bucket policy at all.

stem: A company runs an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster that a packaged third-party application connects to with a static database username and password; the vendor's software cannot use IAM authentication tokens. The application connects as the cluster's master user, whose credentials RDS manages in AWS Secrets Manager. A new security standard requires that the database password be rotated automatically every 30 days, that the password never appear in code or configuration files, and that the rotation proceed without an engineer writing or maintaining any rotation code. The application already retrieves its configuration values at startup through an AWS SDK, so it can read the credential from an AWS service at that point. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Store the password as a SecureString parameter in Systems Manager Parameter Store and build an EventBridge-scheduled Lambda function that rotates the value every 30 days.
Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager and author a custom Lambda rotation function that is based on the generic rotation function template, invoked on a 30-day schedule.
Enable IAM database authentication on the cluster and change the application to request a fresh authentication token before each connection instead of presenting a password.
Enable Secrets Manager managed rotation for the cluster's master user secret on a 30-day schedule, and have the application retrieve the secret at startup through the SDK.

explanation: D is correct. For the master user credentials of supported Amazon RDS and Aurora databases, Secrets Manager offers managed rotation in which the rotation logic is provided and operated by AWS on the configured schedule, so no rotation code is written or maintained, the password lives only in the secret, and the application keeps reading it at startup through the SDK it already uses. A is wrong because it requires building and maintaining exactly the custom rotation code the standard rules out, and Parameter Store has no rotation capability of its own. B is wrong because authoring a function from the generic template is still writing and maintaining rotation code when a no-code managed option exists for Aurora. C is wrong because the packaged application cannot use IAM authentication tokens, so this option violates the vendor constraint regardless of its security merits.

stem: A shared-services account, account A, stores a database credential in AWS Secrets Manager encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager. An application role in a separate workload account, account B, must retrieve the secret. An engineer attached a resource policy to the secret that allows the account B role to call secretsmanager:GetSecretValue, and attached an IAM policy in account B that grants the same action on the secret's ARN. Retrieval attempts still fail, and the AccessDenied error message references AWS KMS rather than Secrets Manager. The company allows changes in either account to fix the problem. Which set of changes will allow the role to retrieve the secret?

options.text: Re-encrypt the secret with a customer managed key in account A whose key policy allows the account B role to call kms:Decrypt, and add kms:Decrypt on that key to the role's IAM policy.

Update the key policy of the aws/secretsmanager managed key in account A so that it allows the account B role to call kms:Decrypt for requests that Secrets Manager makes when the role retrieves the secret.
Add both secretsmanager:GetSecretValue and kms:Decrypt for the managed key to the secret's resource policy so that the secret itself grants every permission the retrieval needs.
Create a replica of the secret in account B so that the application role reads a local copy that is encrypted with account B's own AWS managed key.

explanation: A is correct. Cross-account secret retrieval requires the caller to decrypt the secret with the encrypting KMS key, and the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager can never be used by principals from another account because its key policy cannot be modified. The fix is to re-encrypt the secret under a customer managed key whose key policy admits the account B role, with a matching kms:Decrypt allow in the role's IAM policy. B is wrong because the key policies of AWS managed keys are maintained by AWS and cannot be edited by customers. C is wrong because a Secrets Manager resource policy can grant only secretsmanager actions; kms:Decrypt must be authorized by the key's own policy, not by the secret. D is wrong because Secrets Manager replication copies secrets across Regions within the same account, not across accounts.

stem: A retail group with 40 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations must locate unprotected sensitive data stored in Amazon S3 across the entire organization. The security team needs ongoing, organization-wide visibility into buckets that contain payment card numbers and, in addition, the company's proprietary loyalty-card identifier, which follows a custom 13-character alphanumeric format that no built-in detector recognizes. All findings must flow into the existing central security-tooling account, and coverage must extend automatically to new accounts as the organization grows, without per-account setup work by the individual teams. Several of the group's accounts were created only weeks ago, and more acquisitions are planned for next year. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Run an AWS Glue crawler with a custom classifier for the loyalty-card format across every bucket in the organization and publish the resulting match metrics to CloudWatch dashboards in each member account.

Delegate Macie administration to the security-tooling account, auto-enable Macie with automated sensitive data discovery for all current and future accounts, and add a custom data identifier for the loyalty-card format.
Enable Amazon GuardDuty S3 Protection with the security-tooling account as the delegated administrator, and upload a threat list that describes the loyalty-card identifier format.
Enable Amazon Inspector across the organization from the security-tooling account and configure an assessment that scans the objects in every S3 bucket for the identifier.

explanation: B is correct. Macie is the sensitive-data discovery service for S3: a delegated administrator in the security-tooling account centralizes all findings, the auto-enable setting extends coverage to new accounts as they join the organization, automated sensitive data discovery provides the ongoing visibility, managed data identifiers detect payment card numbers, and a custom data identifier expresses the proprietary 13-character loyalty format. A is wrong because Glue crawlers catalog data structure for analytics; they do not generate security findings, centralize results, or auto-cover new accounts. C is wrong because GuardDuty S3 Protection analyzes access behavior in CloudTrail data events rather than object contents, and threat lists hold IP addresses, not data patterns. D is wrong because Amazon Inspector scans EC2 instances, container images, and Lambda functions for vulnerabilities; it does not inspect S3 object contents for sensitive data.

stem: A broker-dealer must retain trade-confirmation records in Amazon S3 for seven years in a write-once-read-many state to satisfy a financial regulator. The regulator's examiners specifically test whether any identity, including account administrators and the account's root user, can delete a record or shorten its retention before the period ends. The bucket will be created new for this workload, and the ingestion pipeline can set per-object settings at upload time. The compliance team also wants the protection evaluated object by object, so that each record's seven-year clock starts when that record is written. The pipeline writes each confirmation record exactly once, and records are never modified after ingestion. Which configuration meets the regulatory requirement?

options.text: Enable S3 Object Lock on the new bucket and apply a seven-year retention period in governance mode to each object at upload time.
Enable S3 Versioning with MFA delete on the bucket so that permanent deletions require the root user's hardware MFA device to authorize.
Enable S3 Object Lock on the new bucket and apply a seven-year retention period in compliance mode to each object at upload time.
Apply a legal hold to each object at upload time and remove the holds through a controlled change process once seven years have elapsed.

explanation: C is correct. Object Lock in compliance mode is the WORM control that no identity can override: until an object's retention date passes, its version cannot be deleted or overwritten and the retention period cannot be shortened, by anyone, including administrators and the root user, and per-object retention set at upload starts each record's clock at write time. A is wrong because governance mode is bypassable by any principal granted s3:BypassGovernanceRetention, which fails the examiners' specific test. B is wrong because MFA delete only gates deletion behind the root user's MFA device; the root user can still delete records, so the data is not immutable. D is wrong because a legal hold has no retention period and can be removed at any time by anyone with s3:PutObjectLegalHold, so it does not enforce a seven-year term.

stem: A healthcare application connects from Amazon EC2 application servers to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance. An internal standard derived from HIPAA requires that every database connection be encrypted in transit and that clients cryptographically verify they are connected to the genuine database server, rejecting the connection when the server certificate cannot be validated. During a review, engineers discovered that some legacy connection strings disable TLS entirely and still connect successfully. The database must keep accepting the application's existing username and password credentials, and the fix must not require changing the database engine or migrating any data. Which combination of actions enforces the standard for all connections? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable storage encryption for the DB instance by re-creating it from an encrypted snapshot so that its data is protected end to end.
Move the DB instance into a private subnet and restrict its security group to the application servers so that traffic cannot leave the VPC.
