Set the rds.force_ssl parameter to 1 in the instance's DB parameter group so that the server rejects any connection that does not use SSL/TLS.
Install the AWS-provided RDS certificate bundle on the application servers and set the client's SSL mode to verify-full so that the server certificate and host name are validated.
Enable IAM database authentication on the instance and migrate the application to short-lived authentication tokens instead of its stored password.

explanation: C and D are correct. Setting rds.force_ssl to 1 makes the PostgreSQL server itself reject every non-TLS connection, which closes the legacy plaintext paths regardless of client configuration, and installing the AWS certificate bundle with verify-full makes each client validate the server's certificate chain and host name, providing the required server-identity verification. A is wrong because storage encryption protects data at rest on the instance's volumes and has no effect on the network connection. B is wrong because network placement and security groups control who can reach the database, not whether the traffic is encrypted or the server is authenticated. E is wrong because the standard requires keeping the existing username and password, and IAM authentication changes the credential model without forcing TLS onto the remaining password-based connections.

stem: A logistics company enforces encryption in transit for an internal API that runs on Amazon ECS behind an internal Application Load Balancer. A new partner-integration requirement states that the load balancer itself must verify a client certificate on every TLS connection and reject clients whose certificates were not issued by the company's private certificate authority, before any request reaches the API containers. The platform team wants the verification performed natively by the load balancer, wants revoked partner certificates to be rejected, and does not want to run any additional proxy software in front of the load balancer or inside the ECS tasks. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy an AWS WAF web ACL on the load balancer with a rule that inspects the certificate fields of incoming requests and blocks clients whose issuer does not match the private CA.
Enable mutual TLS in passthrough mode on the ALB's HTTPS listener so that client certificates are forwarded in headers for the ECS containers to validate against the private CA.
Apply a strict TLS 1.3 security policy to the HTTPS listener, because negotiating the strictest protocol version requires clients to present certificates chained to a trusted authority.
Configure mutual TLS in verify mode on the ALB's HTTPS listener with a trust store that contains the private CA bundle, and attach the certificate revocation list to the trust store.

explanation: D is correct. ALB mutual TLS in verify mode performs the client-certificate validation natively at the listener: the trust store holds the private CA bundle that issued the partner certificates, connections from clients whose certificates fail chain validation are rejected before any request reaches the targets, and attaching a certificate revocation list makes the ALB reject revoked certificates as well. A is wrong because AWS WAF inspects HTTP request content after TLS termination and has no visibility into the certificate exchange of the TLS handshake. B is wrong because passthrough mode does not validate anything at the load balancer; it forwards the certificate in headers and pushes verification into the ECS tasks, which the requirement forbids. C is wrong because a TLS security policy governs protocol versions and cipher suites for the server side of the handshake; it never requests or verifies client certificates.

stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with the default FullAWSAccess SCP attached to all organizational units. The security team must restrict AWS usage for all existing and future accounts in a specific OU so that resources can be created only in the eu-west-1 Region. A defined set of global services, including IAM, Amazon CloudFront, Amazon Route 53, and AWS Support, must continue to work from their default endpoints. A security engineer will attach a new SCP to the OU. Which SCP meets these requirements?

options.text: A statement with Effect: Allow and Action: "*" that includes a condition of StringEquals aws:RequestedRegion: eu-west-1.
A statement with Effect: Deny and Action: "*" that includes a condition of StringEquals aws:RequestedRegion: eu-west-1.
A statement with Effect: Deny and Action: "*" that includes a condition of StringNotEquals aws:RequestedRegion: eu-west-1.
A statement with Effect: Deny and NotAction set to the global service actions (iam:*, cloudfront:*, route53:*, support:*) that includes a condition of StringNotEquals aws:RequestedRegion: eu-west-1.

explanation: D is correct. The Deny applies to every action except the exempted global service actions, and the StringNotEquals condition makes the Deny fire only for requests outside eu-west-1, so regional usage is confined to eu-west-1 while the named global services keep working; because SCPs attached to an OU apply to every current and future account in that OU, no per-account work is needed. A is wrong because SCPs do not grant permissions, and with FullAWSAccess still attached an additional Allow statement imposes no restriction at all. B is wrong because its logic is inverted: it denies requests that are in eu-west-1, the one Region that should remain usable. C is wrong because it denies all non-eu-west-1 requests with no exemption, which breaks the required global services since their control planes resolve to Regions such as us-east-1.

stem: A company manages 60 AWS accounts with AWS Organizations. Amazon GuardDuty and AWS Security Hub were originally enabled with the management account acting as the administrator account for both services, and security analysts sign in to the management account daily to triage findings. An internal audit cites this as a violation of the company's policy that the management account must be used only for tasks that require it. The security team owns a dedicated security-tooling account that is a member of the organization. The team must move day-to-day administration of GuardDuty and Security Hub out of the management account while retaining organization-wide coverage of all existing and future accounts. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: From the management account, register the security-tooling account as the delegated administrator for GuardDuty and Security Hub, and manage member accounts and findings from the security-tooling account.
Create an IAM role in the management account that the security analysts assume from the security-tooling account, and continue to administer GuardDuty and Security Hub through that assumed role.
Enable GuardDuty and Security Hub independently in every member account, and configure EventBridge rules in each account to forward findings to an event bus in the security-tooling account.
Disable both services in the management account, and use AWS Config aggregators in the security-tooling account to collect security findings from all of the member accounts.

explanation: A is correct. GuardDuty and Security Hub support delegated administration: the management account registers a member account as the delegated administrator, after which that account manages the organization configuration, auto-enables coverage for existing and future accounts, and triages findings, so analysts no longer need to sign in to the management account. B is wrong because the analysts would still perform daily administration inside the management account through the assumed role, which is exactly what the audit flagged. C is wrong because per-account enablement plus per-account EventBridge forwarding must be repeated for every new account and provides aggregation only, not central administration. D is wrong because AWS Config aggregators collect resource configuration and Config rule compliance, not GuardDuty or Security Hub findings, and disabling the services removes the organization-wide coverage the team must retain.

stem: A security engineer attaches a service control policy to the root of an AWS organization. The SCP contains a single statement that denies ec2:CreateInternetGateway and ec2:AttachInternetGateway for all principals so that workload VPCs cannot gain direct internet paths. One week later, a routine review finds a new internet gateway attached to a VPC in the management account. CloudTrail shows that the gateway was created by an IAM role in the management account after the SCP was attached, and the SCP is still attached to the root and enabled. All features are enabled for the organization. What is the reason the SCP did not block this action?

options.text: The SCP must also be attached directly to the management account because policies that are attached to the organization root are not inherited by the management account and must be attached explicitly.
SCPs do not affect principals in the management account; the deny applies only to member accounts, so workloads that must be governed by SCPs should not run in the management account.
The FullAWSAccess policy that remains attached to the root contains an Allow for all actions, and an Allow statement in any attached SCP overrides a Deny statement.
The IAM role's identity-based policy grants administrator access, and identity-based Allow permissions are evaluated after SCPs and therefore take precedence over an SCP Deny.

explanation: B is correct. Service control policies never apply to the management account, regardless of where they are attached in the organization, so the deny cannot block principals operating there; the standard mitigation is to keep workloads out of the management account. A is wrong because attachment is not the issue: the root-level SCP already governs every member account, and no attachment point makes an SCP apply to the management account. C is wrong because an explicit Deny in any applicable SCP always overrides an Allow; FullAWSAccess merely grants the baseline that other statements subtract from. D is wrong because SCPs are evaluated as a guardrail outside the identity policy: an action denied by an applicable SCP is blocked even for principals whose IAM policies allow it.

stem: A financial services company must ensure that accounts in its Workloads OU can use only an approved list of services: Amazon EC2, Amazon S3, Amazon RDS, and Amazon CloudWatch. Today every OU has the default FullAWSAccess SCP attached, and the security team has been maintaining a Deny SCP that lists prohibited services, but auditors found engineers using newly launched AWS services that the deny list had not yet been updated to cover. The team wants any service that is not explicitly approved to be unusable in the Workloads OU by default, including services that AWS releases in the future, without affecting the other OUs. Which change meets these requirements?

options.text: Keep FullAWSAccess attached to the Workloads OU and add a new SCP to the OU that contains Allow statements for only the four approved services.

Expand the existing Deny SCP with an additional statement that denies all actions for any service that AWS adds after the policy's creation date by using a policy condition on the service launch date.
Detach FullAWSAccess from the Workloads OU and attach an SCP that allows only the actions of the four approved services, leaving FullAWSAccess in place at the organization root.
Detach FullAWSAccess from the organization root and attach the allow-list SCP to the root so that every account inherits the approved-services restriction.

explanation: C is correct. An action is permitted only if it is allowed at every level from the root down to the account, so replacing FullAWSAccess on the Workloads OU with an allow-list SCP limits those accounts to the intersection: only the four approved services. Anything not listed, including future services, is implicitly denied at the OU level, while FullAWSAccess at the root keeps other OUs unaffected. A is wrong because multiple SCPs at the same level are evaluated so that an action allowed by any of them is allowed at that level; FullAWSAccess would still permit every service. B is wrong because SCPs have no condition that matches services by release date, which is why deny lists require constant maintenance. D is wrong because a root-level allow list restricts every OU in the organization, and the requirement is to constrain only the Workloads OU.

stem: A company's security team must guarantee that Amazon S3 buckets in all 200 member accounts can be accessed only by principals that belong to the company's AWS organization. Developers manage their own bucket policies, and the team has twice discovered bucket policies that granted read access to an external vendor account. The control must override anything a developer writes in a bucket policy, must apply automatically to buckets in accounts that are added to the organization later, and must not require the team to modify individual buckets. Legitimate access by AWS service principals, such as log delivery, must continue to work. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies all S3 actions when the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key does not match the organization ID.

Deploy an AWS Config organization rule that detects bucket policies granting access outside the organization and triggers an automatic remediation Lambda function that rewrites each noncompliant bucket policy immediately.
Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level in every member account by using a CloudFormation stack set with automatic deployment to new accounts.
Attach a resource control policy to the organization root that denies S3 actions unless aws:PrincipalOrgID matches the organization ID or the caller is an AWS service principal.

explanation: D is correct. Resource control policies are organization-managed guardrails on resources: an RCP at the root caps the access that any bucket in any current or future member account can grant, and it overrides broader grants in developer-managed bucket policies. An exception using aws:PrincipalIsAWSService preserves service-principal access such as log delivery. A is wrong because SCPs restrict what principals inside the organization can do; they place no limit on an external vendor principal that a bucket policy invites in. B is wrong because it is detective: the vendor has access during the window between the policy change and the remediation, and the requirement is a control that cannot be overridden. C is wrong because Block Public Access blocks anonymous and public grants, not authenticated access granted to a specific external account.

stem: During a security review, a company determines that an employee could copy sensitive data from an internal Amazon S3 bucket to an S3 bucket in a personal AWS account by using company credentials, because nothing prevents the company's IAM roles from calling S3 against buckets that other accounts own. The security team must block every principal in the organization from reading or writing S3 buckets that do not belong to the organization. The control must cover access from the console, the CLI, and SDKs on any network, and it must apply to all current and future accounts with a single centrally managed policy. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies S3 actions when the aws:ResourceOrgID condition key does not match the company's organization ID.
Attach a resource control policy to the organization root that denies S3 actions when the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key does not match the company's organization ID.
Add a policy to every VPC gateway endpoint for S3 that denies requests when the aws:ResourceOrgID condition key does not match the organization ID.
Configure the company's S3 bucket policies to deny requests when the aws:SourceOrgID condition key does not match the organization ID.

explanation: A is correct. aws:ResourceOrgID compares the organization of the resource being accessed with the stated value, and an SCP applies to every principal in every member account, so a root-level deny blocks organization identities from touching S3 buckets outside the organization on any access path, including the console and any network. B is wrong because RCPs attach to the organization's own resources; a bucket in an employee's personal account is outside the organization, so no company RCP governs requests to it. C is wrong because a VPC endpoint policy constrains only requests that traverse that endpoint; console sessions and traffic from other networks never pass through it. D is wrong because aws:SourceOrgID is populated for requests made by AWS service principals on a customer's behalf, and policies on company-owned buckets cannot restrict uploads to buckets the company does not own.

stem: A company aggregates AWS service logs from all organization accounts into a central Amazon S3 bucket in a log archive account. The bucket policy grants s3:PutObject to service principals such as cloudtrail.amazonaws.com and delivery.logs.amazonaws.com. A penetration test demonstrates that an attacker who knows the bucket name can configure CloudTrail in the attacker's own AWS account to deliver logs into the company's bucket, because the service principal grant does not distinguish which customer initiated the delivery. The company must restrict delivery so that only resources in its own organization can trigger writes, and new member accounts must be covered without any future policy updates. Which change to the bucket policy meets these requirements?

options.text: Add a condition to the service principal statements that requires aws:PrincipalOrgID to match the company's organization ID.
Add a condition to the service principal statements that requires aws:SourceOrgID to match the company's organization ID.
Add a condition to the service principal statements that requires aws:SourceAccount to match a list of the organization's current account IDs.
Add a condition to the service principal statements that requires aws:SourceIp to match the published IP address ranges for the AWS services.

explanation: B is correct. aws:SourceOrgID is populated when an AWS service makes a request on behalf of a customer resource, and it contains the organization ID of the account that owns that resource, so requiring it to match the company's organization blocks deliveries initiated from any outside account, including the attacker's, while automatically covering accounts that join the organization later. A is wrong because when the principal is a service principal such as cloudtrail.amazonaws.com, aws:PrincipalOrgID is not present in the request context, so the condition would fail for legitimate deliveries. C is wrong because a static list of account IDs satisfies the security goal but must be edited every time an account is created, violating the no-policy-updates requirement. D is wrong because service-to-service deliveries originate from AWS-owned infrastructure that is shared by all customers, so IP restrictions cannot distinguish the attacker's deliveries from the company's.

stem: A rapidly growing company creates several AWS accounts each month for new product teams. Today a cloud engineer creates each account manually with the Organizations console and then spends about a day configuring IAM Identity Center access, a baseline CloudTrail configuration, VPC settings, and mandatory guardrails, and audits have found accounts where steps were missed. The company already runs AWS Control Tower with a landing zone and an OU structure that has preventive and detective controls. The platform team wants product teams to obtain new accounts through a standardized, repeatable process that applies the security baseline and OU controls automatically at creation. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Continue creating accounts with the Organizations API and run a custom Step Functions workflow that applies the baseline configuration and moves each account into the correct OU.
Create a golden AWS account, export its configuration with AWS Config, and use CloudFormation to replicate the captured configuration into each newly created account.
Provision new accounts through AWS Control Tower Account Factory so that each account is enrolled in the landing zone, placed in its target OU, and baselined automatically.
Create new accounts by invitation from the management account and rely on the OU's controls to configure the required baseline inside each invited account.

explanation: C is correct. Account Factory is Control Tower's provisioning capability: each account it creates is enrolled in the landing zone, receives the baseline (including centralized logging and IAM Identity Center access), and lands in the chosen OU where preventive and detective controls apply immediately, eliminating the manual checklist. A is wrong because a custom workflow re-implements what Account Factory already provides and must be maintained, tested, and kept aligned with the landing zone. B is wrong because AWS Config records configuration state for compliance evaluation; it is not a mechanism for cloning an account's setup into new accounts. D is wrong because invited accounts are not automatically enrolled or baselined by Control Tower, and controls attached to an OU constrain and evaluate accounts but do not perform initial configuration such as identity and logging setup.

stem: A company deploys all infrastructure through AWS CloudFormation pipelines in accounts governed by AWS Control Tower. The security team is remediating a recurring problem: application teams occasionally deploy Amazon S3 buckets whose configurations violate policy, such as buckets without server access logging. Detective controls flag the buckets as noncompliant a few minutes after creation, but the company's compliance officer requires that noncompliant buckets never be created at all: the violation must be caught before the resource is provisioned, and the deployment must fail with a clear error that the application team can act on. The team wants to use capabilities that are native to Control Tower. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable additional detective controls on the OU and configure the controls to run continuously rather than on a daily schedule.
Enable preventive controls on the OU, which use service control policies to inspect the configuration properties of the resources that CloudFormation templates declare before deployment.
Deploy an AWS Config custom rule with an automatic remediation action that deletes any bucket that is created without server access logging.
Enable the relevant proactive controls on the OU, which use AWS CloudFormation hooks to evaluate resources and block the deployment before provisioning begins.

explanation: D is correct. Proactive controls are implemented as CloudFormation hooks: when a stack operation declares a resource that would violate the control, the evaluation runs before provisioning, the operation fails with an explanatory message, and the noncompliant bucket is never created, which is exactly the compliance officer's requirement. A is wrong because detective controls evaluate resources that already exist; however frequently they run, the bucket is created first. B is wrong because preventive controls use SCPs, which allow or deny API actions based on the request context; they cannot inspect the configuration properties that a CloudFormation template declares for a resource. C is wrong because deleting the bucket after creation is remediation, not prevention, and the resource still existed in a noncompliant state for a period of time.

stem: A company with 150 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations must roll out a standardized set of roughly 40 AWS Config rules with associated remediation documents to every account. Compliance reporting must treat the rule set as a single unit so that auditors can see at a glance whether each account is compliant with the full package, member account administrators must not be able to delete the rules, accounts that join the organization later must receive the rule set automatically, and the security team must operate everything from its security-tooling account rather than the management account. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Register the security-tooling account as a delegated administrator for AWS Config and deploy an organization conformance pack that contains the rules and remediation documents.
Use CloudFormation StackSets with automatic deployment from the security-tooling account to create the individual Config rules and remediation documents in every account.
Enable a Security Hub standard that contains equivalent controls and use central configuration from the security-tooling account to apply the standard to all accounts.
Publish the rules as a private conformance pack template in an S3 bucket and instruct each account team to deploy the pack in its own account.

explanation: A is correct. An organization conformance pack deploys the rules and remediation documents to every existing and future member account, is reported on as a single compliance unit per account, cannot be deleted by member account administrators because it is managed at the organization level, and delegated administration lets the security-tooling account own the deployment instead of the management account. B is wrong because StackSets creates the rules as individual account-level resources, so there is no packaged compliance view, and drift from local changes must be detected and repaired. C is wrong because Security Hub standards are predefined control sets; they cannot package the company's own 40 Config rules with custom remediation documents. D is wrong because per-account self-service deployment leaves the packs deletable locally, misses new accounts, and depends on every team acting.

stem: A security team must capture management events from every account in an AWS organization for a period of seven years. The requirements state that logging must start automatically for accounts that join the organization, that administrators in member accounts must not be able to stop or reconfigure the logging in their own accounts, and that all log files must be delivered to a single Amazon S3 bucket in a dedicated log archive account. The organization has all features enabled, and the log archive account is an existing member account. The team wants to satisfy these requirements with configuration in as few places as possible. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use CloudFormation StackSets with automatic deployment enabled to create an identical CloudTrail trail in every member account that delivers its log files to the central bucket in the log archive account.
Create an organization trail that delivers to the central bucket in the log archive account, so every existing and future member account logs through a trail it cannot modify.
Enable CloudTrail Lake event data stores in each member account and configure the stores to replicate their events to the log archive account.
Create a trail in the log archive account only and grant it cross-account permission to read management events from the other accounts' event history.

explanation: B is correct. An organization trail is configured once, automatically applies to every current and future member account, delivers all log files to the designated bucket, and appears in member accounts as a trail that member administrators cannot stop, delete, or modify, which covers every stated requirement from a single configuration point. A is wrong because StackSets-created trails are ordinary account-owned trails: a member administrator with CloudTrail permissions can stop logging in that account, and drift must be detected and repaired. C is wrong because CloudTrail Lake stores are per-account analytic stores; they do not deliver log files to S3, and per-account configuration contradicts the single-point requirement. D is wrong because a trail records events only for the accounts it is created for; there is no mechanism for one account's trail to read other accounts' event history.

stem: A company configures its organization trail to deliver logs to an Amazon S3 bucket in the log archive account and must encrypt the log files with AWS KMS. A junior engineer first selected the AWS managed key aws/s3 and found that the trail could not be configured to use it. Security requirements state that the key must be controllable by the security team, that CloudTrail must be able to encrypt new log files, that only one designated analyst role from the audit account may decrypt the logs, and that the trail's delivery must not depend on key permissions granted through IAM identity policies in the log archive account. Which KMS configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Use the AWS managed key aws/s3 in the log archive account and grant the analyst role decrypt permissions in that key's key policy.
Create a customer managed key in each member account and configure the organization trail to encrypt each account's log files with that account's key.

Create a customer managed key in the log archive account whose key policy allows cloudtrail.amazonaws.com to generate data keys for the trail and grants decrypt only to the audit account analyst role.
Create a customer managed key in the log archive account, keep the default key policy, and attach an IAM identity policy to the analyst role in the audit account that grants kms:Decrypt on the key.

explanation: C is correct. A customer managed key gives the security team full control of the key policy; a statement allowing cloudtrail.amazonaws.com to call GenerateDataKey, conditioned on the trail's ARN, lets the trail encrypt new log files, and a statement granting kms:Decrypt to the audit account analyst role authorizes cross-account decryption directly in the key policy, with no reliance on identity policies in the log archive account. A is wrong because the policy of an AWS managed key cannot be edited, so neither the CloudTrail grant nor the analyst grant can be expressed, and CloudTrail SSE-KMS requires a customer managed key. B is wrong because an organization trail encrypts its log files with a single KMS key; per-account keys are not how delivery works and would multiply management effort. D is wrong because the default key policy does not authorize CloudTrail to use the key, and a cross-account principal cannot gain access through an identity policy alone; the key policy must also allow it.

stem: A company must undergo an annual PCI DSS assessment covering workloads spread across 40 AWS accounts. Today, engineers spend roughly six weeks each year taking console screenshots and exporting configuration files, which the compliance team manually maps to individual PCI DSS requirements before handing a package to the external assessor. The compliance team wants continuous, automated collection of evidence from all in-scope accounts, organized by PCI DSS control, with assessment reports that it can generate on demand for the assessor. The solution must also record who reviewed each item of evidence, and the evidence must remain available for review by internal stakeholders throughout the year. Which AWS service meets these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Artifact to download the PCI DSS attestation of compliance and the responsibility summary documents and provide those AWS documents to the external assessor.
Enable the PCI DSS standard in Security Hub across all accounts and export the aggregated findings to provide to the assessor.
Create an AWS Config aggregator covering the in-scope accounts and give the assessor read access to the aggregated resource configuration data.
Create an AWS Audit Manager assessment scoped to the in-scope accounts by using the PCI DSS framework, and generate assessment reports from the collected evidence.

explanation: D is correct. Audit Manager continuously and automatically collects evidence, such as configuration snapshots, compliance check results, and CloudTrail activity, across the in-scope accounts, organizes it under the controls of the chosen PCI DSS framework, tracks review status and delegations for each item, and produces assessor-ready assessment reports on demand. A is wrong because AWS Artifact provides AWS's own audit reports about the AWS side of the shared responsibility model; it contains no evidence about the company's workloads. B is wrong because Security Hub reports pass or fail findings against its PCI checks; it does not assemble evidence by framework control, track evidence review, or generate assessment reports. C is wrong because an aggregator exposes raw resource configuration data, leaving the team to map, package, and track evidence manually, which is the burden being eliminated.

stem: An external auditor performing a SOC 2 examination of a SaaS company asks for documentation proving that the underlying cloud provider's own controls have been independently assessed. Specifically, the auditor wants AWS's most recent SOC 2 Type II report and ISO 27001 certificate to evaluate the provider portion of the shared responsibility model. The company's compliance manager needs to retrieve these documents this week, must keep track of the associated nondisclosure terms, and must be able to pull refreshed versions when AWS publishes reports for new periods. The manager has an IAM role in the organization's management account with the necessary permissions. Where should the compliance manager obtain these documents?

options.text: Download the reports from AWS Artifact after accepting the associated terms, and return to Artifact for updated versions when new reporting periods are published.
Open a case with AWS Support to request the SOC 2 Type II report and the ISO 27001 certificate and ask AWS to set up a recurring delivery subscription.
Create an AWS Audit Manager assessment with the SOC 2 framework and generate an assessment report to give to the auditor.
Export the compliance summary from AWS Security Hub showing the company's passing checks for the relevant standards and share it with the auditor.

explanation: A is correct. AWS Artifact is the self-service portal for AWS's own third-party audit artifacts: it serves the current SOC reports and ISO certificates on demand, gates each download behind the applicable confidentiality terms, and always offers the latest published reporting period, which covers every part of the request. B is wrong because AWS does not distribute these audit reports through support cases; they are delivered through Artifact, and no recurring delivery subscription exists. C is wrong because an Audit Manager assessment evaluates the company's own environment; it cannot produce AWS's independent auditor reports about AWS's controls. D is wrong because Security Hub findings describe the company's resource compliance, which is the customer portion of the shared responsibility model, not evidence about the provider's controls.

stem: A security team inherits an AWS organization of 300 member accounts that were created over eight years. Many member accounts still have root user passwords set, and a credential report review shows that several root users have active access keys. The team must eliminate long-term root credentials across all member accounts, prevent the credentials from being recreated locally, and still be able to perform the rare tasks that require root, such as deleting a misconfigured S3 bucket policy that locks out all principals. The team wants to accomplish this centrally, without signing in to each account's root user. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use the password recovery process to obtain each member account's root password, sign in, delete the access keys, enable multi-factor authentication, and store the new credentials in a break-glass vault.

Enable centralized root access management in IAM from the management account, remove root credentials from member accounts, and use short-lived privileged root sessions for the tasks that require root.
Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies all actions when the aws:PrincipalArn condition key matches a root user ARN.
Deploy an AWS Config organization rule that detects root access keys and invokes a remediation Lambda function that deletes the keys in each account.

explanation: B is correct. Centralized root access management lets the management account or a delegated administrator remove root user credentials from member accounts at scale, blocks password recovery so the credentials cannot be recreated locally, and provides short-lived privileged root sessions for the few operations that still require root, such as repairing a lockout bucket policy, all without signing in as each root user. A is wrong because it requires an interactive recovery-and-sign-in cycle for 300 accounts and deliberately keeps long-term credentials in existence, which the requirements exclude. C is wrong because an SCP can block a member root user's actions but does not remove the password or access keys, does not stop password recovery, and provides no mechanism for the rare permitted root tasks. D is wrong because it addresses only access keys, is detective rather than preventive, and cannot remove root passwords or prevent their recreation.

stem: A company requires that every new Amazon EC2 instance and Amazon EBS volume carry a CostCenter tag at the moment of creation. The governance team created a tag policy in AWS Organizations that defines the CostCenter tag key and its permitted values and attached the policy to all OUs, but a review one month later still finds newly created instances with no CostCenter tag at all. Tagged resources, however, now consistently use the correct capitalization and values. The team must ensure that instance launches and volume creations without the tag are rejected across all member accounts. The solution must not depend on application teams changing their own deployment tooling. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Update the tag policy to enable enforcement for the relevant EC2 resource types so that the tag policy blocks the creation of any resources that are missing the CostCenter tag.
Deploy the required-tags AWS Config managed rule in every account with an automatic remediation action that stops instances that are missing the CostCenter tag.
Attach an SCP that denies ec2:RunInstances and ec2:CreateVolume when the request does not include a CostCenter tag, by using the aws:RequestTag condition key with a Null test.
Attach a resource control policy that denies the creation of EC2 and EBS resources when the CostCenter tag is absent from the request.

explanation: C is correct. An SCP can evaluate tag-on-create requests: a Deny on ec2:RunInstances and ec2:CreateVolume with a Null condition on aws:RequestTag/CostCenter fires whenever the tag is absent from the request, so noncompliant launches are rejected in every member account at creation time. A is wrong because tag policy enforcement prevents noncompliant tagging operations, such as wrong capitalization or disallowed values, but a tag policy never blocks creating a resource that simply has no tag, which is exactly the observed gap. B is wrong because a Config rule evaluates resources after they exist; stopping an instance later is remediation, not the required rejection at creation, and it does not address volumes. D is wrong because RCPs restrict access to resources for supported resource-hosting services; they are not an enforcement mechanism for tag-on-create conditions on EC2 launches.

stem: A company is building a multi-account environment aligned with the AWS Security Reference Architecture. The design must include a home for the delegated administrator of GuardDuty, Security Hub, and Amazon Detective, where security analysts work interactively every day, and a home for the organization's centralized CloudTrail and VPC flow log archive, where data must be immutable and interactive human access is limited to break-glass scenarios. The architects are deciding how to distribute these responsibilities between a security tooling account and a log archive account, both members of the security OU. Both candidate accounts already exist and have no workloads deployed in them. Which distribution of responsibilities follows the AWS Security Reference Architecture?

options.text: Place the delegated administrator duties and the log archive in the same dedicated account so that security analysts can correlate findings with the raw logs without configuring any cross-account access.
Place the delegated administrator duties in the management account and use the log archive account only for storage, keeping analysts out of the member accounts.
Place the log archive in the security tooling account and make the log archive account the delegated administrator for the security services.
Make the security tooling account the delegated administrator that hosts the analysts' daily work, and restrict the log archive account to immutable log storage with break-glass access.

explanation: D is correct. The SRA assigns interactive security operations, including delegated administration of GuardDuty, Security Hub, and Detective and day-to-day analyst work, to the security tooling account, while the log archive account exists solely to hold immutable, centrally collected logs with tightly restricted access, so routine human activity never occurs where the evidence is stored. A is wrong because combining daily interactive analyst access with the immutable archive violates the separation that keeps log integrity defensible; analysts can query logs cross-account instead. B is wrong because the SRA minimizes use of the management account, which should not host security service administration that a member account can perform through delegated administration. C is wrong because it inverts the two accounts' purposes, placing interactive tooling where immutability is required and archival storage where analysts work daily.

stem: A company with AWS Enterprise Support on all 80 of its organization accounts wants a consolidated view of AWS Trusted Advisor security checks, including exposed access keys, security groups that allow unrestricted access to high-risk ports, and public S3 bucket permissions, across the entire organization. The security team wants a single consolidated report of check results for every account, produced without deploying any per-account tooling, and accounts that join the organization later must be included without extra setup. The team has access to the organization's management account for setup and reporting tasks. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Enable trusted access for Trusted Advisor in AWS Organizations from the management account, and use the organizational view feature to create consolidated reports of check results across all accounts.

Register a member operations account as a delegated administrator for Trusted Advisor and generate the organizational view reports from that delegated administrator account instead of the management account.
Create an IAM role in every account that permits describing Trusted Advisor checks, and run a scheduled script in the management account that assumes each role and merges the results.
Enable AWS Security Hub with central configuration across the organization and use its consolidated findings as the organization-wide report of the Trusted Advisor security checks.

explanation: A is correct. Organizational view is enabled by the management account through trusted access for Trusted Advisor, and the management account can then create consolidated reports that aggregate check results, including the security checks, for every current and future account in the organization with no per-account deployment. B is wrong because delegated administrators for Trusted Advisor apply to Trusted Advisor Priority, the Enterprise Support engagement feature; organizational view reports can be created and viewed only from the management account. C is wrong because a fleet of assumable roles plus a merging script is custom infrastructure that must be deployed to each new account and maintained, which organizational view makes unnecessary. D is wrong because Security Hub aggregates its own and integrated findings; it does not ingest the Trusted Advisor check catalog, so checks such as exposed access keys would be missing from the report.

stem: A company established its AWS organization five years ago and recently deployed an AWS Control Tower landing zone into it. The landing zone governs two new OUs, but 40 legacy accounts remain in an existing OU named Legacy that was created long before Control Tower was set up. Each legacy account has an AWS Config configuration recorder and delivery channel that account teams configured manually years ago. Auditors report that the legacy accounts are not enrolled in Control Tower, so the landing zone's controls and baselines do not apply to them. The platform team must bring all 40 legacy accounts under Control Tower governance in place, without recreating the accounts or migrating any workloads, and future accounts placed in the Legacy OU must be governed as well. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Delete the pre-existing AWS Config configuration recorder and delivery channel in each legacy account before registration so that Control Tower can deploy its own AWS Config baseline.

Provision 40 replacement accounts through AWS Control Tower Account Factory, migrate all of the workloads from the legacy accounts into the replacement accounts, and then close the original legacy accounts.
Send organization invitations to the 40 legacy accounts from the management account so that they are joined to the organization that Control Tower governs.
Copy the SCPs that Control Tower manages from a governed OU and attach the copies to the Legacy OU by using the Organizations console.
Register the Legacy OU with AWS Control Tower so that its member accounts are enrolled, and enable automatic enrollment so that accounts placed in the OU later are governed as well.

explanation: A and E are correct. Registering the Legacy OU extends governance to it: Control Tower enrolls the member accounts and applies the landing zone baselines and the OU's controls, and the automatic enrollment feature governs accounts that are placed in the OU later; the AWSControlTowerExecution role does not need to be pre-created, because the Register OU process provisions it in each account automatically. However, enrollment fails while an account still has its own AWS Config configuration recorder or delivery channel, because Control Tower must create and manage those resources itself, so the manually configured recorders and delivery channels must be deleted first. B is wrong because recreating accounts and migrating workloads is exactly what the requirements exclude; enrollment governs accounts in place. C is wrong because the legacy accounts are already members of the organization; invitations apply to accounts outside it. D is wrong because Control Tower manages its own SCPs, manually copied policies are unmanaged drift, and attaching SCPs performs no enrollment and deploys no baselines.

stem: A company stores its organization trail's log files in an Amazon S3 bucket in a dedicated log archive account. External auditors have issued two findings: the company cannot cryptographically demonstrate that individual log files have not been modified or deleted since CloudTrail delivered them, and administrators in the log archive account technically retain the ability to delete log objects. The security team must be able to prove log file integrity to the auditors and must make delivered log files undeletable by any principal, including log archive account administrators, for the seven-year retention period. The bucket already has versioning enabled. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Configure the trail to encrypt log files with a customer managed KMS key whose policy denies kms:Decrypt to the log archive account administrators.
Enable MFA delete on the bucket so that object versions can be deleted only with the bucket owner's hardware MFA device.
Enable CloudTrail log file validation on the organization trail and periodically verify the delivered digest files against the log files.
Enable cross-Region replication of the bucket to a second bucket in another account so that a copy of each log file survives any deletion.
Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on the log bucket with a seven-year retention period applied to delivered log objects.

explanation: C and E are correct. Log file validation makes CloudTrail deliver signed digest files that reference every log file's hash, so the team can cryptographically prove to auditors that files are unmodified and detect deletions. Object Lock in compliance mode makes each object undeletable and unmodifiable until its retention date by every principal, including the log archive account's administrators and root user, covering the seven-year mandate. A is wrong because encryption controls who can read the logs; it neither proves integrity nor prevents an administrator from deleting the encrypted objects. B is wrong because MFA delete only raises the bar to the root user holding the MFA device, so deletion remains possible and no integrity proof is produced. D is wrong because replication preserves a copy but does not make the source undeletable or provide cryptographic evidence, and a surviving replica does not satisfy auditors that the originals are intact.

stem: Security analysts use an IAM role in a company's audit account and must run Amazon Athena queries against the organization's CloudTrail logs. The logs reside in an Amazon S3 bucket in the log archive account and are encrypted with SSE-KMS by using a customer managed key that also resides in the log archive account. The analyst role already has identity-based permissions for Athena, for s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on the log bucket, and for kms:Decrypt on the key. Test queries from the audit account fail with access denied errors on the S3 objects. Which combination of changes will allow the queries to succeed? (Choose two.)

options.text: Attach an additional identity policy in the audit account that grants the analyst role permission to call athena:StartQueryExecution on the log archive account's resources.
Add a statement to the log bucket's policy that grants s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on the bucket and its objects to the analyst role.
Enable object ACLs on the bucket and grant read access to the audit account's canonical user ID for newly delivered log objects.
Create a VPC peering connection between the audit account's VPC and the log archive account's VPC so that Athena can reach the bucket.
Add a statement to the KMS key's policy that grants kms:Decrypt on the key to the analyst role.

explanation: B and E are correct. Cross-account access requires authorization on both sides: the analyst role's identity policies already allow the calls, but the bucket policy in the log archive account must also grant the role s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket, and the key policy must also grant kms:Decrypt, because a KMS key never honors a cross-account identity policy unless the key policy itself allows that principal. A is wrong because the role already has Athena permissions, and Athena queries run in the analyst's own account; the failure is S3 and KMS authorization, not Athena. C is wrong because ACLs are the legacy mechanism, are disabled on buckets with bucket-owner-enforced object ownership, and would require per-object grants that the bucket policy handles cleanly. D is wrong because S3 and KMS are accessed through their APIs; no VPC connectivity between the two accounts is involved in the authorization failure.

stem: A company's security policy for its AWS organization states two requirements for member account root users: root users must be technically prevented from performing any actions in member accounts, and the security team must receive an alert within minutes whenever anyone signs in to a member account as root. The organization has all features enabled, an organization trail is already delivering logs, and the team operates from a delegated administrator account. The company has not yet adopted centralized root access management, and the solution must work with the root credentials that currently exist. Member account teams must not be able to weaken either control from inside their own accounts. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Attach an identity-based policy that denies all actions to the root user in each member account by using an automation script.
Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies all actions when the aws:PrincipalArn condition key matches the root user ARN pattern for any account.
Require hardware multi-factor authentication for every member account root user so that the root users cannot perform any actions without approval from the security team.
Send the organization trail to CloudWatch Logs and create a metric filter and alarm that matches root user ConsoleLogin events and notifies the security team through SNS.
Enable GuardDuty organization-wide so that its finding for root credential usage blocks the sign-in and notifies the security team automatically.

explanation: B and D are correct. SCPs apply to the root user of member accounts, so a root-level Deny on all actions conditioned on aws:PrincipalArn matching arn:aws:iam::*:root technically prevents root activity across every member account, and member teams cannot detach an SCP from inside their accounts. Sending the organization trail to CloudWatch Logs and alarming on a metric filter for root ConsoleLogin events produces the required near-real-time alert from a single central configuration. A is wrong because IAM identity-based policies cannot be attached to the root user; root's permissions cannot be limited that way. C is wrong because MFA strengthens authentication of the same root user; it neither prevents a signed-in root user from acting nor generates an alert, and it is not an approval workflow. E is wrong because GuardDuty is detective: its root credential usage finding can feed a notification, but nothing in GuardDuty blocks a sign-in, so the prevention requirement is unmet.
